Literal: imam — the Chinese Muslim term for mosque leader and scholar
Figurative: From Persian ākhund (scholar, teacher). 阿訇 āhōng is the standard Chinese Muslim term for the mosque's imam and religious authority, combining the functions of prayer leader, teacher, legal counselor, and community elder.

Literal: love it so much you cannot put it down
Figurative: Lit: love-not-release-hand. The standard phrase for something you cannot stop using, reading, or holding: so beloved that your hand refuses to let go. Used for books, gadgets, food, art. 这本小说写得太好了，让人爱不释手 "This novel is so well-written; you can't put it down."

Pinyin: ài měi zhī xīn, rén jiē yǒu zhī
Literal: the love of beauty is universal — everyone has a heart for beauty
Figurative: Classical proverb affirming the universality of aesthetic appreciation. Often used to gently excuse vanity or the appreciation of beautiful people and things.

Literal: willing but unable to help
Figurative: Literally "to love but be unable to aid," used when you sympathize and would gladly help, but cannot. A gracious, slightly rueful way to decline: 我也想帮你，可惜爱莫能助 ("I'd like to help, but sadly it's beyond me"). The 助 again is the aid of 帮助.

Literal: love me, love my dog — love extends to all connected with the beloved
Figurative: Lit: love-house reach-crow. If you love the house, you even love the crow on the roof. Love spreads to everything associated with the beloved, even people or things that would otherwise seem unremarkable.

Literal: to walk calmly in place of riding: to be content with a simple, unhurried life
Figurative: Lit: walk at ease, treat it as a carriage. Here 当 takes the dàng reading, "to treat as." From a Warring-States anecdote: to stroll on foot and reckon it as good as riding, content without luxury.

Literal: to live in peace and be content in one's work: a settled, secure life
Figurative: Lit: peaceful-dwelling, joyful-work. 安居 is to live securely, 乐业 to take pleasure in one's occupation. The classic image of social well-being: a people housed, employed, and at ease. Often invoked as the aim of good governance.
Tags: emotion music culture characters society commerce industry education

Literal: Allah — God in Chinese Muslim usage
Figurative: The standard Chinese transliteration of Arabic Allāh. Chinese-speaking Muslims also use 真主 Zhēnzhǔ (True Lord , a theologically informed Chinese rendering, placing Islamic monotheism in dialogue with Confucian cosmology).

Literal: to follow the proper sequence: to do things step by step in due order
Figurative: Lit: according-to-section, settle-into-rank. Originally a writer's image of arranging material into its right divisions and lines; now it means to proceed methodically by the established order, neither rushing nor skipping steps. Here 部 keeps its old sense of an ordered division.
Tags: society meaning measure-words characters vocabulary conjunction timing communication

Literal: arrogant and rude; haughty and without manners
Figurative: Lit: arrogant-rude-without-courtesy. The social-failure sense of 慢 crystallized into a four-character indictment.

Pinyin: bā xiān guò hǎi, gè xiǎn shén tōng
Literal: the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each showing their powers — everyone uses their own talents
Figurative: The Eight Immortals, crossing the sea, each rely on a different magical skill rather than a single method. The saying describes a group facing a shared task in which every member contributes through their own distinct ability, and is used to praise resourceful, varied teamwork.

Literal: to seize the moment; to grasp the opportunity at the right time
Figurative: 把握 bǎwò (grip; certainty; grasp) + 时机 shíjī (the right moment). A common exhortation in business, speech, and motivational contexts. Also used as a noun: 有把握 yǒu bǎwò = "to be confident, certain" (lit. to have a grip on it). 没有把握 = "not sure, not confident."

Literal: hair gone hoary white: aged, in advanced old age
Figurative: Lit: white-hair-grey-grey. A vivid picture of a head of grizzled white hair, used affectionately or respectfully of the elderly. Again the fà reading, since the phrase is literally about hair.

Literal: a hundred shots, a hundred hits — unerring accuracy
Figurative: 百 (hundred) + 发 fā (to shoot, release) + 百 + 中 zhòng (to hit the mark). A perfect score: every arrow finds its target. From archery contexts in the Warring States period, now applied to any domain where one's predictions, arguments, or shots unfailingly land.

Literal: a hundred feelings converging — a complex rush of mixed emotions all at once
Figurative: Lit: hundred-feelings-intersect-gather. For when emotions are too tangled and complex to name individually. 百 = figurative "many."

Literal: a hundred schools contend — free intellectual debate; a golden age of ideas
Figurative: Lit: "hundred schools contend and cry out." The standard Chinese phrase for the Warring States philosophical explosion. Still used today for any period of open intellectual competition.
Tags: scale language history confucianism classical dynasty ancient politics ritual philosophy classics bronze-age origins legalism statecraft

Pinyin: bǎi wén bù rú yī jiàn
Literal: hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once
Figurative: From the Han Shu (Book of Han), attributed to general Zhao Chongguo (赵充国), who when asked by Emperor Xuan to estimate how many troops would be needed for a campaign said: "Hearing about a situation a hundred times is not as good as seeing it once.

Literal: unbowed after a hundred setbacks — perseverance through repeated failure
Figurative: 百 (hundred) + 折 zhé (to break, to bend; a setback) + 不 (not) + 挠 náo (to scratch; to give way, to yield). Literally: a hundred snappings, yet never yielding. The material image is bamboo or a sword repeatedly bent but not permanently deformed.

Literal: to ruin the family's good name: to disgrace one's household
Figurative: 败坏 (to corrupt, ruin) acting on 门风, a family's reputation and moral tradition. Said of conduct shameful enough to stain the whole family, a phrase out of old domestic and clan morality.

Literal: Showing Off Before the Master
Figurative: Brandishing an axe at Lu Ban's door: the idiom for presuming to display skill before someone who has mastered it.

Literal: half the Analects suffices to govern all under heaven — the centrality of the classics in governance
Figurative: Attributed to the Song statesman 赵普 Zhào Pǔ, who supposedly told an emperor that he governed with only half his knowledge of the Analects and had the other half in reserve.

Literal: half understanding, half not: imperfectly grasped
Figurative: A colloquial set phrase built on the 半A不A frame (half-A, not-A). It marks shaky comprehension, the state of catching the gist of a lecture or a foreign language without truly mastering it.

Literal: half a catty, eight taels — six of one, half a dozen of the other; much the same
Figurative: Under the old measure of sixteen 两 to a 斤, half a catty was exactly eight taels: 半斤 and 八两 are the identical weight. The idiom says two things or two people are essentially the same despite appearing different, usually with a hint that neither is impressive.

Literal: to give up halfway: to abandon a task before it is finished
Figurative: Lit: half-road-and-quit. 而 links the halfway point to the giving-up that follows. Said in reproach of someone who starts strong but lacks the resolve to see a thing through.
Tags: grammar negation syntax conjunction cohesion classical characters

Literal: half believing, half doubting — skeptical; not fully convinced
Figurative: 半 bàn (half) + 信 xìn (to believe; to trust) + 半 bàn (half) + 疑 yí (to doubt; to suspect). The state of being precisely between trust and doubt: believing something enough to entertain it, doubting it enough not to act on it. 我对他说的话半信半疑 = I'm not sure whether to believe what he said.

Literal: to kidnap and extort: to seize a hostage and demand ransom
Figurative: 绑 bǎng = to tie up; to bind. 票 piào = here, a kidnapped person held for ransom (the slang 肉票 ròupiào, a human "ticket" to be cashed in). 勒索 lèsuǒ = to extort; to blackmail. A four-character description, not a classical chéngyǔ, but a fixed legal and news expression for kidnapping for ransom.

Literal: to have weathered wind and frost: hardened by hardship
Figurative: 饱 here means having had a full share of something. The image is a face lined by years of exposure; used of people who have lived through long adversity. Common in literary and journalistic prose.
Tags: food body daily-life characters classics commerce meaning

Literal: to eat one's fill all day: to idle in comfort
Figurative: From the Analects (论语), where Confucius reproaches those who eat their fill the whole day and apply their minds to nothing. A pointed criticism of idleness; carries a moral edge.

Literal: a scholar full of learning: an erudite person
Figurative: 饱 extends from a full stomach to a full mind. 饱学 means saturated with learning; a respectful term for a deeply read scholar. Formal register.

Literal: to treat to a full helping of fists: to give a sound beating
Figurative: A grim joke on the eating sense: instead of a meal, the recipient gets a generous serving of punches. From the Jìn Shū (晋书). Vivid and slightly humorous in tone.

Literal: defend the family, guard the country — patriotic sacrifice
Figurative: 保家 (protect the family) + 卫国 (defend the country). The phrase that encodes the family-state bond as a call to military service: you fight for the country by fighting for your family; you fight for your family by defending the country.

Literal: avenge a wrong and wipe out a grudge
Figurative: 报仇 (take revenge) paired with 雪恨 (wash away the hatred). The standard four-character phrase for settling a blood debt, frequent in martial-arts fiction and historical drama.
Tags: communication society characters nature weather winter

Literal: violent wind and sudden rain — a sudden, overwhelming storm of events
Figurative: Lit: violent-wind-sudden-rain. 暴 means violent, sudden, savage; 骤 means abrupt, arriving all at once. The idiom describes any sudden, overwhelming onslaught: a torrential crisis, a savage attack, a rapid political upheaval.

Literal: sorrows and joys, partings and reunions
Figurative: Literally "grief, joy, parting, union", the full arc of human fortune in four characters. 离 (parting) and 合 (reunion) form the pair at its heart, the comings and goings of a life. From a famous Song lyric by Su Shi on the moon and human separation.
Tags: motion nature characters grammar direction space communication

Literal: the north wind howls in fury — biting cold; adversity
Figurative: 北风 (north wind) + 怒 (furious) + 号 (to howl). A classical weather image used in poetry and prose to evoke bitter cold and desolation. Du Fu's famous poem 茅屋为秋风所破歌 uses the howling north wind as a metaphor for the hardships of his refugee years during the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763 CE).

Literal: original face: a thing's true, unaltered nature
Figurative: Lit: original-face-and-features. A Chan Buddhist phrase for one's true self before all conditioning, now used broadly for the real character of anything once the disguises are stripped away.
Tags: nature meaning measure-words characters chan zen meditation

Literal: to put root and tip in the wrong order: to mistake the essential for the trivial
Figurative: Lit: root-tip-upside-down. 本 (the root) and 末 (the branch-tips) are the two ends of the tree. To reverse them is to spend effort on the minor while neglecting what truly matters.

Literal: forced up Mount Liang — driven to a desperate course
Figurative: From the heroes' repeated path of being pushed by injustice until they have no refuge but the outlaw stronghold of Liangshan. The chengyu now means being driven by circumstance to take a drastic step one would never have chosen freely, the very pattern by which the novel's decent men become rebels.
Tags: literature novels classics classical song rebellion

Literal: the brush moves like dragons and snakes: bold, flowing, vigorous calligraphy
Figurative: Lit: brush-runs-dragon-snake. The line of cursive writing twists and surges with the energy of a dragon and a snake in motion. High praise for a calligrapher whose hand is alive and free.

Literal: the road one must take; the only viable path forward
Figurative: 必 (must) + 由 yóu (to pass through; to travel by way of) + 之路 (the road). The path through which one must pass, with no alternative route. Used when describing the single viable way forward in a difficult situation: 改革是必由之路 (Reform is the only path forward).
Tags: grammar modal logic classical ethics philosophy

Literal: the whip is long but cannot reach — distance defeats even great strength or authority
Figurative: Lit: whip-long-cannot-reach. From the Zuǒzhuàn (左传), a Spring and Autumn period chronicle. A ruler may have power, but he cannot govern what is too distant from him.
Tags: direction geography nature classical analects confucianism

Literal: to alter the base and pile on more: to grow worse than before, to intensify
Figurative: Lit: change-base-add-severity. Said when behavior that was already bad escalates rather than improving, the original measure exceeded and then redoubled.

Literal: change beyond prediction — unpredictable; mercurial; always surprising
Figurative: 莫 mò = no one can; impossible to. 测 cè = measure; fathom; predict. Lit: "the changes cannot be measured." Used to describe weather, markets, political situations, and people whose behavior cannot be anticipated.

Literal: to discern direction and rectify position — to orient oneself correctly before acting
Figurative: From the Zhouli (周礼). The phrase belongs to the rituals of city-founding and palace-construction: before laying the foundations, the official must determine the cardinal directions and align the building correctly. By extension, in any major undertaking, one must first establish one's bearings.

Literal: a burly, powerfully built man
Figurative: Lit: tiger-bodied big fellow. 彪 (a young tiger) lends its image of muscular bulk, so the phrase paints a tall, broad, imposing man, the bodyguard or strongman of a scene.

Literal: outside and inside are as one: consistent in word and deed; the same within as without
Figurative: 表 biǎo = the outside, the surface. 里 lǐ = the inside, the interior. 如一 rú yī = as if one; identical. A person whose outward conduct matches their inner thoughts, who is honest and undivided, with no gap between the surface they show and the substance underneath. A strong compliment to integrity.

Literal: separate lodges and detached palaces: the same scattered residences, with the lodge named first
Figurative: The attested inversion of 离宫别馆, listed as its own form in idiom dictionaries. Putting 馆 first foregrounds the lodging over the palace.

Literal: guests and friends fill the seats: a house full of company
Figurative: Lit: guests-friends fill the seats. 宾朋 pairs guest with friend; the image is a hall packed with visitors. Close kin to 高朋满座, used of a lively, well-attended occasion where every seat is taken.

Literal: refined and courteous in bearing; gracefully well-mannered
Figurative: From the Lúnyǔ (论语·雍也): 文质彬彬，然后君子 ("when refinement and substance are in balance , only then is one a 君子"). 彬彬 bīn bīn names the quality of refined balance , neither rough nor showy.

Literal: ice in the sky, snow on the ground — a frozen, bitterly cold world
Figurative: 冰 bīng (ice) + 天 tiān (sky) + 雪 xuě (snow) + 地 dì (ground). A vivid set phrase for a landscape locked in deep winter, ice above and snow below, everything frozen. Used to describe the far north, high mountains, or any scene of extreme cold. 探险队在冰天雪地里走了好几天。

Literal: troops at the foot of the wall: the enemy at the gates
Figurative: 兵 bīng = soldiers, troops; 临 lín = to arrive at, to overlook; 城下 = below the city wall. The enemy army has reached the base of the wall, the last moment before a siege becomes an assault.

Literal: soldier-and-horse figures — the terracotta army
Figurative: The name breaks down as 兵 bīng (soldiers) + 马 mǎ (horses) + 俑 yǒng (tomb figures, funerary effigies). The key word is 俑: a sculpted human or animal figure made specifically to be buried with the dead in place of living sacrifices.
Tags: nature daily-life characters history qin first-emperor ancient art archaeology dynasty unification legalism statecraft

Pinyin: bīng wú cháng shì, shuǐ wú cháng xíng.
Literal: An army has no fixed configuration, as water has no fixed shape.
Figurative: Sunzi's image for strategic adaptability, strikingly close to the water imagery of the Daodejing.
Tags: classics philosophy statecraft strategy ancient legalism

Literal: Warfare is the way of deception.
Figurative: A blunt rejection of chivalric ideals: success in conflict depends on shaping the enemy's perceptions, concealing one's own strength and intentions, and striking where one is not expected.
Tags: classics philosophy statecraft strategy ancient legalism

Literal: when the illness is desperate, one runs to any doctor
Figurative: A proverb rather than a classical chengyu: desperation abandons judgment. Used far beyond medicine, for panicked job hunts, failing companies grasping at consultants, or students trying every cram school at once. The tone is sympathetic but critical; the flailing rarely works.

Literal: the illness has entered the vitals: beyond cure
Figurative: From the Zuǒ Zhuàn: a duke dreams the disease hides in the 膏肓, the region between heart and diaphragm that no needle or medicine can reach. Used today for any situation, not only medical, that has decayed past saving.

Literal: Boya breaks his strings — the loss of a 知音
Figurative: From the Liezi 列子. After Zhong Ziqi died, Boya destroyed his qin and played no more. 绝弦 juéxián (severing the strings) became the image for grief over the loss of someone who truly understood you.

Literal: universal love; philanthropy — broad, impartial love for all
Figurative: 博 bó = broad, extensive. Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles include 博爱 as a founding ideal. Also the Chinese word for philanthropy and humanitarian love. Related to the Mohist concept of 兼爱.

Literal: broadly gather the strengths of many — to learn from many sources
Figurative: 博 (broad) + 采 (to gather, to select) + 众 (many, the crowd) + 长 (strengths, advantages). A virtue in learning: drawing on the best from many teachers and traditions rather than following a single school. Used for scholarship, artistic development, and leadership style.

Literal: broad, great, refined, and deep — vast and profound
Figurative: 博 (broad) + 大 (great) + 精 (refined, essential) + 深 (deep). The standard four-character formula for describing Chinese culture in formal contexts: 中华文化博大精深 is a set phrase appearing in textbooks, official speeches, and tourist literature.

Literal: widely read and retentive: of broad learning and a powerful memory
Figurative: Lit: broad-hearing-strong-memory. Praise for a person who has read and heard much and remembers it all. Also written 博闻强识, with 识 read zhì in the sense of "to retain."

Literal: not ashamed to ask those below — intellectual humility; willingness to learn from anyone regardless of status
Figurative: From the 论语 (Analects) , Confucius praising the minister Kong Wenzi: 敏而好学，不耻下问，是以谓之'文'也 (Quick-minded and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those of lower rank , this is why he was given the posthumous title 'Wen').
Tags: communication language society characters confucianism virtue social ethics

Pinyin: bú dào chángchéng fēi hǎo hàn
Literal: he who has not reached the Great Wall is not a true hero
Figurative: From Mao Zedong's 1935 poem 清平乐·六盘山. Not technically a 成语 (it is seven characters), but functions as a fixed quotation. Often paired in modern usage with 越长城: to "cross the wall" is to prove oneself. The verb implied is 越 (to cross over) or 到 (to reach).
Tags: history language identity characters movement comparison border geography dynasty great-wall qin ming architecture

Pinyin: bù fēn qīng hóng zào bái
Literal: without distinguishing the colors — to act heedlessly, without regard for right and wrong
Figurative: 不分 bù fēn (not distinguishing) + 青红皂白 (blue, red, black, white). 皂 zào is an old word for black. To plunge into action without bothering to tell the colors apart, that is, without finding out who is actually at fault. 他不分青红皂白就把孩子骂了一顿。

Literal: to part on bad terms: to break up unhappily, the gathering souring
Figurative: Lit: not-joyful-and-scatter. The mirror image of the joyful idioms: a meeting or meal that ends in discord, everyone leaving displeased. 两人话不投机，不欢而散 "the two could not agree, and parted on bad terms."

Literal: neither panicked nor rushed — composed and unhurried
Figurative: Lit: not-panic-not-hurry. Does not contain 慢 but is its most important semantic companion. Where 慢 can carry a negative charge (negligence, arrogance), 不慌不忙 frames the same unhurriedness as mastery: the person who is slow because they are in control, not because they are lazy or contemptuous.

Literal: countless; too many to count
Figurative: Literally "not to reckon their number," so many that counting is hopeless. Used for vast, uncountable quantities, the far end of the scale that 多少 stretches toward. The answer to 多少 when the true reply is "beyond counting."
Tags: quantifiers adverb numbers grammar scale measure-words communication

Literal: to punish without having taught: to penalize people never instructed in the rule
Figurative: Lit: not-teach-yet-punish. From the Analects, a criticism of the ruler who punishes failings the people were never taught to avoid. To hold someone to a standard you never showed them.

Literal: a bond that cannot be untied: an indissoluble tie
Figurative: Lit: a connection 缘 that cannot 不 be untied 解. An unbreakable bond or lifelong affinity, often with a person, a place, or a pursuit. 他和音乐结下了不解之缘 = he formed a lifelong bond with music. Here 解 is "to untie," and the negation makes the tie permanent.

Literal: neither tight nor slow: unhurried, even-paced
Figurative: A steady, measured tempo with no rush and no dawdling. Often admiring, describing someone who keeps composure under pressure.

Literal: to travel without legs — (of news) to spread rapidly on its own
Figurative: A classical chengyu (using 走 in its classical "to run" sense, before 跑 took over). 胫 jìng = the lower leg; the image is of news that has no legs but somehow runs everywhere by itself. Used today for rumors, viral information, and news that spreads without effort.

Literal: cannot be estimated: immeasurable, beyond reckoning
Figurative: 不可 bù kě (cannot) + 估 gū (to estimate) + 量 liàng (to measure, to gauge). So vast or so consequential that no estimate can capture it. Used for losses, impact, or value too large to quantify: 损失不可估量 (the losses are immeasurable), 意义不可估量 (the significance is beyond reckoning).

Literal: inconceivable; unimaginable
Figurative: Literally "cannot be thought or discussed," beyond comprehension, originally a Buddhist term for the ineffable. Here 可 ("can / possible"), the first character of 可能, takes its sense of "able to be": what cannot possibly be grasped by thought.
Tags: grammar negation syntax modal adverb communication

Literal: insufferably arrogant: to think no one in the whole age is one's equal
Figurative: Lit: cannot be matched by anyone of the age. Said of someone so overweeningly proud that they look down on everyone alive, behaving as though the entire era holds no rival worthy of them. Strongly critical in tone.

Literal: to let a matter fade away unresolved; to end without proper conclusion
Figurative: Lit: not-conclude-conclude-it. Uses 了 liǎo as a verb twice , "to not conclude [a matter], to conclude [it anyway]." A set phrase for when a problem or investigation is allowed to dissolve without resolution , bureaucratic negligence, diplomatic evasion, quiet abandonment. 这件事就这样不了了之了。

Literal: not relying on written words — the foundational Chan stance on language
Figurative: One of the four Chan axioms: 教外别传，不立文字，直指人心，见性成佛 , "Special transmission outside the scriptures; not relying on written words; directly pointing to the human mind; seeing the nature, becoming Buddha." 不立文字 does not mean Chan rejected literacy , monks studied extensively.

Literal: to agree without prior consultation: to coincide spontaneously
Figurative: Lit: without-conferring yet-agree. Said when two people arrive at the same view or plan independently, their thoughts fitting together though they never discussed it.

Literal: not seeking deep understanding — reading for pleasure, not to dissect
Figurative: From Tao Yuanming's self-portrait Mr. Five Willows (五柳先生传): 好读书，不求甚解 "He loved to read, but did not press for fine-grained interpretation." The classical defense of reading widely and lightly rather than scholastically.

Literal: leaving no room for doubt: beyond question; indisputable
Figurative: 不容 = leaves no room for; 置疑 = to cast doubt. A fact or conclusion so certain that no doubt can be entertained. The same 不容 pattern as 义不容辞: there is simply no space for the doubt to enter. 这个事实不容置疑。(This fact is beyond dispute.)

Literal: neither one thing nor another — shady, dubious, not upright
Figurative: Lit: not-three not-four. Three and four are "middle" numbers: something that is neither here nor there, neither proper nor improper. Used for shady people or behavior that doesn't conform to standards.

Literal: never forget the original aspiration — keep faith with founding ideals
Figurative: A phrase with pre-revolutionary Buddhist origins (初心 = the first aspiration toward enlightenment) now central to Xi Jinping-era CCP rhetoric. Used in the context of the Cultural Revolution to mean: remember what the revolution was supposed to achieve, and do not let it be corrupted.

Literal: do not violate the farming seasons: act in step with the right time
Figurative: From the Mencius (孟子). The ruler who does not drag farmers off to other work during planting and harvest will have grain enough to feed the realm. Now a general caution against wrong timing.

Literal: neither hear nor ask: to pay no attention to a matter at all
Figurative: Lit: not-hear-not-ask. To stay wholly indifferent, neither listening for news nor inquiring after it. Often a reproach for someone who ignores what should concern them.

Literal: without words, it is understood — self-evident; goes without saying
Figurative: Lit: not-speak-yet-understand. What goes without saying: a truth so obvious that to speak it would be redundant. Contrasts with the power attributed to 语 elsewhere: here, the deepest understanding transcends the need for words.

Literal: to want no face: shameless, brazen
Figurative: Not a classical four-character chengyu but a fixed colloquial phrase: to want no face is to discard all sense of shame. A sharp insult, stronger than it looks in English.

Literal: to fly off without wings: to vanish suddenly
Figurative: Used of objects that disappear inexplicably, as if something with no wings had taken to the air. Also of news that spreads everywhere overnight.

Literal: to agree without prior arrangement: to coincide as if by plan
Figurative: Lit: not-agreed-yet-alike. Without having arranged it (不约), people 而 nonetheless act alike (同). Used when several act or think the same way by sheer coincidence.

Literal: wide of the mark; irrelevant; rambling without getting to the point
Figurative: 不 + 着 zháo (achieve, land) + 边际 (edge, boundary). Literally "not landing on any boundary" , the talk or argument fails to touch the relevant point. Said of speech, writing, or proposals that circle around without engaging the actual issue.

Literal: at a loss what to do
Figurative: Literally "not knowing what to set one's hands to", thrown into confusion and unable to act. It is the inner state behind a panicked 怎么办, the moment when you cannot even begin to choose a course of action.

Literal: deployed with careful thoroughness: arranged in close and complete order
Figurative: 部署 bùshǔ is to lay out forces or tasks in their assigned positions, the military sense of 部; 周密 zhōumì means thorough and tightly planned. Said of a plan or operation set up with every detail in place.

Literal: talent brimming over: overflowing with brilliance
Figurative: Lit: talent-brilliance-spilling-overflowing. 才华 is creative or literary brilliance, and 横溢 paints it as water flooding past its banks. Said of someone whose gifts are too abundant to contain.

Literal: outstandingly talented — ability that stands above the crowd
Figurative: 才能 cáinéng (talent and ability) + 出众 chūzhòng (to stand out from the crowd). 能 here combines with 才 (talent, capacity) to form the compound 才能. Used in recommendations, eulogies, and formal praise. 她才能出众，前途无量 "Her talents are exceptional; her future is limitless."

Literal: quick-witted; rapid and agile in thought and creative expression
Figurative: 才思 cáisī = literary talent and flow of ideas (才 here is the noun "talent," not the adverb). 敏捷 = swift and agile. A high compliment for writers, poets, and scholars who produce brilliant work quickly.

Literal: the blue sea becomes mulberry fields — dramatic change over time; the world transformed beyond recognition
Figurative: From a Daoist tale recorded in 神仙传 (Biographies of Immortals, attributed to Ge Hong, 4th century CE): the immortal Magu tells of having seen the eastern sea turn to mulberry fields three times. 沧海 cānghǎi = the dark blue sea (沧 = cold, dark; vast).

Literal: to act on it too hastily: to rush a matter
Figurative: A gentle warning that someone moved too fast and forced a result before its time. Often used to advise patience: 这件事不能操之过急 (don't rush this).

Literal: to finish a matter hastily and carelessly
Figurative: The doubled 草草 means hurriedly and roughly, borrowing the haste of fast-growing grass. To 草草了事 is to wrap something up sloppily just to be rid of it, the opposite of thorough work.

Literal: to treat human life as cheap as grass: to kill or harm people without regard
Figurative: From the Hanshu account of Jia Yi. 菅 jiān is a coarse wild grass; to regard a person's life as no more than a weed is to be utterly callous about killing. Used of tyrants and reckless rulers.

Literal: grass and trees all look like soldiers: to be so jumpy that every shadow seems a threat
Figurative: From the Battle of Fei River (淝水之战, 383 CE) in the Jin Shu: the routed Former Qin emperor Fú Jiān, in panic, mistook the grass and trees on Mount Bagong for enemy troops. Now describes nervous, paranoid fear that sees danger everywhere.

Pinyin: cèyǐn zhī xīn, rén jiē yǒu zhī.
Literal: The heart of compassion — every person has it.
Figurative: Mencius 6A:6. The full passage lists all four hearts (恻隐、羞恶、恭敬、是非之心) and asserts that all four are universal: "every person has them." This is the foundation of the 性善论 argument: if the moral emotions are universal, they are innate, not learned.

Literal: teahouses and wine-shops: the everyday public houses of a town
Figurative: A four-character set phrase pairing 茶馆 with 酒肆 (the wine-shop) to stand for the street-level places where ordinary people gathered, drank, and talked.

Literal: to weigh words and read faces: to gauge a person's mood and intent
Figurative: Lit: examine-words-observe-expression. The skill of watching what someone says and how they look in order to sense their true feelings, a prized social sensitivity in Chinese life.

Literal: to sing a one-man show: to carry the whole thing alone
Figurative: From opera, where a 独角戏 is a one-actor play. Used when someone is left doing all the talking or all the work while no one else joins in.

Literal: issue an order at dawn and change it by dusk
Figurative: From debates on Han fiscal policy. A sharp criticism of fickle, unstable rule whose constant reversals leave people unable to plan.

Literal: full of youthful vigor: brimming with life and energy
Figurative: Lit: morning-vigor, luxuriant-thriving. 朝气 is the spirit of a new day, 蓬勃 the look of growth in full flush. Said of people, teams, or whole societies that are young and full of drive.

Literal: Qin in the morning, Chu at night — serving different masters; inconsistency and opportunism
Figurative: From the reality of Warring States advisors who moved between states as circumstances changed. The phrase originally described border regions whose allegiance shifted with the military tide. Now a common idiom for fickleness, opportunism, or having no fixed loyalties.
Tags: ancient dynasty history philosophy legalism statecraft politics classics

Literal: three in the morning, four at dusk: fickle, forever changing one's mind
Figurative: From a fable in which a keeper offers his monkeys three nuts in the morning and four at night; they protest, so he swaps it to four and three, and they are content though the total is the same. Now it names someone fickle, who keeps switching with no real difference.

Literal: to think of morning and night; to long for ceaselessly
Figurative: 朝 zhāo (morning; dawn) + 思 sī (to think of; to long for) + 暮 mù (dusk; evening) + 想 xiǎng (to think of; to miss). Thinking at dawn and thinking at dusk: longing that fills the entire arc of a day. Used for intense, sustained yearning: romantic longing, homesickness, or grief for the absent.

Literal: the dust has settled; a situation has finally reached resolution
Figurative: Lit: dust-settle-fixed. Evokes the moment after turmoil when everything finally comes to rest and the outcome is clear. Title of Alai's celebrated Tibetan novel.

Literal: sinking fish and falling geese — describing a woman so beautiful that fish dive and birds fall when she passes
Figurative: From the Zhuangzi, originally a wry critique of relativism in beauty (the fish do not actually find her beautiful , they hide because they are afraid of humans).

Literal: strike the iron while it's hot: seize the moment
Figurative: 趁 while, 热 hot, 打铁 to forge iron. The blacksmith's wisdom, identical to the English proverb. Used to urge acting on momentum before it cools.

Literal: to suit the heart and match the wish: perfectly satisfactory
Figurative: Lit: fitting-the-heart-as-the-wish. Everything turning out exactly as one hoped, in feeling and in fact alike. A warm phrase for contentment, and a common blessing for someone's plans or new beginnings.

Literal: start a family and establish a career — the two milestones of adult life
Figurative: 立业 = to establish one's career or livelihood. The traditional sequence of adult life goals: first you build a home; then you build a livelihood. 他终于成家立业了。(He has finally started a family and established himself.) The phrase encodes a whole theory of the proper human life cycle.

Literal: thousands upon thousands: a vast, countless number
Figurative: Lit: amounting-to-thousands-up-to-ten-thousands. A vivid way to say a great many, used of crowds, stars, raindrops, anything too numerous to count. Here 成 carries the sense of reaching a quantity.

Literal: to form crowds and bands: in droves, in flocks
Figurative: The most common 队 idiom in daily speech. Pictures people or animals gathering thick enough to clump into groups and lines. Used for crowds streaming somewhere: 游客成群结队地涌入古镇.

Pinyin: chéng yě Xiāo Hé, bài yě Xiāo Hé
Literal: rise by Xiao He, fall by Xiao He — the same hand that made you can unmake you
Figurative: Xiao He recommended Han Xin for command (making him); later lured Han Xin into the trap that got him executed (destroying him). Now: a person or factor that is simultaneously the source of your rise and your ruin. Often used in business for a single decision or relationship that cuts both ways.

Literal: carry on the past and open the way for the future
Figurative: To inherit what came before and pass it on, serving as the bridge between earlier and later generations, a 代 to 代 handing-on. Said of a person, work, or era that links what preceded it to what follows, the connective role between ages.

Literal: City God (respectful address)
Figurative: The suffix 爷 yé is an honorific for senior male figures, divine and human: 土地爷, 老天爷. It conveys respectful familiarity rather than formal distance. Worshippers address the City God as 城隍爷 in prayer and casual speech; formal temple documents may use the full title with rank designation.
Tags: folk-religion religion gods culture history ritual ancestors

Literal: eat, drink, play, be merry: a life of indulgence
Figurative: Four verbs of pleasure strung together, with 喝 as the drinking. Usually mildly disapproving, said of someone who does nothing but enjoy themselves.

Literal: to endure hardship and persevere in labor — a core work-ethic virtue
Figurative: The defining work-ethic phrase in Chinese culture. Applied to individuals, generations, and national character. Eating bitterness + tolerating labor = the formula for achievement.

Literal: suffering loss is a blessing — short-term disadvantage leads to long-term benefit
Figurative: A proverb attributed to Zheng Banqiao (Qing dynasty). The Daoist-inflected wisdom: accepting being at a disadvantage cultivates humility and patience, which eventually bring greater good. Widely quoted in Chinese business and parenting contexts.

Literal: four types of malevolent spirits — demons and monsters; all manner of evil beings
Figurative: All four characters share the 鬼 radical, which is itself significant , this is a phrase built entirely within the spirit-world lexicon. 魑 chī: a mountain demon; 魅 mèi: a seductive forest spirit; 魍 wǎng and 魉 liǎng: two water or mountain spirits classified in classical demonology.
Tags: folk-religion religion culture classical symbolism ancestors

Literal: stuff the ear and not hear — deliberately ignoring what is said
Figurative: 充 (to fill, to stuff) + 耳 (ear) + 不闻 (not listening). Plugging the ear on purpose , willful deafness to advice, complaint, or truth. From the Shijing (詩經, Classic of Poetry): the earliest citation describes a ruler who stopped his ears to his ministers' counsel.

Literal: knitted brows and a bitter face: a picture of gloom and worry
Figurative: 愁 (worry) eyebrows over a 苦 (bitter) face. The whole head sags with anxiety. A vivid, everyday way to say someone looks miserable.

Literal: to come out beyond expectation: contrary to what anyone anticipated
Figurative: Lit: come-out-of-reckoning. 意料 is what the mind reckons in advance; to fall 出乎意料 is to land outside it. Its mirror is 不出所料, "just as expected."

Literal: to stand out from the class and rise above the finest — exceptional; head and shoulders above
Figurative: From Mencius (孟子): 出于其类，拔乎其萃. 类 lèi = category; type; peers. 拔 bá = to pull up; to surpass. 萃 cuì = the finest, the gathered best. To emerge beyond one's category and surpass even the finest specimens within it. Classical Confucian praise for moral and intellectual excellence.

Literal: emerge from its unexpectedness — to catch someone off guard; to act when least expected
Figurative: 出 chū (emerge; go out) + 其 qí (their; its) + 不意 bù yì (not anticipated; unexpected).
Tags: grammar classical literary particle language classics philosophy statecraft strategy ancient legalism

Pinyin: chū qí bù yì, gōng qí wú bèi.
Literal: Emerge where unexpected; attack where unprepared.
Figurative: From the first chapter, now the standard chengyu 出其不意 ("catch off guard"). The principle is to direct one's effort at the point and moment the opponent has not anticipated and cannot defend, turning surprise itself into a decisive advantage.
Tags: classics philosophy statecraft strategy ancient legalism

Literal: to achieve victory through surprise — to win by doing the unexpected
Figurative: 出奇 = to deploy the unusual, to emerge with something unexpected. 制胜 = to achieve victory; to control the outcome.

Literal: beyond people's expectation — unexpected; surprising; contrary to what was anticipated
Figurative: Lit: exceed-people-intention-anticipate. One of the most common ways to say "surprisingly" or "unexpectedly" in formal Chinese. 这个结果出人意料，没有人预测到。"This result was unexpected , no one had predicted it." Also appears in the variant 出乎意料 chū hū yìliào with identical meaning.
Tags: motion direction daily-life meaning gift register

Literal: to leave the mundane and enter the magical: superb; consummate; masterly
Figurative: 出 chū = to leave, 神 shén = the divine, 入 rù = to enter, 化 huà = the transformed, transcendent state.

Literal: remove the old, spread the new — ritual clearing and renewal
Figurative: 除 (chú, to remove, to clear away) + 旧 (old) + 布 (bù, to spread, to lay out) + 新 (new). The ritual logic of the Spring Festival: the house is swept, old paper charms are replaced with new ones, debts are settled, quarrels patched over.

Literal: thread the needle and lead the thread: to act as go-between
Figurative: Literally the seamstress's first move. Figuratively, to broker a connection between two parties, matchmaking a deal, a marriage, a meeting.

Literal: to carry on the family line: to continue the ancestral lineage through descendants
Figurative: Lit: pass on the clan, link the generations. The traditional duty of producing heirs so that the family line does not end. 宗 is the ancestral lineage and 代 the generations; 传 and 接 are the passing-on and the picking-up that keep the chain unbroken.

Literal: sturdy ships and sharp guns: overwhelming naval and military might
Figurative: A late-Qing phrase for the foreign gunboats whose strength forced the treaty ports open. Now shorthand for raw technological force.

Literal: boldly moving through south and north — widely traveled; experienced in the world
Figurative: 闯 (to push through boldly) + 南 (south) + 走 (to travel) + 北 (north). A person who has made their way through the whole country, acquiring experience and resilience. The verb 闯 suggests the travel was not comfortable or planned but forced through obstacles.

Literal: riding the spring wind, full of pride: flush with success
Figurative: From Mèng Jiāo's Tang poem on passing the imperial exam. Describes someone on a winning streak, often with a hint that the pride may be premature.

Literal: spring is warm and flowers bloom: the good season has come
Figurative: The stock image of spring at its best. Used literally for the season and figuratively for the right moment, a turn for the better after hardship.

Literal: the words fail to convey the meaning: to express oneself poorly
Figurative: Lit: words-not-reach-meaning. Said when the language a speaker or writer chooses does not match what they meant, so the point comes across muddled or wrong. A common way to apologize for an unclear remark.

Pinyin: cǐ xīn guāngmíng, yì fù hé yán
Literal: this mind is bright and clear — what more is there to say?
Figurative: Wang Yangming's last words, spoken on his deathbed in 1529 when a student asked if he had any final instructions. His response , that his mind was luminous (光明 guāngmíng), and that this was sufficient , encapsulates his entire philosophy.
Tags: wang-yangming mind knowing neo-confucianism confucianism philosophy ethics human-nature history ming

Literal: calm and unhurried: composed under pressure
Figurative: 从容 = calm, leisurely; 不迫 = not pressed, not rushed. To act with poise and no sign of haste even when stakes are high. Here 容 sits in 从容, the word for unflustered composure: someone with room inside to spare. 他从容不迫地回答了所有问题。(He answered every question calmly and without haste.)

Literal: preserve Heavenly Principle, eliminate human desire — Zhu Xi's formulation of moral cultivation
Figurative: Perhaps the most quoted and most criticized phrase in Neo-Confucianism. 天理 tiānlǐ = Heavenly Principle (the universal moral norm); 人欲 rén yù = human desires (not all desires but those that conflict with Heavenly Principle: excessive appetite, selfishness).

Literal: crisscrossed and tangled: intricate and complicated
Figurative: Lit: interlaced-gathered-doubled-mixed. Keeps the "crossing" sense of 错: relationships or situations so interwoven and layered that they are hard to untangle. 错综复杂的关系 "a web of tangled relationships."

Literal: the answer is not what was asked: to give a reply beside the question
Figurative: Lit: answer-not-what-asked. A reply that fails to address the actual question, whether from evasion or misunderstanding. A near neighbor of 文不对题, but about spoken answers rather than written work.
Tags: education meaning communication characters language society

Literal: to stand up for the wronged; to right injustices
Figurative: 打 (to strike at) + 抱 (to hold) + 不平 (unfairness). To beat back unfairness, to intervene on behalf of someone being treated unjustly. The righteous stranger who steps in. A heroic frame common in wuxia literature.

Literal: to beat the grass and startle the snake — to tip off the target through careless action
Figurative: One of the 36 Stratagems (三十六计). The grass is struck and the snake hiding inside is alerted. Used to warn against premature or clumsy action that reveals your intentions and lets the target escape or prepare. Common in military, political, and business contexts.

Literal: great timber put to small use — talent wasted on a trivial task
Figurative: Lit: great-timber small-use. A large structural beam cut down for use as a chopstick. The standard expression for overqualification or talent misallocation. Said politely of others, rarely of oneself. The 小 here measures not the person but the scope of the task assigned to them.
Tags: cosmology scale daily-life confucianism adjectives daoism philosophy grammar

Literal: to eat and drink lavishly: feast extravagantly
Figurative: The doubled 大 stresses excess. Modern usage often flags wasteful banqueting or living beyond one's means.

Literal: greatly and especially wrong: utterly, completely mistaken
Figurative: Lit: big-error-particularly-error. An emphatic doubling that drives home how badly someone has misjudged: 你这样想就大错特错了 "if you think that, you are gravely mistaken."

Literal: generous and unaffected; poised and at ease in manner
Figurative: The reduplicated form of 大方 dàfang (generous; gracious; not stingy or awkward). Said in praise of someone whose bearing is relaxed and dignified rather than petty or self-conscious.

Literal: the eldest shouldn't mock the second: pot calling the kettle black
Figurative: A proverb on shared flaws: 大哥 and 二哥 are equally at fault, so neither has standing to criticize the other. The Mandarin take on glass houses.

Literal: utterly fair and selfless: putting the common good above all private interest
Figurative: Lit: great-public-without-private. The highest praise for an official or leader who holds to the public good and lets no personal interest sway the judgment. 公 and 私 stand at the two poles of the phrase.

Literal: the great work is accomplished — mission complete
Figurative: Lit: great-achievement-announce-accomplished. A formal declaration that a major undertaking (a construction project, a campaign, a long creative work) has been completed. Often used with a tone of proud announcement: 大功告成！(We did it!).
Tags: culture history aspect particle tense mastery time martial-arts

Literal: the great and beautiful rivers and mountains; the magnificent homeland
Figurative: The near-synonym of 大好江山, using 河山 héshān (Yellow River and mountains) instead of 江山 (Yangtze and mountains). 河 hé specifically refers to the Yellow River , 黄河 Huáng Hé , the cradle of northern Chinese civilization.

Literal: to give a great shout: bellow once, loudly
Figurative: Here 喝 takes its hè reading, "to shout". A stock phrase in classical fiction and storytelling, the warrior or judge who freezes a room with a single roar.

Literal: the great river flows east — time and history flow on; the brilliant figures of the past are gone
Figurative: From Su Shi's 苏轼 famous ci poem "Niannujiao · Red Cliff Nostalgia" (念奴娇·赤壁怀古): 大江东去，浪淘尽，千古风流人物. "The great river flows east; its waves wash away the brilliant figures of a thousand ages." Invoked for historical grandeur and the irreversible passage of time.

Literal: big streets and small lanes: everywhere in town
Figurative: The standard way to say all over the city, every street and back alley. Neutral register, extremely common in news and speech: 大街小巷都挂满了灯笼, lanterns hung all over the streets.

Literal: top sister: a commanding, dominant woman
Figurative: A colloquial trigram, not a classical idiom, for the female leader of a group or a forceful, authoritative woman. Carries a half-admiring, half-wary tone.

Literal: to make a big fuss over nothing — overreacting to small things
Figurative: Lit: big-shock small-wonder. To be shocked and amazed by things that are actually trivial. A mild criticism of someone who overreacts or lacks perspective.

Literal: to greatly open one's horizons — to have one's eyes opened
Figurative: Lit: greatly-open-eye-boundary. The standard phrase for the experience of suddenly seeing something new and broadening one's outlook. Said after a trip, a museum visit, a striking piece of work.

Literal: greatly satisfying to the people's hearts — a righteous outcome that pleases everyone
Figurative: Lit: greatly-fast/free-people's-hearts. Used when a wrongdoer receives punishment, a long-overdue verdict is handed down, or a corrupt official is finally removed. The 快 here is squarely in the "heart released from obstruction" sense: justice has cleared away what was blocking everyone.

Literal: havoc in Heaven — the Monkey King's great rebellion
Figurative: The celebrated early episode in which Sun Wukong storms the celestial palace, defeats Heaven's armies, and helps himself to the food and treasures of the gods.
Tags: literature novels classics classical buddhism pilgrimage

Literal: dramatic rises and falls — extreme volatility and turbulence
Figurative: Lit: great-rise great-fall. For lives, markets, or dynasties marked by dramatic swings: the roller-coaster image. Common in financial commentary and biographical writing.

Literal: to be greatly let down: bitterly disappointed in what one had hoped for
Figurative: Literally "greatly to lose what one hoped for." Used when reality falls far short of expectation and the disappointment is severe, as when an eagerly awaited result turns out badly. The intensified form of plain 失望.
Tags: perception feeling evaluation characters vocabulary daily-life communication

Literal: big hands and big feet — extravagant; throwing money around
Figurative: Lit: big-hand-big-foot. Said of someone who spends lavishly without thinking, makes large gestures, lives beyond their means. Mildly disapproving, the opposite of 节俭 jiéjiǎn (frugal).

Literal: full of the greatest righteousness — awe-inspiring moral authority; unshakeable in the face of evil
Figurative: 大义 dàyì (the greater righteousness; overriding moral principle) + 凛然 lǐnrán (awe-inspiring; commanding; cool and stern; the quality of moral authority that makes others straighten up).

Literal: very promising; full of hope
Figurative: Literally "to greatly have hope," said of a person or prospect with bright chances: 这个项目大有希望 ("this project is very promising"). A warm, encouraging phrase built directly on 希望, the bright mirror of 大失所望.

Literal: the Grand Canal
Figurative: The Sui's enduring monument: 运 yùn (to transport) + 河 hé (river), a man-made transport river. Built at terrible human cost under Emperor Yang, it linked the rice-rich south to the political north and remained the backbone of Chinese internal trade for over a millennium.
Tags: history dynasty unification statecraft classical tang

Literal: great wisdom appears foolish; the truly wise seem simple
Figurative: 大 dà (great; profound) + 智 zhì (wisdom; discernment) + 若 ruò (appears like; seems as if) + 愚 yú (foolish; simple-minded). The phrase appears in its classical form in the 老子 Laozi, Chapter 45: 大直若屈，大巧若拙，大辩若讷 , and in the later formulation 大智若愚 that crystallizes the pattern.
Tags: cosmology scale daily-life philosophy buddhism confucianism knowing

Literal: to treat people and handle affairs: the way one conducts oneself with others
Figurative: Lit: treat-people-engage-things. The whole manner of dealing with others and managing matters; said in praise of someone whose conduct is gracious and well judged.

Literal: to decide decisively at the right moment; not to hesitate when the time comes
Figurative: Lit: facing-the-opportunity-immediately-decide. The complement of 把握时机 , not just grasping the moment but acting on it decisively. 断 here means to cut through, to decide without wavering. The virtuous counterpart to 犹豫不决 (hesitating and unable to decide).
Tags: meaning timing society characters syntax object disposal

Pinyin: dāngjú zhě mí, pángguān zhě qīng
Literal: those involved are confused; bystanders see clearly
Figurative: 当局者 = the one who is in the situation; the person directly involved + 旁观者 = the one standing to the side watching. 迷 = confused, lost / 清 = clear, perceptive. Two contrasting 者 nominalizings set in opposition: the agent inside the situation vs. the observer outside it.

Literal: a staff-blow and a shout to the head — a jolt that wakes someone up
Figurative: From Chan pedagogy at its most physical: Master Deshan was famous for the staff, Master Linji for the shout, both deployed to shatter a student's conceptual dithering. Now any sharp warning that snaps a person out of a bad course: a failed audit, a doctor's blunt sentence.

Literal: stirring the breath and coiling the gut: deeply moving, soul-stirring
Figurative: Lit: surging-breath-coiling-innards. Said of music, writing, or a story so moving that it seems to turn one's very insides. 回 keeps its coiling sense here.

Pinyin: dào bù tóng bù xiāng wéi móu
Literal: those who follow different ways cannot work together — fundamental value divergence ends cooperation
Figurative: From the Analects: when the fundamental principles (道) that govern a person's life diverge, strategic cooperation becomes impossible. Used when parting ways with a colleague, organization, or ally over principle , not personal dislike but incompatible directions.

Pinyin: dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào.
Literal: The Way that can be spoken is not the constant Way.
Figurative: The opening line of chapter 1, and the most famous sentence in the entire text. It establishes at once that the 道 lies beyond the reach of fixed language: any 道 that can be fully captured in words is already a limited, conditioned thing, not the constant, nameless source.
Tags: daoism laozi classics philosophy wuwei cosmology daodejing

Literal: heard on the road, told on the path — hearsay; rumor; unverified gossip
Figurative: 途 tú = road; path (in transit). Things overheard on the road, passed on without verification. The road is a place of unfiltered information, strangers, and half-truths. 不要相信道听途说。(Don't believe hearsay.) Used to dismiss rumors or unverified claims.

Literal: the righteous have many helpers — moral legitimacy generates real-world support
Figurative: From Mencius (孟子). Full phrase: 得道多助，失道寡助 (Those who have the Way have many helpers; those without the Way have few). Moral legitimacy is not merely symbolic , it creates tangible coalitions. Those who govern well attract support; those who govern badly find themselves isolated.

Literal: handy and skillful: to do something with effortless mastery
Figurative: Lit: the hand answers the heart. What the mind intends, the hand at once carries out. Praise for a skill so practiced it feels automatic. Here 应 takes the yìng reading, "to respond."

Literal: so pleased with oneself that one forgets propriety — overweening pride
Figurative: Lit: obtain-pleasure-forget-form/shape. 得意 = satisfied, pleased (here 得 is the full verb "to get/obtain," not the particle). 忘形 = to forget one's bearing/form. Used for someone carried away by success or compliments.

Literal: to have both virtue and talent; the ideal of the capable and morally upright person
Figurative: 德 dé (virtue; moral character) + 才 cái (talent; ability; practical capability) + 兼 jiān (simultaneously; to combine) + 备 bèi (to possess; to be equipped with). The ideal of the complete person , someone who is not only capable and skilled (才) but also genuinely good (德).
Tags: ability timing meaning characters philosophy ethics confucianism

Literal: of lofty virtue and weighty reputation — a venerable elder
Figurative: Lit: virtue-high, reputation-heavy. The standard four-character honorific for a respected senior figure , a teacher, a scholar, a community elder. Used at retirement banquets, in obituaries, and in introductions of distinguished guests.

Literal: vast land, abundant resources — used of China's territory
Figurative: Lit: land-great-things-abundant. The 地 here is the full noun "land, earth" (dì, 4th tone), not the adverbial particle de. Appears frequently in descriptions of China's natural endowment. A reminder: 地 has a full semantic life beyond its particle function.
Tags: things science nature characters particle complement adverb

Literal: indeed; certainly — a frozen adverb containing 的
Figurative: 的确 is pronounced dí-què (not de), showing that 的 in fixed compounds retains its old full pronunciation. 这的确是个好主意 "This is indeed a good idea." A reminder that 的 has a fuller historical identity beyond its grammatical particle role.
Tags: grammar copula logic daily spoken language etiquette particle complement adverb focus cleft past

Literal: red lamps and green wine: gaudy nightlife
Figurative: The glow of pleasure quarters, often tinged with disapproval. Describes a city of bars and neon, sometimes implying decadence or excess.

Literal: lamps blazing splendidly: brilliantly lit
Figurative: A hall or street ablaze with light, suggesting wealth, festivity, or grandeur. A common way to paint a banquet or a lit skyline.

Literal: lamps lit all through: every light blazing
Figurative: A house, street, or ship lit up from end to end, not one window dark. Plainer than 灯火辉煌: it stresses that everything is lit rather than that the light is splendid.

Literal: to ascend the rolls and place in the rankings: to succeed in the civil-service exam
Figurative: Lit: mount-the-roster-reach-rank. 登科 is to have one's name posted on the pass list, 及第 to be ranked within it. A set phrase of congratulation for examination success.

Literal: wait and see; you'll find out (a mild challenge or prediction)
Figurative: 等着 (keep waiting, durative 着) + 瞧 (to look, see). The 着 holds the waiting in place: don't stop waiting, the answer is coming.

Literal: lower the voice, lower the breath — to speak with extreme humility; to be submissive in order to placate someone
Figurative: 低声 (lower the voice) + 下气 (bring down one's breath/spirit). The physical image is precise: a person who speaks quietly and exhales slowly is physiologically in a submissive, de-escalated state.

Literal: dripping water bores through stone: persistence wins
Figurative: The image of a single drip, repeated for years, drilling a hole in rock. The standard idiom for patient, steady effort overcoming a hard obstacle.

Literal: to invert black and white — to deliberately confuse right and wrong
Figurative: 颠倒 diāndǎo (to turn upside down) + 黑白 hēibái (black and white). To knowingly call wrong right and right wrong, twisting the truth for one's own ends. Stronger and more accusatory than simply lying: it charges the speaker with corrupting the very standard of judgment. 他为了脱罪，竟然颠倒黑白。

Literal: to invert right and wrong; to call black white and white black
Figurative: Lit: overturn-invert-right-wrong. A severe accusation: to deliberately misrepresent the facts, to claim something wrong is right and vice versa. The logical extreme of a bad-faith 是…的 , not just correcting a focus, but inverting the entire reality. Common in political rhetoric and moral arguments.

Literal: to touch stone and turn it to gold: to transform the ordinary into the priceless
Figurative: Lit: touch-stone-become-gold. From Daoist immortal lore, the touch that turns base rock to gold. Now used of an editor, teacher, or craftsman who makes something dull suddenly shine.

Literal: to wither and fall — to fade and drop away; (of people) to pass away
Figurative: 凋 (to wither) + 零 (to fall in drops). Strictly a two-character word rather than a four-character chengyu, but a fixed literary expression worth knowing.

Literal: head touching heaven, feet on earth — a person of complete integrity and heroic stature
Figurative: 顶 dǐng = to stand at the top of; to press against from below. 立 lì = to stand; to be upright. The image is of a person so morally complete that they fill the entire vertical axis of the universe , feet firmly planted on earth, head pressing against heaven.
Tags: nature geography cosmology taoism philosophy heaven classical existence

Literal: to render great help: a respectful thanks for another's strong assistance
Figurative: Lit: with-tripod-strength-to-help. 鼎 is the massive bronze ritual tripod, so 鼎力 is great strength. A polite phrase used to acknowledge or request another person's powerful support.

Literal: lose people, show eyes — to make a spectacle of oneself; disgraceful public behavior
Figurative: Lit: lose-person-expose-eyes. A stronger and more colorful version of 丢脸 , specifically about embarrassing public display. 现眼 (to expose one's eyes to public ridicule) adds the dimension of being stared at and judged.

Literal: running east and dashing west — to rush around in every direction
Figurative: A four-character formula combining 奔 and 跑 across the directional pair 东 dōng / 西 xī. Used for someone constantly on the move, often in service of obligations or in pursuit of a livelihood.

Literal: rushing east, running west — frantically busy everywhere; constantly in motion
Figurative: Lit: east-rush-west-walk. Describes someone perpetually in motion, always somewhere else, never settled. Often implies exhausting, stressful busyness with little to show for it. 他为了这件事东奔西走了好几年。"He spent years running all over the place trying to make this happen."
Tags: directions nature cosmology buddhism colloquial things

Literal: pieced together from east and west — cobbled together from miscellaneous sources
Figurative: 东拼 (stitched from the east) + 西凑 (gathered from the west). Something assembled by scraping together bits and pieces from wherever they could be found. Used for a speech that draws from random sources, a meal made from leftovers, or a budget patched together with emergency measures.
Tags: directions nature cosmology buddhism colloquial things

Literal: rise again from the Eastern Mountain — to make a comeback after defeat
Figurative: From the biography of Xiè Ān (謝安, 320–385 CE), a Jin dynasty statesman who retired to 东山 (Eastern Mountain, in present-day Zhejiang) and refused office for years. When the court fell into crisis, he was recalled and restored Jin to stability.

Literal: to imitate blindly without understanding, and make things worse
Figurative: A homely woman copies Xi Shi's famous frown and clears the street: Zhuangzi's parable about form without essence.

Literal: looking east and west — glancing around nervously or curiously; gawking
Figurative: Lit: east-look-west-gaze. Used for someone whose eyes dart around, whether out of nervousness, suspicion, or simple distraction. The four-character structure vividly enacts the scanning motion itself. 他在街上东张西望，好像在找人。"He was looking all around the street as if searching for someone."

Literal: to move hands and feet: to get physical, to grope or rough up
Figurative: Lit: move-hand-move-foot. To put one's hands on someone, either to start a fight or to touch improperly. The doubled 动 spreads the action across hands and feet alike.

Literal: bridal chamber and wedding candles: the wedding night
Figurative: 洞房 is the bridal chamber, the deep inner 房 of the house; 花烛 are the red wedding candles. The set phrase stands for a marriage celebration, often paired as 洞房花烛夜, the night of the wedding.

Literal: the injustice done to Dou E — a metonym for any terrible, heaven-shaking wrong
Figurative: From Guan Hanqing's most famous play. 比窦娥还冤 bǐ Dòu É hái yuān, "more wronged than Dou E herself", is a common colloquial expression for extreme injustice. 比窦娥冤 appears in everyday speech whenever someone protests they have been treated unfairly.

Literal: a unique school's matchless skill: a signature technique known to no one else
Figurative: Lit: sole-school-unmatched-skill. 门 here is a school or lineage of practice. A 独门绝技 is the secret art that belongs to one tradition or master alone.

Literal: to come in first; to stand at the apex
Figurative: Lit: to stand alone on the giant turtle's head. 鳌 áo is the mythical sea turtle whose head is the highest point, corresponding to the top of the imperial examination standings. Metaphor: to take first place.

Literal: read until ten thousand scrolls are worn through — saturate yourself in reading
Figurative: From Du Fu's "Twenty-Two Rhymes Presented to Vice-Director Wei" (奉赠韦左丞丈二十二韵): 读书破万卷，下笔如有神 "Read until ten thousand scrolls are worn through, and your pen will move as if inspired." The classical statement of how literary skill is built.

Pinyin: dú wàn juàn shū, xíng wàn lǐ lù
Literal: read ten thousand scrolls of books, walk ten thousand li of road — learn from text and from travel both
Figurative: A Ming-dynasty saying attributed to the painter and theorist Dong Qichang. The pairing of 读 and 行 as the two halves of an educated life: book-knowledge and lived experience as equally necessary, neither sufficient alone.
Tags: learning language education literacy culture calligraphy

Literal: short weapons meet: close-quarters combat, a fierce face-to-face clash
Figurative: From the Chu Ci. Now applied figuratively to any direct, intense confrontation, including debate and competition.

Literal: a short-lived dynasty
Figurative: The standard description of the Sui, paired in Chinese historical thinking with the 秦朝 Qin: brilliant, transformative, and brief, doing the hard work of unification and building before collapsing and yielding to a long, glorious successor.
Tags: history dynasty unification statecraft classical tang

Literal: playing the qin to a cow — speaking to someone incapable of understanding
Figurative: From a Han dynasty text attributed to 牟融 Móu Róng. A musician plays the most refined music for a cow; the cow goes on eating grass. The problem is not the cow's intelligence but the category mismatch: the music is addressed to the wrong kind of listener.
Tags: arts music classical confucianism literature nature food characters vocabulary

Literal: prescribe according to the symptoms; tailor the remedy to the problem
Figurative: 对 (match) + 症 (symptoms) + 下药 (administer medicine). From the case lore of the Han physician Hua Tuo, who gave two patients with identical headaches different prescriptions because the causes differed.

Literal: of many talents and many skills: versatile, multitalented
Figurative: Lit: much-talent-much-skill. High praise for a person gifted in several arts at once, the painter who also writes and plays music. 艺 yì is craft or art, the paired half of 才.

Literal: one unnecessary action too many — to do something superfluous
Figurative: 多 (extra, unnecessary) + 此 (this) + 一举 (one action). An extra action that wasn't needed , wasted effort that doesn't improve the result. A gentle criticism of overcaution or unnecessary elaboration: 你不用解释，多此一举 ("you don't need to explain , that's unnecessary").

Literal: the more the better
Figurative: Literally "more and more is the more beneficial," the more the merrier. From a remark attributed to the general Han Xin, who said that as a commander he could lead troops 多多益善 ("the more the better"). Built on the 多 ("many") of 多少.
Tags: adjectives scale grammar measure-words communication numbers spoken vocabulary

Literal: an eventful autumn: a troubled time, full of upheavals
Figurative: Lit: many-matters' autumn. Autumn was the season of harvest reckoning and of war, so a "many-matters autumn" came to mean a period crowded with crises and disturbances, a turbulent, eventful time for a state or a person.

Literal: to repay kindness with enmity: to bite the hand that feeds you
Figurative: 恩 (kindness) is met with 仇 (enmity) as its 报 (return). A sharp condemnation of ingratitude, common in everyday speech to call out a betrayer.

Literal: ears and eyes completely renewed — a refreshingly new impression
Figurative: 耳 (ear) + 目 (eye) + 一 (completely) + 新 (new). All your senses reset , everything seems fresh and surprising. Used for places recently renovated, new presentations, or any experience that resets one's perception. The compound treats ears and eyes as a pair, the full perceptual system.

Literal: ears soaked, eyes stained — influenced by constant exposure
Figurative: 耳濡 (ear soaked/wetted) + 目染 (eye stained). The effect of growing up surrounded by something , gradually absorbing it through the senses without formal instruction. Often used for children who learn by immersion: 耳濡目染，自然就会了 ("soaked by ears and eyes, one naturally learns").

Literal: ears listening in all eight directions — alert and perceptive to everything around
Figurative: 耳 (ears) + 听 (listening) + 八方 (the eight directions , north, south, east, west, and the four diagonals; by extension, all sides).

Literal: heard with the ear, seen with the eye — witnessed firsthand
Figurative: 耳 (ear) + 闻 (heard) + 目 (eye) + 睹 (seen). Both the ear and the eye were present and active. A marker of direct personal testimony, as opposed to hearsay. Used in legal testimony, journalism, memoir, and any context where the authority of a claim depends on personal presence.

Literal: two tigers fight — when two powerful forces clash, both suffer
Figurative: The full form is often 两虎相争，必有一伤 liǎng hǔ xiāng zhēng, bì yǒu yī shāng: "when two tigers fight, one is certain to be wounded." Used to counsel against unnecessary conflict between equals, and to describe political or commercial battles where both sides bleed.
Tags: cosmology philosophy daoism yin-yang grammar vocabulary

Literal: without a second word: at once, without hesitation or argument
Figurative: Lit: a-second-word-not-said. Said of someone who acts immediately, raising no objection and wasting no breath: 他二话不说就答应了 "he agreed without a moment's hesitation."

Literal: to carry forward and make flourish: to develop a good thing to its fullest
Figurative: Lit: send-forth-raise-bright-great. Said of carrying on a tradition, virtue, or fine quality and making it grow even greater. The fā reading: to bring something forth and develop it. 把好传统发扬光大 "to carry a good tradition forward."

Literal: the law shows no favor to the noble — law applies equally regardless of rank
Figurative: From Han Feizi. 阿 ē = to show favoritism, to bend. 贵 guì = the noble, the powerful. The complete saying continues: 绳不绕曲 shéng bù rào qū , "the carpenter's line does not bend around curves." Law, like a measuring line, must be straight.

Literal: the law allows no room for sentiment: justice must not bend to feeling
Figurative: Lit: law-not-tolerate-feeling. The principle that the law must be applied evenly, without softening for personal ties or sympathy. The level standard of the water radical made into a maxim.

Literal: to overturn rivers and upend seas: overwhelming, world-shaking force
Figurative: Lit: overturn-river topple-sea. Said of a power great enough to churn the waters of the world, and by extension of turbulent emotion or upheaval: 心里翻江倒海 "the heart in utter turmoil."

Literal: to cross mountain ridge after mountain ridge — to traverse difficult terrain, by extension, to overcome great obstacles
Figurative: A four-character compound combining 翻越 (to climb over) split across 山 (mountain) and 岭 (ridge). Used both literally (an arduous mountain journey) and figuratively (overcoming a series of difficulties to reach a goal). Frequent in war-history and biographical writing. 他翻山越岭，终于来到了家乡。

Literal: to flip back and forth with no constancy: fickle and unpredictable
Figurative: Lit: repeatedly-without-constancy. A criticism of someone whose moods, promises, or positions keep changing, so that no one can rely on them.

Literal: turn from guest to host: to seize the initiative and take control
Figurative: Lit: reverse-guest-become-host. Once a stratagem of war: the side that arrives in a weaker, guest-like position turns the tables and takes command. Now used of anyone who flips a passive role into a controlling one.

Literal: return to the unpolished, restore the authentic — strip away ornament for plain truth
Figurative: Lit: return-uncarved-restore-real. Daoist in spirit. 璞 = uncarved jade. The aesthetic and ethical movement back from elaboration to unworked simplicity.

Literal: a space of mere inches; a tiny place — also: one's heart and mind
Figurative: Lit: square-inch-of-ground. 方寸 = one square cun (about an inch). Used literally for extremely small physical spaces, and metaphorically for the heart/mind (one's inner space).

Literal: Fáng plans, Dù decides: a perfect pairing of complementary talents
Figurative: From the Tang statesmen Fáng Xuánlíng, famed for strategy, and Dù Rúhuì, famed for decisiveness. Here 房 is the surname Fáng; the idiom praises two people whose strengths complete each other.

Pinyin: fàng xià tú dāo, lì dì chéng fó
Literal: lay down the butcher's knife and become a Buddha on the spot — radical redemption is always possible
Figurative: The full form of 立地成佛. Rooted in the Chan teaching that Buddha nature is present in all beings, even the most hardened. Used both seriously (in discussions of rehabilitation, forgiveness, religious conversion) and ironically (with skepticism about a villain's sudden change of heart). 只要放下屠刀，立地成佛.

Literal: cast one's eyes across all-under-heaven — to think broadly; to have a global perspective
Figurative: 放眼 fàng yǎn (to let one's gaze range freely; to look far) + 天下. To look beyond one's immediate circumstances, neighborhood, or nation and think on a civilizational or global scale. The opposite of 鼠目寸光 (shǔ mù cùn guāng , mouse-eyes seeing only an inch; short-sightedness). 要放眼天下，不能只看眼前。

Literal: Feihuang gallops upward: to rise rapidly in rank
Figurative: 飞黄 (Fēihuáng) is a legendary divine steed; the phrase pictures a career rising as if riding it skyward. The standard idiom for a meteoric rise in office or fortune.

Literal: no small matter: serious, of great importance
Figurative: Lit: not-the-same-as-trivial. 小可 means a small or trivial thing, and 非同 negates it: this is not on a par with the trivial, so treat it with weight. 这件事非同小可 "this is no small matter."

Literal: those not of our kin; those outside our group
to forget sleep and meals (in one's work)
Figurative: Literally "to neglect sleep and forget to eat," so absorbed in work or study that one loses track of basic needs. Used to praise total dedication, though modern usage sometimes carries a gentle warning about overwork. The image of the scholar bent over the desk through the night.

Pinyin: fēn jiǔ bì hé, hé jiǔ bì fēn.
Literal: What is long divided must unite; what is long united must divide.
Figurative: The opening philosophy of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, stating the cyclical rhythm of Chinese political history between unity and fragmentation. It is one of the most quoted sentences about Chinese history as a whole, used to frame any long swing between consolidation and breakup.
Tags: literature novels classics classical history strategy dynasty han statecraft

Literal: to fight for every minute and second: to lose not a moment
Figurative: Lit: minute-second-must-contend. Said when time is so pressing that each unit counts, in a race, an emergency, a deadline. 争分夺秒 is the common variant.

Literal: burn the books and bury the Confucians — state censorship and intellectual repression
Figurative: The four-character condemnation of the Qin cultural purges of 213–212 BCE. Still the standard Chinese phrase for any government suppression of thought or culture. Note that 坑 kēng (pit) also functions in modern colloquial Chinese as a verb meaning "to trap" or "to screw over someone" , e.g.
Tags: qin unification first-emperor history dynasty legalism statecraft

Literal: favorable weather: good conditions for a harvest
Figurative: Lit: the wind is well-tuned and the rain comes in due course. A set wish for a year of mild, timely weather and a good harvest, often paired with 国泰民安 (the country at peace and the people content). Here 调 takes the tiáo reading, "to harmonize," the weather brought into balance.
Tags: music communication change characters cosmology geomancy space

Literal: the wind is calm and the waves are still: calm seas, a tranquil situation
Figurative: Lit: wind-level-waves-quiet. The sea at perfect rest, used both literally and for any situation that has settled into calm after trouble has passed.

Literal: feng shui rotates in turn — fortunes change; cycles of luck; the wheel keeps turning
Figurative: The most common figurative use of 风水. Used to express acceptance of change, comfort in adversity, or (more pointedly) schadenfreude when an opponent's luck runs out. 三十年河东，三十年河西，风水轮流转 (thirty years east of the river, thirty years west , the wheel of fortune keeps turning).

Literal: to weather a storm in the same boat
Figurative: Literally "wind and rain, the same boat", to stand together through hardship, sharing the danger. From the Sunzi Bingfa, which notes that even old enemies in one storm-tossed boat will help each other. The deepest form of being 在一起, bound by shared trial.

Literal: to dole out titles and make promises: to buy support with offers of office
titles for the wife, privilege for the sons: rank and honor extended to one's family
Figurative: The reward of high office under the empire: a man's success earned a title for his wife and protected status for his sons. Evokes the prestige of the old examination-and-rank system.

#fields:Hanzi: 烽火连三月，家书抵万金
Pinyin: fēnghuǒ lián sān yuè, jiāshū dǐ wàn jīn
Literal: beacon fires for three months; a letter from home worth ten thousand gold
Figurative: Du Fu's couplet from 春望 (Spring View), written during the An Lushan Rebellion while imprisoned in rebel-held Chang'an (756 CE). Among the most quoted lines in Chinese literature: a complete world of wartime separation compressed into fourteen characters.

Literal: lighting the beacon fires to toy with the lords — crying wolf at the cost of a dynasty
Figurative: From the story of King You and Bao Si: the beacon fires lit for entertainment, the vassal lords who stopped responding, and the Quanrong attack that ended Western Zhou. Used to describe any deception that destroys the credibility needed in a real crisis.
Tags: history ancient confucianism classical dynasty ritual philosophy bronze-age

Literal: after extreme obstruction (yin) comes peace (yang) — when things hit rock bottom, improvement follows
Figurative: From the Yijing hexagrams 否 pǐ (stagnation; obstruction , a yin hexagram) and 泰 tài (peace; harmony , a yang hexagram). The cosmological law: forces cycle, yin cannot dominate forever, the turn of yang is inevitable. A comforting phrase in hard times: 否极泰来，好日子还在后面。

Literal: the husband sings and the wife follows: a harmonious married couple
Figurative: Literally "the husband leads, the wife accompanies." A traditional image of marital harmony in which the couple act in accord, one taking the lead and the other in step.
Tags: communication culture characters family society humanity

Pinyin: fú wú shuāng zhì, huò bù dān xíng
Literal: blessings don't come in pairs; misfortunes never come alone
