Figurative: The Chinese equivalent of "when it rains it pours," and its optimistic inverse. Fortune is rare and singular; misfortune clusters. A paired proverb that encodes Chinese realism about luck.

Literal: the star of fortune shines from above — to be under a lucky star
Figurative: 福星 fúxīng = the star of fortune (one of the three auspicious stars 福禄寿). 高照 = shining from on high. A blessing used at New Year, weddings, and new ventures.

Literal: the father kind, the son filial: the reciprocal duty between generations
Figurative: A Confucian formula for the father-son relationship, paired in the classics with 兄友弟恭 (elder brother caring, younger respectful). Authority and obedience are framed as mutual obligations, not one-way command.

Literal: the father's debt, the son repays: a debt or wrong passes down the line
Figurative: Once a literal expectation in family law, now used figuratively for any burden inherited from a previous generation. Carries a tone of grim inevitability.

Literal: enrich the country, strengthen the army — national power as a policy goal
Figurative: 富国 (enrich the state) + 强兵 (strengthen the army). The paired goals of realist statecraft, traceable to the Legalist ministers of the Warring States period (especially Shāng Yāng of Qin, died 338 BCE).

Literal: wealthiest in the whole region: the richest man around
Figurative: 甲 here means "to rank first." Said of a local magnate whose fortune tops everyone in the district. Admiring, slightly old-fashioned register.

Literal: wealth that can rival a state: fabulously rich
Figurative: 敌 means "to match." A private fortune so vast it equals a kingdom's treasury, applied to tycoons past and present.

Literal: rich, beautiful, grand and imposing: sumptuous and magnificent
Figurative: Describes a palace, mansion, or banquet hall dazzling with luxury. Common in travel writing and architecture description today.

Literal: to change dynasty and era: a change of regime
Figurative: Lit: change-dynasty, swap-era. 朝 and 代 are the dynasty and its age. The phrase names the fall of one ruling house and the rise of another, and by extension any sweeping change of who holds power.
Tags: dynasty history direction characters generation society motion daily-life politics philosophy worldview

Literal: change the head, swap the face: a superficial makeover
Figurative: Originally Buddhist, on the soul taking a new body. Now usually pejorative: the form is redone but the substance is unchanged, like a rebranded scam.

Literal: change the string and retune — fundamental reform, not adjustment
Figurative: 改弦 = to change the string (of a stringed instrument); 更张 = to restring and retune. The 更 is gēng, first tone. A musician who only retunes (改弦) is making incremental adjustments; one who also rerestrings (更张) is starting fresh.
Tags: grammar adverb comparison degree timing classical

Literal: change the bowstring, switch the wheel-rut — to change direction; to take a new approach
Figurative: 改 (change) + 弦 (xián, bowstring) + 易 (change) + 辙 (zhé, wheel-rut). The two halves are parallel images of changing tools and changing track. Used for any decisive shift in policy, method, or life-direction.

Literal: to abandon the crooked and return to the straight: to mend one's ways
Figurative: Lit: change-evil-return-upright. Said of someone who gives up wrongdoing and comes back to honest living. 邪 (crooked, evil) is the standing opposite of 正.
Tags: society communication characters ethics aspect meaning

Literal: dare to do, dare to act — bold and decisive; willing to take initiative and responsibility
Figurative: 敢 (to dare) + 作 (to do) + 敢 (to dare) + 为 (to act). The positive image of 为 as confident, owned action , the opposite pole from 无为. Where 无为 counsels releasing the forcing quality of striving, 敢作敢为 describes the quality of someone who acts decisively and stands behind what they do. 这个领导敢作敢为，大家都很佩服。
Tags: grammar classical taoism philosophy daoism wuwei syntax

Literal: to dare to act and dare to answer for it — to own one's actions
Figurative: 敢 gǎn (to dare) + 做 + 敢 + 当 dāng (to bear, to take responsibility). The mark of a person of integrity: bold enough to act, and equally willing to shoulder the consequences. The phrase praises moral courage paired with accountability, the refusal to act and then duck the blame.

Literal: so grateful the tears fall — moved to tears by gratitude; deeply thankful
Figurative: 感激 (deep gratitude) + 涕 (tears) + 零 (to fall in drops). Here 零 returns to its literal verb sense, "to fall in drops," applied not to rain but to tears: gratitude so overwhelming that the tears come down. The phrase describes being moved to weeping by another's kindness or favor.
Tags: emotion perception gratitude language science cosmology

Literal: ten thousand emotions surging — overwhelmed by bittersweet feeling at life's passage
Figurative: Go-to phrase for homecomings, reunions, and witnessing great change. Appears constantly in memoirs and personal essays.

Literal: to feel it as if one's own body received it; deep empathy
Figurative: Originally a formula of thanks on another's behalf (I feel your kindness to them as if I received it myself); modern usage has shifted it to empathy generally, feeling someone's pain as one's own.
Tags: emotion perception gratitude body health daily-life vocabulary

Literal: too high to climb — unattainable; inaccessible
Figurative: 高 (high) + 不可 (cannot) + 攀 (to climb, to reach by climbing). So elevated that it is beyond reach , a person, position, standard, or price that cannot be attained.

Literal: neither high nor low will do — too picky; unable to settle; rejecting both good and mediocre options
Figurative: 高低 (high and low, all options across the spectrum) + 不就 (will not take, will not accept).

Literal: lofty bearing and shining integrity: noble character of the highest order
Figurative: Lit: high-wind-bright-node. Here 节 is integrity, the firm node that does not bend. High praise for a person of unbending principle and selfless conduct.

Literal: distinguished friends fill the seats: a gathering of honored guests
Figurative: Lit: high-friends fill the seats. 高朋 are eminent guests, the 高 marking rank or worth. The phrase from Wang Bo's preface to the Tengwang Pavilion praises a host whose hall is full of distinguished company, a warm word for a well-attended feast.

Literal: high mountains, flowing water — finding someone who truly hears you
Figurative: The piece Boya played when Ziqi first identified the mountains and rivers in his music. As a chengyu, 高山流水 has two uses: the meeting of a 知音 (someone who understands you perfectly), and more broadly, music or artistry of the very highest order.
Tags: arts music classical confucianism literature vocabulary

Literal: to talk loftily and expansively: to hold forth grandly, often emptily
Figurative: Literally "lofty talk, broad discoursing." Describes someone holding forth at length on grand themes, frequently with the implication that the talk is more impressive than substantial. Can be neutral (spirited, wide-ranging conversation) but often carries a faint edge of "all talk."

Literal: look high and see far — farsighted vision; strategic perspective
Figurative: 高 (high) + 瞻 (to look up, to look ahead) + 远 (far) + 瞩 (to gaze at closely). Looking from an elevated position and therefore seeing farther: the physical metaphor for strategic or visionary thinking. Used to praise leaders, planners, and thinkers who see beyond immediate circumstances.
Tags: adjectives scale direction geography nature classical analects confucianism

Literal: high pillow, no worries — sleeping soundly; feeling at ease
Figurative: 高枕 (high pillow , sleeping comfortably) + 无忧 (no worry). Resting with one's head high , which you can only do when there's nothing to worry about. From the Zhànguó Cè: a strategist tells a king that if he follows the right policy, he can "sleep on a high pillow" without concern.

Literal: the two of us are tight: a toast and a drinking-game call
Figurative: A finger-guessing drinking call and a stock phrase for two close male friends. 俩 (liǎ) is "the two of us," so the whole thing means "we two brothers are solid."

Literal: cede territory and pay indemnities — the formula of defeat in unequal treaties
Figurative: Lit: cut-land-compensate-money. The standard shorthand for what unequal treaties required of China: territorial concessions (割地) combined with massive financial reparations (赔款). The phrase encodes the humiliation of the treaty system in four characters.

Literal: sing of deeds and praise virtue: to lavish flattering praise
Figurative: Here 歌 works as a verb, to sing the praises of. Now usually critical, marking hollow or sycophantic eulogy of those in power.

Literal: reform the old, establish the new
Figurative: From the Book of Changes. The more active, transformative counterpart to 与时俱进; where 与时俱进 describes keeping pace, 革故鼎新 describes active renovation. The 鼎 (bronze tripod) is a symbol of legitimate authority; 鼎新 means to inaugurate a new order as one would inaugurate a new dynasty.
Tags: history change classical daily-life chengyu idioms modern culture politics philosophy

Literal: investigate things to extend knowledge — the Neo-Confucian epistemological program
Figurative: From the 大学 Dàxué (Great Learning). 格 gé = to probe, to arrive at; 物 wù = things and affairs; 致 zhì = to extend, to bring to completion; 知 zhī = knowledge.
Tags: neo-confucianism zhuxi principle philosophy confucianism taoism cosmology nature heaven humanity classical

Literal: each and every one; all of them
Figurative: Reduplicating the measure word makes it mean "every single one without exception." 他们个个都很努力 "every one of them works hard." A vivid, emphatic way to say "all."

Literal: individualism
Figurative: 个人 (the individual) + 主义 (-ism). The modern term for individualism, the doctrine that puts the single person ahead of the collective. Its standing contrast is 集体主义 jítǐ zhǔyì (collectivism).

Literal: the flavor within: the inner experience only the one who lived it can know
Figurative: Lit: the-taste-within-this. 个中 means "within this matter," and 滋味 is flavor. The phrase points to feelings or hardships that an outsider cannot fully grasp, known only to the person who went through them.

Literal: each fully deploying what it is suited for — every component serving its proper function
Figurative: 各 gè = each; every. 尽 jìn = fully; to exhaust. 所用 = what it is for; the use to which it is suited. A principle of social and organizational coordination: when each person, each resource, each role operates at full capacity within its proper domain, the whole system functions well.

Literal: each airs his own view: everyone speaks their mind freely
Figurative: Lit: each-express-own-view. Said of a discussion where every participant is free to put forward their own opinion, the ideal of open and frank exchange. 抒 shū means to express or pour out.

Literal: each has its own beauty — beauty takes many forms
Figurative: A pluralist aesthetic principle: different things, places, or people each have their own kind of beauty. Used to avoid ranking or comparisons. The civilized response to "which is better?"

Literal: each has their own abilities — everyone has something they're good at
Figurative: Lit: each-has-what-[they]-can[do]. A Confucian-flavored observation about the distribution of talent. Used to affirm that different people excel in different domains , a polite and diplomatic formula. 人各有所能，没什么好比较的 "Everyone has their own abilities; there's nothing to compare."

Literal: every kind and every sort: all manner of things
Figurative: Lit: each-kind-each-sort. The standard everyday phrase for "all kinds of," stressing variety: 各种各样的人 "all sorts of people," 各种各样的问题 "every kind of problem."

Literal: so devoted to the common good as to forget oneself
Figurative: Lit: public-and-forget-private. Praise for one who throws themselves into public duty to the point of neglecting personal interest. A close cousin of 大公无私.

Literal: to handle official business by the book: no favors, no shortcuts
Figurative: Lit: public-matter-public-handle. To deal with official affairs strictly on their merits, without bending the rules for friendship or private gain. Often said with a touch of formality or coolness.

Literal: fair and selfless: impartial, with no private interest
Figurative: Lit: fair-upright-without-self. The ideal of the just official or judge who holds to the line without bending it toward kin, friends, or personal gain.

Literal: achievement complete and fame attained: to have made it
Figurative: Lit: merit-accomplished-name-attained. The classical picture of a fulfilled career: the work is done and the reputation is secured. Often paired with the idea of retiring gracefully afterward (功成身退, to withdraw once the work is achieved).

Literal: effort does not fail the determined person — hard work pays off; persistence wins
Figurative: One of the most commonly cited Chinese sayings about effort. 有心人 = a person with resolve and intention. The saying frames determination as the prerequisite: effort pays off for those who truly commit to it. 只要坚持，功夫不负有心人。

Literal: to fail for the lack of one final basketful: to fall short at the very end
Figurative: Lit: achievement-short-one-basket. From the image of building a mound and stopping one last basket of earth before completion. From the Book of Documents (尚书). The lesson: do not abandon a near-finished effort, or all the work before it is wasted.
Tags: mastery ability evaluation characters time martial-arts

Literal: to scheme and intrigue against each other — hooks, hearts, and clashing horns
Figurative: Originally described the complex interlocking eaves of palace architecture: each bracket hooking into another, each corner clashing. Now means: workplace backstabbing, political maneuvering, scheming rivalry.

Literal: a cornered dog leaps the wall: desperation breeds reckless acts
Figurative: The image is a trapped dog that, with no escape, hurls itself over a wall it could never normally clear. Used of people pushed past the edge who lash out wildly. Common in spoken and written warnings.

Literal: patching a sable robe with a dog's tail: a shabby sequel to a fine work
Figurative: From the Jìn Shū, where lavish marten-fur posts ran short and dog tails were used instead. Now a self-deprecating or critical term for an unworthy continuation of something excellent.

Pinyin: gū yīn bù shēng, dú yáng bù zhǎng
Literal: lone yin cannot generate; solitary yang cannot grow — nothing thrives in isolation; complementarity is necessary for life
Figurative: The cosmological principle stated with maximum directness: neither yin nor yang can sustain life alone. Life requires both.

Literal: of antique flavor: redolent of the past in look and feel
Figurative: Literally "ancient color, ancient scent." Praises a building, room, or object that has a tasteful, antique character, steeped in the atmosphere of an older age. A favorite for describing a classical garden, a tea house, or an old street that has kept its period charm.
Tags: ancient history classics characters perception food daily-life

Literal: from ancient times to the present
Figurative: Literally "the ancient goes, the present comes," spanning all of history up to now. Used to introduce a truth that has held across the ages: 古往今来，人人都怕死 ("from ancient times to now, everyone fears death"). Here 今 is the classical single character for "the present, now."
Tags: ancient history classics characters grammar direction motion communication vocabulary time daily-life timing

Literal: make the past serve the present
Figurative: To draw on the heritage of antiquity for present-day purposes, using old wisdom, forms, or techniques in modern life. Often paired with 洋为中用 ("make the foreign serve China"), the two together forming a well-known formula for selectively adapting the old and the foreign to modern Chinese needs.
Tags: vocabulary time history modern era daily-life

Literal: cheap grain hurts the farmer: low crop prices ruin the people who grow them
Figurative: A piece of classical economics still quoted in policy debates: when a bumper harvest crashes prices, the farmer who grew it earns less, not more.

Literal: bone and flesh joined together: bound by blood kinship
Figurative: The image is that bone and flesh cannot be pulled apart. Used for the inseparable bond between family members, and figuratively for a homeland and its people.

Literal: to confine oneself to old ways: to be complacent and refuse to progress
Figurative: Literally "wall yourself in with your old footsteps." 封 here is the self-imposed boundary. A common criticism of stagnant institutions or people who resist new ideas.

Literal: to deliberately mystify: to make something seem more obscure or profound than it is
Figurative: 故 (deliberately) + 弄 (nòng, to play with, to manipulate) + 玄 (xuán, mysterious, dark, profound) + 虚 (xū, empty, unreal). To purposely dress something up as mysterious in order to confuse or impress, when in fact there is little substance behind it.

Literal: attend to this and lose that — unable to manage everything at once
Figurative: 顾 gù (to attend to; to look after) + 此 cǐ (this) + 失 shī (to lose) + 彼 bǐ (that; the other). Fix your attention on one thing and something else slips away. Describes resource constraints, divided attention, and the predicament of managing competing priorities.

Literal: when the melon is ripe, the stem falls — things happen at the right natural moment
Figurative: Lit: melon-ripe-stem-fall. Things should not be forced; they will happen naturally when conditions are right. The Daoist principle of naturalness encoded in a harvest image.

Literal: wipe the eyes and look again — to see someone with new respect after they've changed
Figurative: 刮目 (to wipe / rub the eyes) + 相看 (to look at each other; to regard). Clear your eyes and look again at the person in front of you , because they are no longer who you thought they were.

Literal: relationship close and tight — closely connected; intimately related
Figurative: A descriptive fixed phrase rather than a classical 成语, but widely used as a set expression in formal Chinese writing and speech. 这两家公司的关系密切，共享很多资源。"These two companies are closely connected and share many resources." The closeness can be personal, institutional, or strategic.

Literal: corrupt officials drive the people to revolt
Figurative: The phrase that captures the whole moral logic of Water Margin: rebellion springs not from the people's wickedness but from the oppression of corrupt officials who leave them no other choice.
Tags: literature novels classics classical song rebellion

Literal: open, upright, and honest — nothing to hide
Figurative: Lit: light-bright-correct-great. Used to describe someone who acts with complete transparency and moral integrity. 他做事光明正大 "He does things openly and uprightly."

Literal: time flies like an arrow — the days pass with frightening speed
Figurative: 光阴 guāngyīn (time, light-and-shadow) + 似 sì (resembles) + 箭 jiàn (arrow). Time shoots past like a loosed arrow, gone before you can grasp it. Usually paired with its twin 日月如梭 (the sun and moon shuttle by like a weaver's shuttle). 光阴似箭，日月如梭，一晃十年就过去了。
Tags: cosmology nature weather tense aspect time

Literal: bring glory to the clan and illuminate the ancestors
Figurative: 光 (illuminate) + 宗 (clan lineage) + 耀 (cause to shine) + 祖 (ancestors). The foundational aspiration of Chinese family-oriented ambition: achievement is owed to and shared with those who came before. Used sincerely in formal contexts; with ironic distance among younger generations.

Literal: to return to the root and settle the bottom: in the final analysis, when all is said and done
Figurative: Lit: return-root-conclude-bottom. Used to introduce the fundamental point after stripping away the surface: 归根结底，还是钱的问题 "in the end, it still comes down to money." Here 结 carries the settling sense.

Literal: the country is prosperous and the people are at peace
Figurative: The classical blessing for a nation: 泰 tài (great peace) + 民安 (the people are secure). Used in toasts, New Year wishes, and political rhetoric. The Confucian ideal of good governance.

Literal: cross the river, then tear down the bridge
Figurative: A vivid picture of ingratitude: discarding the very means or person that got you across once you are safely over. A sharp accusation in modern speech.

Literal: to roar with laughter: a full belly laugh
Figurative: 哈哈 is the sound of laughter itself, 大笑 a big laugh. The everyday, vivid way to say someone burst out laughing. Common in narration and casual speech alike.

Literal: the sea does not surge — peaceful passage; a stable, unchallenged realm
Figurative: Lit: sea-not-raise-waves. A classical phrase for the ideal of peaceful sea passage , exactly what Mazu provides. Used in Mazu temple inscriptions and ritual prayers.

Literal: till the seas run dry and the rocks crumble: forever, unchanging
Figurative: Lit: sea-dry stone-rot. A vow of eternal constancy, used in oaths of love and loyalty: even when the impossible happens and the ocean dries up, the feeling will not change.

Literal: the sea is wide and the sky is open: boundless; (of talk) freewheeling and unconstrained
Figurative: Lit: sea-wide sky-empty. It paints limitless space, hence both a feeling of total freedom and a way to describe rambling, anything-goes conversation: 海阔天空地聊 "to chat about everything under the sun."

Literal: sea-sized capacity: a vast tolerance or a huge amount
Figurative: 海 hǎi (sea) + 量 liàng (capacity). A capacity as large as the sea. Traditionally a generous compliment for someone of great tolerance, whether a magnanimous temperament (大人有海量, your honor is broad-minded) or a formidable drinking capacity at the table.
Tags: nature geography meaning characters measure-words evaluation

Literal: a horse that harms the herd: one bad apple
Figurative: From the Zhuāngzǐ, where the Yellow Emperor is told to govern by removing whatever harms the herd. Now the person who spoils a group or organization.

Literal: to hold pungency and swallow bitterness: to endure every hardship
Figurative: 茹 (rú) means to eat. Almost always said of parents, especially mothers, who suffer silently for years to raise their children.

Literal: losing your own way while trying to imitate another's — ending up with neither
Figurative: From the Zhuangzi (秋水 chapter). The problem: imitation so total that it erases the imitator's original competence. Used for people who pursue a foreign or fashionable style so completely that they lose their own footing.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms mastery arts aesthetics learning

Literal: cold window, bitter study
Figurative: The archetypal image of examination preparation: the scholar sitting through winter nights by a cold window, studying by lamplight, without heat or comfort.
Tags: history confucianism tang song ming qing

Literal: to sweat the oxen and fill the rafters: a vast number of books
Figurative: Coined by the Tang writer Liǔ Zōngyuán. So many volumes that hauling them makes the oxen sweat and stacking them fills the house to the roofbeams. Praise for a great library or prolific output.

Literal: without the slightest problem; absolutely fine
Figurative: A stronger, more emphatic version of 没问题, using 毫无 ("not the slightest"). It asserts that something is completely fine or certain, with no doubt or difficulty whatever. Common in confident assurances and formal contexts.

Literal: a wise fellow avoids a loss he can plainly see coming
Figurative: Lit: a good-fellow does not eat the loss before his eyes. Folk wisdom that real courage includes the sense to step back from a fight you cannot win, rather than charging in for pride.

Literal: good times don't last — a beautiful scene cannot endure
Figurative: Lit: good-scenery-not-long. An expression of Buddhist impermanence and Chinese realism about fortune. Used when pleasant circumstances are ending or were brief.

Literal: the Song of Good and Done — the vanity of worldly craving
Figurative: The song sung by a tattered Daoist near the start of the novel, teaching that all the things people chase (rank, gold, lovers, children) end in nothing, and that 好 (good) and 了 (finished with, let go of) are ultimately the same.
Tags: literature novels classics classical qing romance

Literal: good things take time — good outcomes require much grinding and effort
Figurative: Lit: good-things-much-grinding. Used to console someone experiencing delays or obstacles on the path to something valuable. The consolation: friction is the price of worth.

Literal: take good care of yourself; do well for yourself
Figurative: A formal farewell or parting injunction: "do well in your own conduct." Can be warm (a mentor to a student) or pointed (a warning to behave). Context determines whether it is affectionate or admonishing.

Literal: to drink the northwest wind: have nothing to eat, go hungry
Figurative: A vivid colloquial idiom: with no food, all you can swallow is the cold wind. Said wryly of poverty or a failed livelihood, "我们都去喝西北风了".

Literal: in keeping with feeling and reason: fair and reasonable
Figurative: Lit: accords-with-feeling, accords-with-reason. Said of a decision or request that satisfies both human sentiment and good sense, so no one can fault it. The doubled 合 stresses that it fits on every count.

Literal: vertical alliance and horizontal linkage — coalition against a dominant power, or accommodation with it
Figurative: The two grand strategic options of the Warring States endgame. Used today in geopolitics, business competition, and organizational dynamics to describe the choice between forming a coalition against a dominant player and making separate deals with it.
Tags: ancient dynasty history philosophy legalism statecraft politics classics

Literal: which way to turn; what course to take
Figurative: Literally "where to go, what to follow", the weighing of a hard choice between paths. A more literary cousin of 怎么办, asking not just "what to do" but "which direction to commit to". Here 何 is the classical "how / what" that 怎么 replaced in everyday speech.

Literal: to soften one's light and share the dust: to blend in and live among ordinary people
Figurative: From the Daoist classics: to dim one's brilliance and mix with the common crowd rather than stand apart. A vision of how the wise move within society, joining its dust instead of towering over it. The ideal of fitting unobtrusively into the social whole.

Literal: harmony brings wealth — a gentle manner attracts prosperity
Figurative: 和气 héqi (harmony of manner; friendliness) + 生 shēng (to generate) + 财 cái (wealth). The principle that amicable dealings create the trust and goodwill that sustain business. Posted in shops across the Chinese-speaking world.

Literal: the lioness of Hedong roars: a fierce, jealous wife
Figurative: From a Song poem by Su Shi teasing his friend Chen Jichang (Chen Zao), whose wife's temper made him quail. 河东 (Hedong) names her clan's home east of the Yellow River. Still used, half teasing, for a domineering spouse.

Literal: the river runs clear and the sea is calm: peace under good rule
Figurative: Since the Yellow River is famously muddy, its running clear is a near-impossible omen of a sage age. Paired with a calm sea, it stands for an era of order and prosperity. Formal, literary register.

Literal: a crane standing among chickens: head and shoulders above the rest
Figurative: The tall white crane towering over a yard of squat fowl. Said of a person whose talent or bearing makes them stand out from an ordinary crowd.

Literal: red-red fire-fire — flourishing, booming, and full of warmth
Figurative: A doubled, emphatic form of 红火. The image is a scene so prosperous and lively it seems to glow like fire.

Literal: red cheeks, thin fate — a beautiful woman is destined for a hard or short life
Figurative: 红颜 hóngyán (rosy cheeks, a beautiful woman) + 薄命 bómìng (thin or meager fate). A fatalistic literary trope: great beauty seems to attract misfortune, and the most celebrated beauties of history met tragic ends. 自古红颜多薄命。

Literal: the Feast at Hong Gate — a banquet set as a trap
Figurative: The Shiji's most famous set-piece: the banquet at which Xiang Yu's faction plotted to kill the future Han founder Liu Bang, where the sword-dance of 项庄 (项庄舞剑) masked an assassination attempt and Liu Bang escaped by a hair.
Tags: classics history han literature ancient biography

Literal: the worry of looking back — concern for what you leave behind; anxiety about what is happening at the rear
Figurative: 后 (behind; the rear) + 顾 (to look back; to attend to) + 之 (classical possessive particle) + 忧 (worry; anxiety).

Literal: the latecomer occupies the top — the newcomer surpasses those who came first
Figurative: 后来 (later arrival) + 居上 (occupies the upper position). From the Shǐjì (史记), the court historian Sima Qian. A newly promoted official sitting above older ministers in court: the latecomer had outranked his seniors.

Literal: the young are to be feared — the next generation will surpass those before them
Figurative: From the Analects of Confucius (论语·子罕): 后生可畏，焉知来者之不如今也？(The young are to be feared , how do we know the ones still to come will not surpass those of today?) 后生 = those born later, the younger generation. 可畏 = worthy of awe, of apprehension.

Literal: profound virtue bears all things; great moral force sustains everything it carries
Figurative: 厚 hòu (thick; deep; generous; substantial) + 德 dé (virtue; moral force) + 载 zài (to carry; to bear; to support) + 物 wù (things; the ten thousand things; all beings).

Literal: to favor the past over the present: to esteem antiquity and slight the modern
Figurative: Literally "thick toward the ancient, thin toward the present." Criticizes the habit of prizing everything old while dismissing the contemporary. Its mirror is 厚今薄古, valuing the present over the past. A pointed term in debates over tradition and modernity.

Literal: fox-friends and dog-companions: a bad crowd
Figurative: Lit: fox-friends, dog-friends. 狐 fox and 狗 dog stand for the sly and the low. The phrase scorns worthless drinking companions and hangers-on, the kind of friends who lead you nowhere good. A parent's word of warning.

Literal: lake light and mountain hues: beautiful lake-and-mountain scenery
Figurative: A set phrase praising scenic landscape, the stock compliment paid to West Lake and its kin.

Literal: the Humen Opium Destruction — Lin Zexu's burning of British opium in 1839
Figurative: Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of 1,200 tons of British-owned opium at Humen (虎门), Guangdong, in June 1839. The act that triggered the First Opium War. Commemorated as a patriotic symbol in Chinese history education. The date (June 26) is marked as China's National Anti-Drug Day (中国禁毒日).

Literal: flowers in full bloom, moon perfectly round — a moment of perfection and happiness
Figurative: The classic wedding blessing and New Year wish. Flowers (spring beauty) + full moon (reunion, completeness) = the ideal of a happy, complete life. Often inscribed on wedding gifts and red envelopes.
Tags: nature culture meaning characters radical poetry time

Literal: flowers red, willows green — a riot of bright spring color
Figurative: 花 huā (flowers) + 红 hóng (red) + 柳 liǔ (willow) + 绿 lǜ (green). A set image of late spring at its most colorful: red blossoms against green willows. By extension it describes anything gaudy and brightly multicolored, sometimes with a faint hint of being overdone. 公园里花红柳绿，游人如织。

Literal: the year of the flowery cycle — age sixty
flower streets and willow lanes: the pleasure quarters
Figurative: A classical euphemism for the red-light district, where 花 (flower) and 柳 (willow) stand for courtesans. Literary and old-fashioned; appears in Ming and Qing fiction.

Literal: when the flower blooms, the Buddha is seen — sudden illumination after patient waiting
Figurative: Originally a Pure Land image (the lotus flower opening in the Pure Land to reveal the practitioner reborn there, seeing Amitābha), adopted by Chan as a metaphor for sudden enlightenment: the moment when all the conditions are right and understanding blooms.
Tags: chan zen meditation pure-land amitabha faith

Literal: flowery words and clever speech: sweet, deceptive talk
Figurative: Lit: flowery-words-clever-speech. Honeyed, ornamented talk meant to flatter or deceive. Here 花 carries its "showy, dressed-up" sense, words made pretty to mislead rather than to tell the truth.

Literal: to turn danger into safety: to avert a crisis; to come through unscathed
Figurative: 化 huà = to transform, 险 xiǎn = danger, peril, 为 wéi = into, 夷 yí = level ground, flatness, safety. Lit: "transform the perilous into the level." Describes turning a dangerous, threatening situation into a safe one, often through skill, calm, or good fortune. 在关键时刻，他冷静地化险为夷。

Literal: turn the whole into pieces — to break something large into small scattered parts
Figurative: 化 (to transform) + 整 (the whole) + 为 (into) + 零 (the scattered pieces). To disperse one large thing into many small ones: a big force split into small units that move unseen, a large task divided into manageable bits, a lump sum paid in installments.

Literal: to draw a cake to ease hunger: to comfort oneself with empty fantasy
Figurative: Lit: draw-cake-fill-hunger. A painted cake feeds no one. The idiom mocks any plan or promise that satisfies in imagination only, offering the picture of a thing in place of the thing itself.

Pinyin: huà hǔ bù chéng fǎn lèi quǎn
Literal: tried to paint a tiger, ended up with a dog
Figurative: Colloquial proverb for the same failure: aiming high, imitating without understanding, producing something worse than the original and worse than doing nothing.

Literal: drawing a dragon and dotting the eye — the small finishing touch that brings the whole alive
Figurative: From a Tang anecdote: the painter Zhang Sengyou painted dragons but refused to add eyes; when pressed, he dotted the eyes of two , and they immediately flew off the wall. The dot is what brings the form to life. Used today for the small but decisive move that makes a piece of work click.
Tags: measure-words time food characters arts calligraphy culture body perception

Literal: Drawing Legs on a Snake
Figurative: He finished first, so he kept drawing, and lost the prize. The idiom for ruining a good thing by overdoing it.

Literal: the talk does not meet: the conversation does not click
Figurative: Lit: words-not-matching-the-moment. Said when two people simply cannot find common ground in conversation. The fuller saying 话不投机半句多 adds that "when talk does not click, even half a sentence is too much."

Literal: there are words within the words: a remark carries a hidden meaning
Figurative: Lit: inside-the-words-there-are-words. Said when someone speaks with an implied second meaning, hinting at more than the surface remark admits.

Literal: to harbor talent yet meet no chance: gifted but unrecognized
Figurative: Lit: cradle-talent-not-encounter. The lament of the able person who never finds a ruler, patron, or era that will use their gifts. A recurring theme in classical poetry, where the unemployed scholar mourns his wasted ability.

Literal: bad people and bad deeds: wrongdoers and their misdeeds
Figurative: A set four-character phrase pairing 坏人 with 坏事, often in the formula 与坏人坏事作斗争, "to struggle against wrongdoers and wrongdoing." Carries a formal, almost official register.

Literal: wild with joy: overjoyed, beside oneself with delight
Figurative: Lit: joy-Heaven-glad-Earth, joy that fills the whole sky and ground. Said of someone bursting with happiness at good news, a reunion, or a festival. 一家人欢天喜地过新年 "the family rang in the New Year overjoyed."

Literal: elated and inspired: filled with joy and high spirits
Figurative: Lit: joyful-glad-drum-dance, so cheered that one beats the drum and dances. Used of a group lifted and energized by good news or a great event, joy that rouses people to action.

Literal: eunuch domination of state power — when palace servants usurp the emperor's authority
Figurative: A recurring theme in Chinese historiography across multiple dynasties, but reaching its most extreme form in the late Ming. 专权 (monopolize power) is always pejorative. The phrase is invoked whenever insiders with access but no mandate accumulate power.

Literal: a friend made in times of hardship — a friend in adversity
Figurative: A friendship forged through shared difficulty, prized in Chinese culture as the truest kind. 患难 huànnàn means hardship and danger; 交 jiāo here is the noun "friendship, bond." The related proverb is 患难见真情 ("adversity reveals true feeling"): you learn who your real friends are when times are hard.

Literal: completely transformed to something new — completely renewed; a total makeover
Figurative: 焕然 (huànrán, resplendently bright; the appearance of something that has been renovated or refreshed) + 一新 (completely new). The appearance of something that has undergone a total transformation: 装修完工后，房间焕然一新 (after the renovation was complete, the room was completely transformed).
Tags: logic cohesion meaning characters adjectives change modern

Literal: imperial relatives and royal in-laws
Figurative: The emperor's kin and the families connected to the throne by marriage, the privileged inner circle of the imperial house. Now used, often with a sardonic edge, for anyone who enjoys protection or privilege through family connections to power.
Tags: vocabulary history emperor imperial statecraft royalty

Literal: suddenly, greatly awakened — the flash of realization
Figurative: 恍然 (in a flash) + 大悟 (great awakening, 悟 being the enlightenment verb of Chan Buddhism and the Monkey King's name 悟空). The eureka moment: the detective's final chapter, the student when the proof clicks. Chinese lets you borrow the vocabulary of enlightenment for algebra.

Literal: turn your head and there is the shore: it is never too late to repent
Figurative: Lit: turn-the-head-is-shore. From the Buddhist 苦海无边，回头是岸 ("the sea of suffering is boundless; turn back and the shore is there"). To stop a wrong course and come back is itself salvation.

Literal: to turn the heart and shift the will: to change one's mind, to relent
Figurative: Lit: turn-heart-shift-intent. Said of someone who softens, reconsiders, or comes back to a relationship or decision they had set aside.

Literal: painting both sound and color: vivid and lifelike (of a description)
Figurative: Lit: paint-sound-paint-color. Of telling or describing something so vividly that the listener seems to hear and see it. High praise for a gripping, animated account.

Literal: seamlessly whole as if formed by nature: without a trace of artifice
Figurative: Lit: wholly-so-Heaven-made. Praises a work of art or writing so unified that it seems made by nature rather than by human hands, with no visible seams or effort. 浑然 means "in one undivided whole."

Literal: alive and bouncing about: brimming with health and energy
Figurative: Lit: alive-leaping-wildly-jumping. The image of a fish on the deck or a healthy child who cannot keep still. Used for someone bursting with vitality, often after recovering from illness.

Pinyin: huó dào lǎo, xué dào lǎo
Literal: live until old, learn until old — lifelong learning
Figurative: The most common proverb for lifelong learning: you learn for as long as you live. An encouragement to keep studying at any age, and a gentle reminder that no one has ever learned enough to stop. Equivalent in spirit to the English "you're never too old to learn."

Literal: vivid and lifelike: so vivid it seems to come alive before you
Figurative: Lit: alive-spirit-alive-appearing, with 活 doubled for emphasis. Describes a story, performance, or portrait so vivid and animated that the thing depicted seems present in the room. High praise for vividness.

Literal: to add oil to the fire — to make a bad situation worse
Figurative: Lit: fire-above-add-oil. The Chinese equivalent of "adding fuel to the fire." 你别火上加油了 "Don't make things worse." The equivalent English idiom "add fuel to the fire" has exactly the same logic.

Literal: fiery golden eyes — seeing through deception
Figurative: The Monkey King's eyes, hardened in the furnace of the Daoist god Laojun, that let him see through every demon's disguise to the true form beneath. The chengyu now means sharp, penetrating discernment, the ability to see through falsehood and recognise the real nature of a person or situation.
Tags: literature novels classics classical buddhism pilgrimage

Literal: genuine goods at a fair price: the real thing, no fakery
Figurative: Lit: goods-genuine-price-real. A merchant's pledge that the wares are authentic and honestly priced. By extension it certifies anything as the genuine article, not a counterfeit or an exaggeration.

Literal: to pick bones out of an egg: to nitpick, to find fault where there is none
Figurative: A vivid colloquial saying: an egg has no bones, so hunting for one means inventing flaws. Used of a critic or boss who complains about everything.

Literal: the hen flies off and the eggs break: to lose everything, ending up empty-handed
Figurative: A botched scheme where both the chicken and its eggs are lost. Said when an attempt to grab more leaves you with nothing at all.

Literal: chickens fly and dogs leap: utter chaos and uproar
Figurative: A farmyard thrown into panic, hens flapping and dogs bolting. Describes a household or scene in total disorder. Lively and colloquial.

Literal: chicken feathers and garlic skins: trivial, petty matters
Figurative: The kitchen sweepings nobody bothers with. Used to dismiss a quarrel or complaint as not worth the fuss: 别为这点鸡毛蒜皮的事吵架.

Literal: errors accumulated until they harden into accepted norm
Figurative: Lit: accumulate-wrong-become-right. When a mistake or deviation is repeated so long it calcifies into convention. Applied in linguistics (describing language change), ethics, and institutional analysis. A cautionary concept: not all norms are correct simply because they persist.

Literal: accumulated slander dissolves bones
Figurative: From the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian): repeated criticism, even if each instance is minor, accumulates into something that can destroy a person entirely. This is the specific personal consequence that Pang Cong feared, and that happened to him.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms logic rhetoric communication media society

Literal: accumulate goodness, achieve virtue — individual good acts build character over time
Figurative: From Xunzi (荀子): 积土成山…积善成德，而神明自得，圣心备焉。 "Pile earth to make a mountain; accumulate goodness to achieve virtue, and the divine intelligence arrives of itself, the sage's mind becomes complete." Virtue on this account is a slow deposit, not a bolt of insight.
Tags: ethics virtue confucianism human-nature philosophy buddhism taoism

Literal: accumulate the few and it becomes the many
Figurative: The thrift-and-study chengyu: small savings, daily vocabulary reviews, and minor improvements compound. The financial-app era has given it a second life in savings-product marketing, and teachers deploy it against the student who dismisses ten minutes of practice as pointless.

Literal: to pass the exam and make a name: to win rank and renown at once
Figurative: Lit: reach-rank-become-famous. The double prize of the imperial scholar, to place in the examination and so earn lasting reputation. The dream that drove generations of candidates to the 科举.

Literal: eager for quick merit and near-term gain: shortsighted opportunism
Figurative: Lit: anxious-merit-near-profit. A criticism of those who chase immediate results and quick profit at the expense of long-term, sustainable success. The opposite of the 功夫 ethic of patient, foundational effort.
Tags: mastery ability evaluation characters emotion feeling

Literal: urgent as a shooting star — desperately urgent
Figurative: Lit: urgent-like-shooting-star-fire. A shooting star (流星) appears briefly and is gone: something that needs to be acted on instantly before the moment passes. Used in military dispatches and urgent appeals.

Literal: wisdom born from urgency — a bright idea in a crisis; thinking fast under pressure
Figurative: 急 jí (urgent; pressed; crisis) + 中 zhōng (within; in the midst of) + 生 shēng (to be born; to arise) + 智 zhì (wisdom; clever idea). The intelligence that surfaces specifically when there is no time to think: the flash of insight that saves a situation.
Tags: emotion feeling characters confucianism ethics virtue philosophy buddhism

Pinyin: jǐ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén
Literal: do not impose on others what you yourself do not want — the Silver Rule
Figurative: Analects 15.24. Confucius called this 恕 shù (reciprocity, forgiveness), the negative formulation of the Golden Rule. One of the most famous sentences in Chinese. Appears in the UN Declaration of Human Rights as a cross-cultural parallel. 己 = oneself; 施 = to impose/apply; 于人 = onto others.
Tags: grammar classical syntax passive literary particles confucianism analects ritual ethics

Pinyin: jǐ suǒ bù yù, wù shī yú rén.
Literal: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
Figurative: Appears twice in the Analects (12.2, 15.24) as the Confucian formulation of the negative Golden Rule. Called the doctrine of 恕 shù (sympathetic understanding). This formulation was inscribed on the UNESCO building in Paris as one of humanity's foundational ethical principles.

Literal: the memory is still fresh: as vivid as if it just happened
Figurative: Lit: memory-still-new. Said of an event or scene one recalls so clearly that time seems not to have dulled it. 至今记忆犹新 "to this day it remains fresh in my mind."

Pinyin: jì shēng yú, hé shēng liàng?
Literal: Since you bore Zhou Yu, why also bear Zhuge Liang?
Figurative: The dying lament attributed to the Wu commander 周瑜 Zhou Yu, repeatedly outmatched by his rival Zhuge Liang.
Tags: history dynasty han statecraft strategy classical

Literal: an everyday home meal: a common, unremarkable occurrence
Figurative: Lit: home-ordinary-simple-meal. Literally plain home cooking, used figuratively for anything that happens so routinely it is no big deal: 加班对他来说是家常便饭 "working late is routine for him."

Literal: home with only four walls — extreme poverty; owning nothing
Figurative: Lit: home-merely-four-walls. 徒 = only; merely; bare. The household contains nothing but the four walls themselves. Used in literature to describe destitution. Often contrasted with 家财万贯 jiācái wànguàn (immense family wealth). A stock phrase for total financial ruin.

Literal: known to every household — a household name; universally known
Figurative: Lit: family-understood-household-known. 喻 = understood; 晓 = known; aware. Every family understands it; every household knows it. 这首歌已经家喻户晓了。(This song is now known to everyone.) The go-to phrase for "universally famous" in Chinese.

Literal: worth a string of cities: of immense value
Figurative: From the Warring States tale of the 和氏璧 jade, which King Zhao of Qin offered fifteen cities to obtain. To be worth 连城 is to command a value beyond ordinary reckoning.

Literal: firm and unshakable
Figurative: Literally "firm and settled, not shifting", steadfast in resolve, never wavering. The 定 ("settled, fixed") at its heart is the same 定 in 一定; here it describes a will that has fixed on its course. The deepest form of the resolve 一定要 voices.

Literal: the gap admits not a hair: a situation of extreme danger or urgency
Figurative: Lit: the-gap-does-not-allow-a-hair. The interval is so narrow not even a single hair could fit, so the margin for error is none at all. Here 间 takes the jiān reading for the gap itself.

Literal: love all under Heaven impartially — the Mohist manifesto in four characters
Figurative: 兼 jiān (jointly; all together) + 爱 ài (love) + 天下 tiānxià (all under Heaven; the world). The compressed statement of Mozi's central ethical position: love extended equally to every person without gradation by family, state, or social proximity.
Tags: mohism universal-love philosophy history classical ethics virtue confucianism statecraft ancient

Literal: to study and refine through relentless, focused effort
Figurative: From the Zhanguo Ce account of Su Qin reading until he was exhausted, jabbing his own thigh with an awl to stay awake. 练 carries the sense of working material over and over until it is honed.

Literal: simple, clear, and gripping the essentials: succinct and pointed
Figurative: 简 simple, 明 clear, 扼要 to grip the crux. Common in formal evaluation of summaries and briefings, marking a text that wastes no words.

Literal: to see someone dying and not save them
Figurative: The harshest social indictment in the 救 family: standing by while another perishes. Used today to condemn indifference, whether a bystander ignoring an accident or an institution refusing aid.

Literal: to be laughed at: forgive my poor effort
Figurative: Lit: be-seen laughed-at. A set humble phrase: 让您见笑了 ("I've let you laugh at me") deflects praise for one's own work or skill. Polite, slightly formal register.

Literal: see righteousness and act with courage — to step up when others need help
Figurative: 见 jiàn (to see; to perceive) + 义 yì (righteous action; what is right) + 勇 yǒng (courage; bravery) + 为 wéi (to do; to act). From the Analects (论语): 见义不为，无勇也 , "To see what is right and not do it is a want of courage" (Confucius, 2.24).

Literal: a wandering swindler, a roving con artist
Figurative: The 江湖 of itinerant healers and fortune-tellers turned into a label for a charlatan who works the crowds.
Tags: nature settlement characters wuxia culture society

Literal: Jiang's talent is exhausted — creative powers have run dry; the burnt-out genius
Figurative: From the Southern Qi dynasty writer Jiang Yan (江淹), famed for his prose, who stopped producing good work later in life. Legend says he dreamed that a man demanded his writing brush back; after that, his talent was gone. 他感觉自己江郎才尽了。

Literal: rivers and mountains like a painting; the land is breathtakingly beautiful
Figurative: From Su Shi's 念奴娇·赤壁怀古 (Remembering Chibi, to the tune of Nian Nu Jiao), written in 1082 at the site of the famous Three Kingdoms battle. 江山如画，一时多少豪杰 (the rivers and mountains like a painting , how many heroes in that one moment).

Literal: the rivers, mountains, and altars of soil and grain: the whole realm, the state
Figurative: Literally "rivers and mountains, the altars of soil and grain." 江山 the land and 社稷 the altars together name the entire country a ruler holds in trust. A grand, classical phrase for the state as a whole, the territory and the legitimacy that come with it.

Pinyin: jiāngshān yì gǎi, běnxìng nán yí
Literal: easy to change the landscape, hard to change one's nature; a leopard can't change its spots
Figurative: The full proverb. 易 yì (easy) + 改 gǎi (to change; to alter) / 难 nán (difficult) + 移 yí (to shift; to move; to transplant). The contrast is between the external world , rivers and mountains, the landscape of history , and the internal: 本性, innate character, the temperament you were born with.
Tags: human-nature identity mind characters history politics geography

Pinyin: jiāng shān yì gǎi běn xìng nán yí
Literal: territory is easy to change; fundamental nature is hard to move — a leopard cannot change its spots
Figurative: Classic proverb about human nature used in resignation or rueful acknowledgment. 他就是这样的人，江山易改本性难移。(He's just that kind of person; a leopard can't change its spots.) Often invoked by someone who has tried to change another person and given up.

Literal: to take the mistake and run with it: to leave a wrong thing as it is
Figurative: Lit: take-the-error-go-with-the-error. Rather than undo a mistake already made, one accepts it and proceeds on that footing, often because correcting it would cost more than living with it.

Literal: heads together, ears joined: to whisper privately
Figurative: Two people lean in until one mouth nearly touches the other's ear. The image of leaning close to murmur in secret, often disapproving when done during a meeting or class.

Literal: feet planted on solid ground: down-to-earth, steady and practical
Figurative: Lit: feet-tread-solid-ground. High praise for someone who works steadily and realistically rather than chasing empty schemes. The 实 here is the solid earth underfoot.
Tags: nature geography meaning evaluation quality characters

Pinyin: jiào wǒ rúhé bù xiǎng tā
Literal: How could I not think of her — Liu Bannong's 1920 poem, set to music by Zhao Yuanren
Figurative: Not classical, but the most famous early appearance of 她 in print. The poem is addressed to "her", variously read as a lover, the homeland (Liu was abroad in Britain when he wrote it), or both. The song became one of the defining works of early modern Chinese music.

Literal: teaching and learning grow each other: the teacher learns by teaching
Figurative: Lit: teach-learn-mutually-grow. From the Liji (Record of Rites). Teaching exposes what the teacher does not yet understand, so instructing others deepens one's own knowledge; the two advance together.

Literal: all are greatly delighted — everyone ends up happy
Figurative: Originally the closing formula of Buddhist sutras, where the assembly rejoices at the teaching and departs; now the phrase for win-win endings, amicable settlements, and comedies. It is also the standard Chinese title of Shakespeare's As You Like It, a translation with better provenance than most.
Tags: emotion culture characters feeling family spoken daily-life

Literal: one after another: coming in quick succession
Figurative: Literally "joining the second, linking the third," counting events as they pile up. Describes things happening in rapid, repeated succession, most often a run of incidents or problems: 接二连三地出事 (one mishap after another).
Tags: motion connections daily-life characters cohesion even

Literal: linked and unbroken: continuous, without interruption
Figurative: 接连 doubles the sense of joining; 不断 says the chain never breaks. Describes rain, applause, or news that keeps coming.

Literal: to raise a pole and rise up — to start a popular rebellion
Figurative: 揭 (raise, lift) + 竿 (pole, bamboo staff) + 而起 (and rise up). The idiom originates in the Qin dynasty collapse (221–206 BCE), when the rebel leader Chen Sheng reportedly rallied followers with nothing but a raised pole: no weapons, no banners, no organization, just the act of standing up.

Literal: street talk and lane discussion: common gossip, popular chatter
Figurative: The talk of the town, idle public discussion of an affair. Carries a faintly dismissive tone, the chatter of ordinary streets as opposed to considered opinion.

Literal: street corners and lane ends: all about town, on everyone's lips
Figurative: Names the public places where people gather and gossip. Often used of news or rumor that has spread everywhere: 这件事在街头巷尾传开了, the story spread to every corner of town.

Literal: rising section by section — steady, continuous increase
Figurative: 节 jié = section; segment; node. Each node advances the rise. Used for prices, temperatures, performance metrics, or any quantity that climbs steadily over time. Common in economic and news reporting.

Literal: a branch sprouts from the joint: new complications arise unexpectedly
Figurative: Lit: joint-outside-grow-branch. A side branch springs from the node of a stalk where none was wanted. Said when an already settled matter throws up fresh, unwelcome problems.

Literal: to scrimp on clothes and food: to live frugally and pinch every penny
Figurative: Lit: economize-clothing-cut-back-food. To deny oneself even basics in order to save, said of those who tighten the belt hard, often to support a family or reach a goal.

Literal: to knot grass and carry rings: to repay a kindness, even after death
Figurative: Lit: tie-grass-hold-ring. From two old tales of gratitude: a ghost knotted grass to trip an enemy and save his benefactor, and a magpie brought jade rings to repay a rescuer. Together they stand for never forgetting a debt of kindness.

Literal: deep sisterly affection
Figurative: A common modern four-character set phrase for the strong bond between sisters or close female friends. Frequent in titles, toasts, and warm descriptions of female friendship.

Literal: borrow a knife to kill a man: destroy a rival by another's hand
Figurative: The third of the Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六计). You stay clean while a third party does the deed; still vivid in business and political commentary today.

Literal: borrow the wind to sail the boat: turn outside conditions to your own ends
Figurative: A close cousin of 顺水推船, stressing the borrowed force: you let someone else's momentum carry your own plan forward.

Literal: use the past to satirize the present
Figurative: A classic mode of Chinese writing: cloak criticism of present rulers in a story about an ancient dynasty. Long the safest way to speak truth to power.

Literal: to offer flowers borrowed from another — presenting something that isn't yours
Figurative: Used with self-deprecating humor when giving a gift that wasn't originally yours , passing along a recommendation, re-gifting, or presenting another person's work as an offering. The image: lacking flowers of your own to offer at the Buddhist altar, you borrow someone else's.
Tags: religion buddhism culture social daily-life characters transmission history

Literal: seize on a topic to make a wider point: use a pretext to vent
Figurative: Literally "borrow the subject to elaborate." Common for someone who turns a small matter into a platform for a bigger grievance.

Pinyin: jīn guó bù ràng xū méi
Literal: the woman's headdress yields nothing to the man's beard — a woman who is the equal of any man
Figurative: 巾帼 jīnguó , a woman's hair ornament, by metonymy "woman." 须眉 xūméi: beard and brows, by metonymy "man." Used in praise of female generals (Mulan, Hua Mulan; Liang Hongyu), athletes, and accomplished women.

Literal: heroine — a woman of exceptional courage and achievement
Figurative: Lit: kerchief-hood hero. 巾帼 jīnguó is the traditional women's headdress, used by extension to mean women collectively. A 巾帼英雄 is a female hero, a woman who has achieved what is extraordinary even by the standards of men. Hua Mulan 花木兰 is the archetype. Used to praise exceptional women in any field.

Literal: the present cannot compare with the past
Figurative: Literally "today is not what the past compared to," meaning things have changed greatly, usually for the better, so that now far surpasses before. 今 (now) versus 昔 (former times). A common way to mark dramatic progress or transformation.

Literal: one's name inscribed on the golden list — exam success
Figurative: The 金榜 was the yellow placard of palace-exam graduates posted outside the examination compound. Classical culture counted it among life's four great joys, alongside the wedding night, rain after drought, and meeting an old friend far from home. Today it captions every gaokao congratulations post.
Tags: history confucianism tang song ming qing learning daily-life culture vocabulary

Literal: to keep a beauty in a golden house — to keep a mistress in luxury
Figurative: From a Han dynasty story: Emperor Wu as a child said he would build a golden house for the girl Ah Jiao (阿娇) if she became his wife. Now means to keep a mistress in a secret dwelling. A literary idiom that appears in Tang poetry and classical fiction.

Pinyin: jīn wú zú chì, rén wú wán rén
Literal: no gold is pure, no person is perfect
Figurative: Pure 24-karat gold is too soft to be durable; impurity is what makes gold useful. The proverb uses this fact to excuse human flaws: perfection is neither achievable nor desirable. Used to express tolerance of others' shortcomings.

Literal: words of gold and jade — invaluable advice
Figurative: Lit: gold-jade-fine-words. Used to praise someone's counsel or wisdom. "Your words are truly 金玉良言" = "That is genuinely valuable advice." The pairing of gold and jade 金玉 represents the two most precious materials.
Tags: nature radical wuxing culture virtue confucianism aesthetics royalty classical

Literal: do what you can as a human, then accept Heaven's decree
Figurative: The natural paired response to 事与愿违. Where 事与愿违 names the gap between intention and outcome, this phrase names the correct attitude toward that gap: maximum effort, then acceptance of what lies beyond one's control. The two phrases together describe the full Confucian-Daoist response to adversity.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy fate daily-life pragmatics colloquial

Literal: utterly good and utterly beautiful — perfection achieved
Figurative: Confucius used this phrase to evaluate music: the highest praise for something that excels in both moral virtue and aesthetic form. Used today for flawless work, ideal relationships, and perfect events.

Literal: tight gongs and dense drums: intense, busy preparation
Figurative: From the loud, crowded percussion that builds before an opera's climax. Modern usage describes a project being driven forward at full, urgent pace behind the scenes.

Literal: a crucial, critical juncture
Figurative: The pivotal moment when everything hangs in the balance. Common in news and narrative for the turning point of a crisis or contest.

Literal: adding flowers on top of brocade — making something excellent even better
Figurative: Brocade (锦 jǐn) is already the finest silk, already decorated with woven patterns. Adding flowers on top of it is a gift that was not needed but is delightful. Contrasted with 雪中送炭 (sending coal in the snow), helping someone in genuine need. 锦上添花 is the luxury gesture; 雪中送炭 is the necessary one.
Tags: nature culture meaning characters direction grammar motion

Pinyin: jìn zhū zhě chì, jìn mò zhě hēi
Literal: those near red become red; those near ink become black — environment shapes character
Figurative: Two parallel 者 constructions: 近朱者 = the one(s) near vermilion / 近墨者 = the one(s) near ink. The argument is that proximity to good or bad influences changes a person's nature, just as a white object held near ink absorbs its color.
Tags: direction geography daily-life history grammar classical syntax literary compounds

Pinyin: jìn zhū zhě chì, jìn mò zhě hēi
Literal: near vermilion turns red, near ink turns black — you become like the company you keep
Figurative: 近 jìn (close to) + 朱 zhū (vermilion) + 者 zhě (one who) + 赤 chì (red); 近 + 墨 mò (ink) + 者 + 黑 (black). Whoever stays near red dye turns red; whoever stays near ink turns black. A classic statement that environment and company shape character, attributed to the Jin-dynasty writer Fu Xuan 傅玄.

Literal: hard to advance and hard to retreat: caught in a dilemma
Figurative: Lit: advance-retreat-both-hard. To be stuck where neither going forward nor falling back will do, the classic no-win bind. The 进 / 退 pairing makes the trap vivid.

Literal: to endure long without fading: standing the test of time
Figurative: Lit: pass-through long, not declining. Said of a song, a brand, a custom, or a reputation that stays popular and vigorous over many years rather than fading away.

Literal: the startled spirit has not yet settled: still shaken after a fright
Figurative: Lit: startled-soul-not-yet-settled. Describes someone whose nerves are still rattled in the aftermath of a shock or narrow escape, the heart not yet returned to rest.

Literal: startling heaven, shaking earth — earth-shaking; of tremendous power or significance
Figurative: 惊 jīng (to startle; to alarm) + 动 dòng (to move; to shake). When something is so significant that heaven is startled and earth trembles, the hyperbole names genuine magnitude. Used for historic events, monumental achievements, and powerful works. 他们完成了一项惊天动地的壮举。
Tags: movement motion energy characters cosmology taoism philosophy nature heaven classical existence

Literal: diligent and careful in one's work
Figurative: A phrase of high praise for someone who does their work with constant care and seriousness, never cutting corners. 兢兢 conveys cautious diligence; 业业 the steady attention to one's 业 (work, duties). Common in performance reviews and tributes, the model of the conscientious worker.
Tags: society commerce industry education vocabulary daily-life communication

Literal: to unite with wholehearted sincerity: to stand together in good faith
Figurative: Lit: pure-sincere-unite. A call for a group to bond in genuine, undivided solidarity rather than in mere appearance. 结 here is the uniting sense, the bond made fast among people.

Literal: serve the country with utmost loyalty — the supreme patriotic commitment
Figurative: The four characters said to have been tattooed on Yue Fei's back by his mother (精忠 = utmost loyalty; 报国 = repay/serve the country). Whether the tattooing story is historical or legendary, the phrase became the supreme expression of Chinese patriotic loyalty.
Tags: politics society culture song economy innovation

Literal: to revere ancestors and honor the lineage
Figurative: A set phrase expressing the core ethic of ancestor veneration: to show reverence (敬 jìng) to direct ancestors (祖) and to honor the lineage (宗) as a whole. Used in ritual speeches, genealogy prefaces, and New Year ancestral hall ceremonies.

Literal: the Jingkang Humiliation — national shame that demands redemption
Figurative: The capture of the Song imperial family by the Jurchen Jin dynasty in 1127 CE. Invoked by Yue Fei and every subsequent patriot as the wound that must be avenged. Still appears in modern Chinese political rhetoric when national pride or territorial integrity is at stake.

Literal: the eighty-one tribulations — a long sequence of trials that must all be passed
Figurative: From 西游记: the pilgrims must survive exactly eighty-one ordeals (九九, "nine nines," a number of completeness) before the scriptures can be won.
Tags: history tang buddhism pilgrimage translation silk-road biography

Literal: one hair from nine oxen — a trifling amount; a drop in the bucket
Figurative: 九牛 (nine oxen) and 一毛 (a single hair). A lone hair plucked from nine whole oxen is utterly negligible against the mass it comes from. The phrase comes from Sima Qian, who wrote that his own death would weigh on the world no more than one hair lost from nine oxen.
Tags: cosmology culture language nature food characters

Literal: nine deaths, one life — a narrow escape from death; surviving against all odds
Figurative: 九死 (nine chances of death) against 一生 (one chance of life). To come through a danger in which the odds of dying were nine to one, a hair's-breadth survival. Used of soldiers, explorers, and patients who pull through against overwhelming odds: 九死一生，终于活了下来.

Literal: beyond the ninth heaven and the clouds — utterly out of mind; flung far away
Figurative: 九霄 (the ninefold heaven, the top of the sky) plus 云外 (beyond the clouds). To cast something to the ninth heaven and past the clouds is to banish it completely from thought: 把承诺忘到九霄云外 (to forget a promise entirely).

Literal: long illness makes the patient a doctor
Figurative: Chronic experience becomes expertise. Said of patients who know their condition better than junior doctors, and by extension of anyone whose long exposure to a problem has made them its reluctant expert: the veteran user who knows the software's bugs better than the developers.

Literal: the old departs, the new arrives — natural renewal and change
Figurative: 旧 jiù (old; worn; the previous) + 去 qù (departs) + 新 xīn (new) + 来 lái (arrives). The cycle of replacement: what has aged goes away, what is fresh comes in. Used for seasons (winter's cold 去, spring 来), generations, technologies, fashions.

Literal: to bring up an old matter again: to reopen a settled affair
Figurative: Lit: old-matter-again-raise. The chóng reading, again. Said when someone dredges up a past issue better left closed.

Literal: to relieve suffering and rescue from peril
Figurative: A Buddhist phrase, the standing epithet of the bodhisattva 观音 (Guānyīn), 救苦救难 (one who relieves the suffering and saves from calamity). Now also figurative for any savior figure.

Literal: save the dying, aid the wounded
Figurative: 救 (save) the 死 (dying), 扶 (support) the 伤 (wounded). The classic motto of medicine and the Red Cross spirit, naming the doctor's and rescuer's duty in four characters.

Literal: to use local materials; to make do with what is immediately available
Figurative: Lit: just-ground-take-materials. 就地 = "right here on the spot" (from 就 = to approach what is near). 取材 = to gather materials. The idiom celebrates resourcefulness , using what is immediately at hand rather than waiting for something better. The 就 captures the "readiness without delay" quality.

Literal: dwelling in safety, think of danger: stay alert in good times
Figurative: From the Zuǒ Zhuàn. The classic counsel of prudent statecraft: when secure, prepare for the threat that has not yet come. A staple of formal and editorial Chinese.

Literal: to hold a chess piece without setting it down: to hesitate and waver
Figurative: Lit: raise-chesspiece-not-settle. The image of a player holding a piece in the air, unable to commit to a move. Said of anyone caught in indecision who cannot fix on a choice.

Literal: world-famous: renowned throughout the whole world
Figurative: Lit: the whole world has heard the name. 举世 means the entire world taken together, 闻名 means to be known by name. Said of a person, place, or work whose fame reaches everywhere, as in the Great Wall or a celebrated master.

Pinyin: jǔ tóu sān chǐ yǒu shénmíng
Literal: three feet above your head there are divine spirits — you are always watched
Figurative: A foundational folk-religion moral warning: the gods are always observing human conduct; no action goes unseen. Functionally identical to the Western "God is watching." Used to caution against wrongdoing, especially in private. The full proverb: 举头三尺有神明，不畏人知畏己知。

Literal: to argue strongly on principle: to stand on reason and contend hard for it
Figurative: Lit: rely-on-principle-strongly-contend. To take one's stand on what is right and fight for it in argument, not backing down so long as reason is on your side.

Literal: the exemplary person is not a vessel
Figurative: Confucius says the junzi is not a utensil: not defined by function, not limited to one use. The Analects' argument against reducing a person to their usefulness.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms confucianism confucius analects virtue ethics education philosophy

Literal: the friendship of noble people: plain as water, lasting and unselfish
Figurative: Lit: noble-person's friendship. From the saying 君子之交淡如水, "the friendship of the noble is bland as water," meaning a true bond needs no flattery or gifts and so never sours.

Literal: to enlighten the people; to awaken popular wisdom and intelligence
Figurative: 开启 kāiqǐ (to open; to initiate; to unlock) + 民 mín (the people; the populace) + 智 zhì (wisdom; intelligence; discernment).

Literal: to split open heaven and cleave earth — to create the world; a groundbreaking, unprecedented achievement
Figurative: From the Pangu myth (盘古 Pángǔ). In the beginning, all was 混沌 hùndùn: undifferentiated chaos. Pangu broke it open. The light, clear elements rose and became Heaven; the heavy, turbid elements sank and became Earth. Pangu stood between them for 18,000 years until the separation was permanent.
Tags: cosmology taoism philosophy nature heaven classical existence

Literal: the Glorious Era of Kaiyuan — the High Tang at its zenith
Figurative: The reign-era name 开元 (713–741 CE) under Emperor Xuanzong gave its name to the period of Tang's greatest cultural and economic flourishing. Population reached approximately 50 million; the examination system produced its greatest talents; Chang'an was at its most cosmopolitan.

Literal: open up the source and restrain the flow: increase income and curb spending
Figurative: Lit: open-source-restrain-flow. The classic principle of sound finance: widen what comes in while narrowing what goes out. Applied to household budgets, companies, and the state alike.

Literal: the flourishing era of Kangxi and Qianlong — the Qing golden age
Figurative: The compound reign-name shorthand 康乾 (Kangxi-Qianlong) with 盛世 (flourishing era, golden age).

Literal: the imperial examination system
Figurative: The system of selecting officials by competitive written examination, which the Sui began and later dynasties developed into the central institution of Chinese government.
Tags: history confucianism tang song ming qing dynasty unification statecraft classical yuan mongol kublai ritual ethics learning daily-life culture vocabulary classics philosophy literature analects confucius

Literal: worthy of song and worthy of tears — so moving as to deserve both celebration and mourning
Figurative: 可 + 歌 (to sing) + 可 + 泣 (to weep). Used for heroic, sacrificial stories: deeds of such weight they call for both elegy and lament. 革命先烈的事迹可歌可泣。(The deeds of the revolutionary martyrs are worthy of song and tears.) High formal register.
Tags: grammar modal ability permission classical syntax

Literal: can be seen but not reached — within sight but out of grasp
Figurative: 可望 (can be hoped for/seen) + 不可即 (cannot be approached). Used for goals, dreams, and people that seem close but remain permanently out of reach. Often carries a wistful rather than bitter tone.
Tags: grammar modal ability permission classical syntax

Literal: overcome the self, return to rites — the Confucian definition of humaneness
Figurative: From Analects 12.1: 克己复礼为仁. "To overcome the self and return to rites is to achieve 仁." One of the foundational statements of Confucian ethics. The phrase is quoted whenever the relationship between self-discipline and social form is under discussion.

Literal: Carving the Boat to Find the Sword
Figurative: He marked the boat where his sword fell into the river. When the boat reached the shore, he dived where the mark was.

Literal: the Empty Fort Strategy — bluffing strength from weakness
Figurative: Zhuge Liang, holding an undefended town against a vastly superior army, flings the gates open and sits calmly playing the zither on the wall. The enemy commander, certain so bold a display must conceal an ambush, retreats.
Tags: literature novels classics classical history strategy

Literal: empty before, cut off behind — unprecedented and unrepeated; without equal in all of history
Figurative: 空 kōng (empty; void) + 前 (before; the past) + 绝 jué (cut off; without) + 后 (after; the future). Nothing like it has existed in the past (the front is empty of precedent) and nothing like it will exist in the future (the back is cut off from repetition).

Literal: the mouth says yes but the heart says no — saying one thing while thinking another
Figurative: Lit: mouth-yes-heart-no. The classic expression for hypocrisy or false agreement: when outward words and inner feelings are opposites. Used for people who agree to your face while disagreeing inside, or who say what they think you want to hear rather than what they actually believe.

Literal: bitterness ends, sweetness comes: hardship gives way to better days
Figurative: 苦 (bitter) and 甘 (sweet) frame a full turn of fortune. The standard consolation offered to anyone enduring a long hard stretch; the reward is built into the saying.

Literal: bitter mouth, grandmotherly heart: to urge earnestly and patiently
Figurative: Describes someone who repeats hard advice tirelessly out of genuine care, the way an old woman nags her grandchild for their own good.

Literal: to span seas and cross oceans — to travel vast distances
Figurative: A modern four-character compound that pairs 跨 and 越 in parallel slots: exactly the kind of construction Chinese loves. Used for international trade, transcontinental travel, or any long voyage. Not classical, but stylistically formal enough to appear in policy speeches and ceremonial writing.

Literal: to mount one's horse and lift one's blade — to ride out armed and ready
Figurative: A four-character battle-formula common in classical novels and modern wuxia. The image is a general or knight-errant hoisting himself astride his horse with weapon drawn: the moment of departure for combat.

Literal: crossing fiscal years — spanning more than one annual cycle
Figurative: Bureaucratic and accounting vocabulary, not classical, but ubiquitous in modern policy and business documents. 跨年度项目 (a project spanning fiscal years), 跨年度预算 (multi-year budget). Useful as a tag of how 跨 has migrated from the body's stride into the calendar's accounting.

Literal: whip a fast horse — press on faster when already moving well
Figurative: Lit: fast-horse-add-whip. The image is of a courier or cavalry rider who is already galloping but spurs the horse harder anyway. Metaphorically: when momentum is good, don't coast. Used to encourage continued effort or accelerated progress, often in workplace or project contexts.

Literal: a cornered beast still fights: desperate last-ditch resistance
Figurative: From the Zuǒ Zhuàn. A trapped animal will fight on even with no hope, so the phrase warns that a cornered opponent is dangerous. Used of enemies making a final stand.

Literal: to learn through hardship and act through effort
Figurative: From the Zhōngyōng (Doctrine of the Mean). Knowledge won the hard way, by struggle, and conduct sustained by force of will. Praises perseverance over native talent.

Literal: to have enough time; to make it in time
Figurative: A potential complement construction: 来 (come/arrive) + 得 + 及 (reach in time). The negative 来不及 is one of the highest-frequency colloquial expressions. 来不及了！ "There's no time!" Both forms exemplify the potential complement use of 得/不.

Literal: of unknown origin: provenance unclear, background not established
Figurative: 来历 láilì = origin, background, where something or someone came from (历 here is the path-walked-through that produced the present state); 不明 bù míng = not clear. Said of a person whose background cannot be verified, or an object whose provenance is suspect. It carries a note of suspicion.

Literal: coming and going as one pleases — complete freedom of movement; unhindered
Figurative: 来去 (coming and going, the full freedom of movement) + 自如 (naturally; freely; as one wishes). The ideal of total freedom: moving in any direction without restriction or obstacle.

Literal: the days to come are still long — there is still much time ahead
Figurative: 来日 = the coming days, the future (days that come toward us). 方长 = just beginning to be long. A comfort phrase: things not accomplished now can still be done; relationships not deepened yet have time. 我们来日方长，不必着急 "We still have plenty of time ahead , no need to rush."
Tags: direction motion grammar complement tense aspect time

Literal: turn no one away; welcome all comers; refuse nothing that comes
Figurative: 来者 = those who come + 不拒 = do not refuse. Originally a statement of generous hospitality or all-accepting policy. Used in commercial contexts (a shop that accepts all customers), in descriptions of a person with an open-door policy, and ironically for someone who takes on too much work.
Tags: direction motion grammar complement classical syntax literary compounds

Literal: faking the yu-pipe to fill out the ensemble — an impostor padding the numbers
