Literal: to achieve one's wish; things went as hoped
Figurative: The positive counterpart: wishes fulfilled, intention and outcome aligned. 如愿以偿 and 事与愿违 are natural antonyms: the same structure (relation of wish to outcome) with opposite results. Pairing them in commentary about uncertain situations (whether things went well or not) is a common rhetorical move.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy fate daily-life pragmatics colloquial

Literal: entering the earth brings peace — may they rest in peace
Figurative: Lit: enter-earth-become-peaceful. The traditional Chinese expression for the peace of burial: entering the earth is how the deceased find rest. Used in discussions of funerary customs and in consoling the bereaved.

Literal: too sharp to be withstood: an irresistible force
Figurative: Lit: so sharp it cannot be matched. Here 当 means to stand against or block. Said of an advance, an army, or a momentum that nothing can stop.

Literal: a timely snow foretells a good harvest
Figurative: 瑞 ruì (auspicious) + 雪 xuě (snow) + 兆 zhào (to portend) + 丰年 fēngnián (a year of abundance). A farmer's proverb with real agronomy behind it: a heavy winter snow insulates the wheat from killing cold, kills overwintering pests, and melts into spring soil moisture.

Literal: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse
Figurative: His horse ran off. His neighbours grieved. He shrugged. The Daoist parable that became China's word for the unknowability of fortune.

Literal: the governance of the Three Dynasties — the Confucian golden age
Figurative: The Three Dynasties (Xia, Shang, Zhou) collectively were idealized by Confucians as the golden age of moral government, a standard against which all later dynasties were measured and found wanting. 三代 remains a byword for ideal antiquity in Chinese intellectual discourse.

Literal: the dead of night — the third watch, past midnight
Figurative: 三更 (third night watch, 11 pm to 1 am) + 半夜 (middle of the night). The 更 is gēng, first tone. A fixed phrase for any unreasonably late hour. 你三更半夜打电话干什么? "What are you calling at this hour for?" Still in active everyday use; most speakers do not connect it to the premodern watch system.
Tags: grammar adverb comparison degree timing classical

Literal: three visits to the thatched cottage — to seek out a person of talent with great persistence and sincerity
Figurative: The most celebrated episode from Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Liu Bei, ruler of Shu, visits the hermit Zhuge Liang three times at his remote thatched cottage before Zhuge Liang agrees to leave seclusion and serve as his strategist.
Tags: cosmology philosophy language history dynasty han statecraft strategy classical

Literal: the Three Principles of the People — nationalism, democracy, livelihood
Figurative: Sun Yat-sen's political program, still the official ideology of the Republic of China (Taiwan). The phrase is so embedded in Chinese political vocabulary that it functions almost as a set term.

Literal: three people make a tiger
Figurative: A minister warns his king: if three people all claim there is a tiger in the marketplace, even the skeptical will believe it. The Zhanguo Ce parable of rumor that outlasts the warning against it.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms logic rhetoric communication media society

Pinyin: sān rén xíng, bì yǒu wǒ shī
Literal: where three walk together, one of them is sure to be my teacher
Figurative: From the Analects (论语). Confucius's most-quoted statement on learning: in any company of three people, there will be something to learn , from the better among them by emulation, from the worse by avoidance.

Literal: three heads and six arms — superhuman ability; able to do many things at once
Figurative: 三头 (three heads) and 六臂 (six arms), the form of certain fierce Buddhist and Daoist deities such as Nezha, who can fight and act on many fronts at once.

Literal: three hearts, two intentions — indecisive; half-hearted; wavering
Figurative: Three hearts pulling in different directions, two sets of intentions competing: the image is of someone who cannot commit. Used to criticize a lack of decisiveness or sincerity in a relationship, a task, or a position. 做事不能三心二意 (You can't do things half-heartedly).
Tags: cosmology philosophy daoism yin-yang grammar vocabulary language meaning mind emotion characters

Literal: three words, two phrases — in a few words; briefly
Figurative: 三言 (three words) and 两语 (two phrases): just a handful of words, said briefly. Used to mean something can be (or cannot be) explained in a sentence or two: 三言两语说不清 (it can't be explained in a few words).
Tags: language literature communication characters grammar daily-life

Literal: three yang lines open into prosperity: an auspicious fresh start, a New Year blessing
Figurative: From the hexagram 泰 (peace) in the Book of Changes, whose lower three lines are 阳, marking yang rising as winter turns to spring. A traditional New Year greeting wishing renewal and good fortune for the year ahead.

Literal: fierce in appearance but cowardly within — all bark and no bite
Figurative: Lit: color-fierce-inside-timid. A Confucian observation from the Analects: those who appear stern and imposing externally (色厉) but are weak-willed inside (内荏). The opposite of the virtuous person, whose outer bearing matches inner substance.

Literal: many monks, little porridge — too many claimants for scarce resources
Figurative: The monastery breakfast as economic model. Used for job markets (百个人抢一个岗位，僧多粥少), housing, research funding, and concert tickets. The pictorial economy of the phrase, one queue and one pot, is why it beats the abstract word for scarcity in daily speech.

Literal: kill the chicken to warn the monkey: punish one to frighten the rest
Figurative: Make an example of a minor offender so the watching crowd falls into line. Common in talk of office discipline and political crackdowns.

Literal: to smear blood on the lips as an oath — to seal a solemn covenant
Figurative: The ritual procedure of the Spring and Autumn covenant assembly (盟会 ménghuì): participants touched their lips with the blood of a sacrificial animal , usually a bull or horse , while swearing the covenant terms. The act bound the parties through ritual sanction, not just political agreement.
Tags: history confucianism classical dynasty ancient politics ritual philosophy classics

Literal: mountains high, water long — virtue or reputation that endures across time
Figurative: From a Northern Song memorial by Fan Zhongyan (范仲淹) describing the legacy of a virtuous official: 云山苍苍，江水泱泱；先生之风，山高水长 ("the cloudy mountains stretch dark; the rivers run wide; the master's spirit , high as the mountains, long as the rivers").

Literal: Mountains Clear, Waters Lovely
Figurative: Clear mountains, lovely waters. The standard Chinese phrase for a picturesque landscape: four characters that compress the whole aesthetic vocabulary of natural beauty.

Literal: the mountains are exhausted, the waters are at their end — at the end of one's resources
Figurative: From Lu You (陆游, Song dynasty), 游山西村: 山穷水尽疑无路，柳暗花明又一村 ("when the mountains are spent and the waters are done and there seems to be no road , there, beyond the dim willows and bright flowers, is another village").

Literal: mountains piled on mountains, waters winding through waters — a seemingly hopeless impasse
Figurative: From a poem by Lu You 陆游. Full line: 山重水复疑无路，柳暗花明又一村, "Mountain on mountain, water on water, seemingly no path; then through dark willows and bright flowers, a village appears." The proverb for finding hope when all seems lost.

Literal: cut the complex and move toward the simple: prune the excess
Figurative: 删 to delete, 繁 the complicated, 就 to go toward, 简 the simple. An editor's motto, applied to prose, procedures, and design alike.

Literal: good and evil are rewarded accordingly — karmic accounting
Figurative: The foundational moral logic of the City God's record-keeping function. 善 shàn = virtue; 恶 è = evil; 有报 yǒu bào = has retribution/reward. The phrase asserts that no deed escapes accounting, even if human courts miss it, because the City God has the complete ledger.
Tags: folk-religion religion gods culture history ritual ancestors

Literal: good beginning, good ending; to see something through properly from start to finish
Figurative: Lit: good-start-good-end. The virtue of completing what one begins, and completing it well. 终 zhōng (end, conclusion) is the Classical Chinese counterpart to the grammatical 了 , both mark the reaching of an end. This idiom captures the moral weight of completion.
Tags: ethics virtue confucianism human-nature philosophy buddhism taoism aspect particle tense vocabulary adverb timing communication

Literal: to wound heaven and harm reason: utterly immoral
Figurative: An act so cruel it offends both heaven and natural law. Strong condemnation of conscienceless deeds.

Literal: the highest good is like water — effortless giving that sustains without striving
Figurative: Daodejing, Chapter 8. Functions as a classical four-character literary phrase rather than an everyday idiom. Cited in calligraphy, philosophy, and any context invoking the Daoist ideal of natural, uncontending benefit.
Tags: ethics virtue confucianism human-nature philosophy buddhism taoism daoism religion immortality

Literal: The highest good is like water.
Figurative: From chapter 8. Water is the master image of the Daodejing: it benefits all things without contending, it seeks the low places that everyone else disdains, and in this very humility it comes closest to the 道.
Tags: daoism laozi classics philosophy wuwei cosmology daodejing

Literal: hands moving up and down — to manipulate facts; to connive
Figurative: From the Zuǒzhuàn (左传), Spring and Autumn period. A general signaled with his hand upward or downward to indicate whether a captured soldier was high-ranking (ransom-worthy) or low-ranking (irrelevant) , the signal determined the truth, not the facts.

Literal: what the top does, the bottom imitates — those in power set the moral tone
Figurative: A foundational principle of Confucian political thought: the ruler's virtue or vice flows downward through society. If the one above is corrupt, those below will follow. If the one above is upright, the people will follow that too. 上 and 下 carry the full social hierarchy in two strokes.

Literal: please wait a moment
Figurative: A polite, slightly formal way to ask someone to wait briefly, 片刻 ("a short moment") being the written cousin of 一会儿. Heard in service settings and on the phone, the courteous register where 等一会儿 would be too casual.

Literal: seen little, amazed by much — making a fuss about ordinary things
Figurative: 少见 (having seen few things) + 多怪 (finding much to be strange/surprising). When you haven't seen much of the world, ordinary things seem remarkable. A mild criticism of provinciality or naïvety: someone who marvels at things a more experienced person takes for granted.

Literal: to sacrifice oneself for others: selfless devotion to others' good
Figurative: Lit: give-up-self-for-others. The highest praise for selflessness, setting one's own interests aside for the sake of other people. The 己 here is exactly the self that 舍 (to give up) renounces.

Literal: to give up one's life and forget death; to face danger without thought of self
Figurative: A standard high-register chengyu for selfless courage, used for soldiers, rescue workers, doctors during epidemics. The phrase doesn't contain 命 directly but belongs to its semantic field: it names the willingness to set down the command-to-live for something larger.

Literal: if not I, then who? — the burden falls to me
the body is not controlled by oneself — driven by circumstances beyond one's will
Figurative: 身 shēn (body; self) + 不 bù (not) + 由 yóu (controlled by; following from) + 己 jǐ (oneself). One's own body belongs to external forces , obligation, circumstance, social pressure, or fate. The counterpart to agency: when 他 (the other, external) overrides 己 (the self).
Tags: grammar humanity social modern passive syntax agent

Literal: to practice with one's own body and strength; to live what one preaches
Figurative: 身 and 体 here are both verbs in the classical grammar: to embody personally (身) and to enact (体力行, carry out with strength). The Confucian ideal of the teacher whose conduct is the curriculum. Modern usage praises leaders who do rather than direct: 环保不能只喊口号，要身体力行。
Tags: energy ability meaning characters body health daily-life vocabulary

Literal: deep thought, mature deliberation — to think long and carefully before acting
Figurative: 深 shēn (deep) + 思 sī (think) + 熟 shú (mature; thoroughly cooked) + 虑 lǜ (to deliberate; to consider). A four-character description of the deliberative ideal: thought that has gone deep and has been given time to mature, like food that has cooked through completely.

Literal: appearing like a deity, vanishing like a ghost — moving unpredictably, appearing and disappearing without warning
Figurative: Lit: spirit-emerge-ghost-disappear. 出 is to emerge, appear; 没 is to sink, vanish. The pairing of 神 (divine, above) and 鬼 (ghostly, below) creates a complete spectrum of supernatural unpredictability , appearing from nowhere, vanishing the same way.
Tags: folk-religion religion culture classical symbolism ancestors gods popular

Literal: careful attention to death rites and honoring distant ancestors
Figurative: From the Analects (论语): 慎终追远，民德归厚矣. "When the people are careful about death rites and diligently honor distant ancestors, the virtue of the people will return to richness." Confucius's most concise statement of why ancestor veneration matters: it cultivates moral seriousness in the living.

Literal: living dragon, active tiger — bursting with energy and vitality
Figurative: 生 shēng (alive; living) + 龙 lóng + 活 huó (active; lively) + 虎 hǔ (tiger). Used to describe a person , especially a child, an athlete, or anyone at the peak of their physical vitality , who radiates robust, irrepressible energy. 这些孩子个个生龙活虎，根本停不下来。

Literal: life generating life without ceasing — the endless renewal of existence
Figurative: A Daoist cosmological phrase: life perpetually generating more life. Used in nature writing, philosophical prose, and speeches about cultural continuity.

Literal: to share life and death together — a bond through the deepest adversity
Figurative: Lit: life-death-with-together. Used for close comrades, soldiers, and couples who have endured extreme hardship. The deepest statement of loyalty.

Pinyin: shēng yú yōuhuàn, sǐ yú ānlè.
Literal: One lives through hardship and worry; one dies from comfort and pleasure.
Figurative: Mencius 6B:15. The full passage argues this through historical examples: great figures of the past were all tempered through adversity before they could accomplish anything.

Literal: feign east, strike west — strategic deception; misdirection before attacking
Figurative: Lit: declare-east-strike-west. A classic military stratagem from the Sun Tzu tradition , make noise in the east to draw attention, then attack from the west. Used broadly for any deceptive misdirection tactic in business, politics, or argument. 他用声东击西的策略迷惑了对手。
Tags: directions nature cosmology phonology perception communication characters colloquial things language vocabulary

Literal: ten years at a cold window — long, austere years of study
Figurative: The image of the exam candidate reading through winters without heat. The full couplet adds the payoff: ten years at the cold window unknown, one exam success and the world knows your name (十年寒窗无人问，一举成名天下知). Modern parents invoke it during gaokao season with full sincerity.

Pinyin: shí nián shù mù, bǎi nián shù rén
Literal: ten years to grow a tree, a hundred years to cultivate a person — education takes far longer than any other cultivation
Figurative: From the classical text 管子 Guǎnzi. Growing a tree requires ten years of patience: planting, watering, waiting. Cultivating a human being , educating, civilizing, forming character , requires ten times longer. The century-scale horizon is a deliberate rebuke to impatience.

Literal: perfect in every way — ten-complete and ten-beautiful, with nothing lacking
Figurative: The most-used idiom of perfection in Chinese. The doubling of 十 means completeness is measured twice , in wholeness and in beauty , so that neither a technical nor an aesthetic standard is left unmet.
Tags: meaning evaluation characters quality language cosmology science

Literal: time will not wait for me — seize the moment; there is no time to lose
Figurative: Lit: time-not-me-wait. A classical inversion , the subject (时, time) is placed before the negation, with "me" as object, producing the archaic feel of a proverb. The phrase frames time as an agent with no personal loyalty: it moves whether you are ready or not.

Literal: time passes, circumstances change — things are different now; that was then
Figurative: 时过 (time has passed) + 境迁 (the situation has shifted , 境 jìng: circumstances, context; 迁 qiān: to move, to change). Used to acknowledge that what was true, appropriate, or possible in the past no longer applies , without judgment, simply as a statement of temporal fact.

Literal: the hour is not early: it is getting late
Figurative: A common set expression rather than a classical chengyu. Used to signal politely that time has slipped on, often as a cue to wrap up or take one's leave: 时候不早了，我该走了 "it is getting late, I should go."

Literal: when the time comes, fortune turns — one's luck changes for the better
Figurative: Lit: time-comes fortune-turns. Fortune is not fixed; it turns like a wheel. Used when someone's luck dramatically improves after a period of misfortune. The Daoist wheel of fortune encoded in a four-character phrase.

Literal: the times produce their heroes
Figurative: Great figures are made by the conditions of their age, not by innate destiny alone, the circumstances create the opportunity for greatness.

Literal: to seek truth from facts — address problems realistically
Figurative: A classical phrase, later a famous modern slogan, meaning to approach a 问题 on the basis of facts rather than wishful thinking or ideology. 实事 (real matters) + 求是 (seek what is so). The standard expression for a pragmatic, evidence-based way of analysing and solving problems.
Tags: meaning evaluation quality characters society daily-life focus cleft past vocabulary adverb communication rhetoric

Literal: to harbor a wicked scheme: to act with malicious intent
Figurative: A colloquial set phrase, 使坏 (to scheme) plus 心眼 (mind, intention). Describes someone secretly plotting harm rather than acting openly. Everyday spoken register, not classical.

Literal: scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant: the four classes of old society
Figurative: The traditional ranking of occupations, with the farmer placed second only to the scholar and above the merchant, a clue to how high agriculture stood in the Confucian moral order.

Literal: the eighth wonder of the world
Figurative: The popular epithet attached to the terracotta army since foreign dignitaries applied it after the discovery.
Tags: history qin first-emperor ancient art archaeology

Literal: generation after generation: for all the generations to come
Figurative: A doubling of 世 (age) and 代 (generation), each repeated for emphasis. Describes something passed down or continuing without break across every generation, as in a craft, a duty, or a family living on the same land.

Literal: a haven of peace: an idyllic refuge cut off from the troubled world
Figurative: Lit: a peach-blossom spring beyond the world. From Tao Yuanming's fable of a fisherman who stumbles on a hidden valley untouched by war and time. Now any tranquil place sheltered from the strife and bustle of ordinary life.

Literal: half the work, double the result: maximum output from minimum effort
Figurative: Lit: work-half-achievement-double. The ideal of efficiency: accomplishing more by working smarter. From Mencius (孟子). Its mirror image is 事倍功半 shì bèi gōng bàn (double the work, half the result), wasted, inefficient effort.
Tags: mastery ability evaluation characters culture history society daily-life meaning time martial-arts

Literal: double the effort, half the result
Figurative: A related but distinct phrase: where 事与愿违 says the outcome diverged from the wish without specifying the ratio, 事倍功半 specifically describes disproportionate effort yielding inadequate results.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy fate daily-life pragmatics colloquial

Literal: nothing happens more than three times — the third time is the last; do not push beyond three
Figurative: A folk saying rather than a classical text quotation: three is the outer limit of tolerance or recurrence.

Literal: everything happens for a reason
Figurative: Literally "when a matter arises, there is a cause", nothing comes out of nowhere. It is the quiet conviction behind every 为什么: ask the question and there will be a 因 (cause) to find. The 因 here is the same one in 因为 ("because").

Literal: now that things have come to this
Figurative: Literally "matters have arrived at the present," a set opener used when a situation has reached its current, often difficult, point and one must face it: 事到如今，只能这样了 ("now that it's come to this, this is all we can do"). Built on 如今 (nowadays, the present).

Literal: the affair has passed and the circumstances have changed
Figurative: 事 (the matter) 过 (has passed) 境 (circumstances) 迁 (have shifted). Note 过 in its full verbal sense, the same morpheme that grammaticalized into the experiential particle. Used to wave off old grievances: 事过境迁，别再提了 "It's all in the past, don't bring it up again."

Literal: things go contrary to ones wishes
Figurative: Traced to Ruan Ji of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove: a literary formulation of the gap between intention and outcome, resigned rather than accusatory, with no blame assigned.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy fate daily-life pragmatics colloquial

Literal: things depend on human effort — nothing is impossible with effort
Figurative: Lit: matters-located-in-human-doing. The outcome of things lies in human action, not fate or circumstance. An optimistic proverb of agency: no matter how difficult, the result is in human hands. 不要灰心，事在人为。

Literal: bound to happen; imperative
Figurative: Literally "the momentum lies in must-be-done", a course of action that circumstances make unavoidable. It is certainty of the necessary kind, the 必 ("must") that 一定 and 必须 both touch, applied to events that simply have to proceed.

Literal: right and wrong turned upside down — moral inversion
Figurative: Lit: right-wrong-overturned-upended. Used when injustice prevails, when blame is assigned to the innocent, or when someone deliberately distorts moral reality. 他把是非颠倒，让人无法接受。Strong condemnation in formal and classical register.

Literal: right and wrong, correct and incorrect — the full moral spectrum of a situation
Figurative: Lit: right-wrong-correct-incorrect. A compound of two pairs: 是非 (right/wrong as a classical pair) and 对错 (correct/incorrect as a modern pair). Used to describe careful moral judgment of a complex situation. 分清是非对错 = "to clearly distinguish right from wrong in the situation."

Literal: right and wrong clearly divided: drawing a sharp line between them
Figurative: Lit: right-wrong-divide-clear. Said in praise of someone with firm moral judgment who does not blur what is right with what is wrong.

Literal: right and wrong, crooked and straight: the true merits of a case
Figurative: Lit: right-wrong-crooked-straight. The four poles by which a dispute is judged. To 分清是非曲直 is to sort out who is truly in the right, free of bias.

Literal: to praise the ancient and disparage the present
Figurative: Lit: right-ancient-wrong-present. The bias of treating old things as inherently superior to contemporary ones. Appears in debates about tradition versus modernity, canonical texts versus living practice. Qin Shihuang's advisors warned him about scholars guilty of this very tendency.

Literal: hand never releasing the scroll — to be an insatiable reader
Figurative: Lit: hand-not-release-scroll. To be so devoted to books that you never put them down. A compliment for scholars. 卷 juǎn = scroll; the classical form of the book.

Literal: the hand arrives and the capture is made — easily accomplished
Figurative: Lit: hand-arrives-capture-comes. Used to describe a task accomplished with ease and confidence , the expert reaches out and the thing is done. An expression of mastery making difficulty look effortless. 对他来说，这件事手到擒来 "For him, this was a cinch."

Literal: hands busy, feet disordered — flustered and disorganized
Figurative: Lit: hands-busy-feet-chaotic. The image of someone scrambling in a panic, hands and feet moving in disordered haste. Used to describe being overwhelmed and disorganized: the opposite of calm competence. 他一到过年就手忙脚乱 "Around New Year, he's always running around in a flustered state."
Tags: body movement space perception emotion characters culture

Literal: hands and feet without placement — at a complete loss, not knowing what to do
Figurative: 手 (hands) + 足 (feet) + 无措 (nowhere to place them). So flustered that your hands and feet don't know where to go. From the Analects (Book XIII): Confucius warns that without ritual propriety, the people will be 手足无措.

Literal: the affection of hands and feet: the bond between brothers and sisters
Figurative: Lit: hand-foot's-feeling. 手足 (hands and feet) is a classical image for siblings, who are as inseparable as one's own limbs. The phrase names the deep tie between brothers and sisters.

Literal: to have kept watch for a long while: to wait faithfully and at length
Figurative: Lit: keep-watch-much-time. Said of someone who has been standing by patiently for a long stretch, often awaiting a person or an awaited moment. 守候 pairs the vigil of 守 with the waiting of 候.

Literal: to watch out for and help one another
Figurative: From the Mencius: neighbors keeping watch and lending aid to each other, the ideal of a community that protects its own. 守望 (to keep watch) + 相助 (to help one another). Invoked for solidarity in hard times.

Literal: Guarding the Stump, Waiting for Rabbits
Figurative: A rabbit ran headlong into a tree stump. The farmer dropped his plough and watched the stump for the rest of his life.

Literal: the first finger you bend to count: second to none, the very best
Figurative: Lit: first-bend-one-finger. When you count off the best on your fingers, this is the one you bend down first. Used to rank a person or thing as the foremost in its field. 他在这个行业首屈一指 "He is second to none in this industry."

Literal: to be controlled by others; to be subject to another's power
Figurative: Lit: receive-control-by-people. The standard formal expression for being under another's power, being constrained by external forces rather than acting freely. Common in diplomatic, strategic, and business contexts. The grammatical structure 受…于 is classical , modern equivalent would be 被人控制.

Pinyin: shū tóng wén, chē tóng guǐ
Literal: unified script, standardized axle widths — the rhetorical formula of systemic national unity
Figurative: Still quoted in policy arguments about national standards: language standardization, infrastructure compatibility, technical regulation. The pairing condenses the Qin unification logic: physical connectivity (roads) plus cultural connectivity (writing) equals empire.

Literal: a family with a fragrance of books — a family of scholars and learning
Figurative: Lit: book-fragrance-door-lineage. A family where books are the tradition and education runs through the generations. High cultural prestige in Chinese society. 书香 shūxiāng "the fragrance of books" is itself a vivid compound.
Tags: literacy culture calligraphy perception food daily-life characters

Pinyin: shú dú Táng shī sān bǎi shǒu
Literal: read three hundred Tang poems until you know them by heart — and you'll be able to compose poetry yourself
Figurative: From the preface to the famous Qing-dynasty anthology Three Hundred Tang Poems: 熟读唐诗三百首，不会作诗也会吟. The locus classicus for the Chinese theory of learning by saturated recitation. The full saying ends "even if you can't compose, you'll be able to chant" , competence emerges from soaking in the corpus.

Literal: recite the classics but forget your ancestors
Figurative: From the Zuozhuan: a minister who could cite all historical precedents of his state but could not name his own ancestral lineage was mocked with this phrase. Used for ingratitude, forgetting one's origins, or adopting foreign ways at the expense of one's own heritage.

Literal: when water flows, a channel forms
Figurative: Literally "when the water arrives, the channel is made", success comes naturally once conditions ripen, with no forcing. It is the gentle counterpart to 终于's hard-won arrival: the long-awaited outcome that, in the end, simply falls into place.
Tags: meaning evaluation change characters vocabulary adverb timing communication

Literal: water drips and the stone is bored through: small force, long time
Figurative: The same image reordered, traced to the Han text Hàn Shū. Stresses the result, the worn-through stone, as proof that small efforts accumulate.

Literal: water and fire cannot coexist — irreconcilably opposed
Figurative: Water extinguishes fire; fire evaporates water. The two simply cannot occupy the same space. Used for people, factions, or ideas in absolute opposition. 他们两人水火不容 "Those two are completely incompatible."

Literal: not even water can leak through: packed solid; completely blocked or surrounded
Figurative: 水 shuǐ (water) + 泄 xiè (to leak; to drain out) + 不 bù (not) + 通 (to pass through). So densely packed that not even a drop of water could trickle out.

Literal: when the water rises the boat rises too: gains that lift everything along with the tide
Figurative: Originally a Chán Buddhist phrase. Used when one rising element pulls others up with it, whether prices, status, or a whole industry.

Literal: fishing the moon out of water — chasing an illusion
Figurative: Lit: water-inside-fish-moon. The moon's reflection in a pond looks real but cannot be grasped. Used for futile efforts chasing something impossible. A Buddhist parable: mistaking the reflection for reality.

Literal: with the wind, with the water — smooth sailing; everything going well without obstruction
Figurative: A wish and a description: wind at your back, current in your favor , nothing impeding progress. 祝你顺风顺水！(Wishing you smooth sailing!) is a common departure blessing. The 风水 imagery is natural: when wind and water cooperate, travel is easy; when they oppose, nothing moves.

Literal: let things take their natural course; go with the flow; accord with what is self-so
Figurative: 顺 shùn (to follow; to go along with; to accord with; to flow downstream) + 其 qí (its; their; that) + 自然 zìrán (nature; the natural; self-so , 自 zì = self, 然 rán = thus/so: what is so of itself, without external imposition). The modern everyday expression for the principle underlying 无为.
Tags: daoism daodejing laozi wuwei philosophy buddhism fate romance

Literal: push the boat along with the current: go with the flow and make the easy move
Figurative: When circumstances already lean your way, you give a light push and take the credit. Often used for a decision that costs nothing because the moment favors it.

Literal: accord with Heaven, respond to humanity — acting in alignment with both cosmic order and popular sentiment
Figurative: Lit: accord-Heaven-respond-humanity. A classical formula used to describe righteous political action or revolution: the actor is both aligned with Heaven's pattern and responding to the genuine needs of the people.
Tags: philosophy confucianism taoism cosmology nature heaven humanity classical

Pinyin: shuō Cáo Cāo, Cáo Cāo dào
Literal: speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives — speak of the devil
Figurative: The exact Chinese equivalent of "speak of the devil." Said the instant someone shows up just as you were talking about them. It is the most common everyday phrase in which Cao Cao's name survives, owed to his reputation, in the stories, for moving with sudden speed.
Tags: history han biography warlord poet poetry statecraft strategy

Pinyin: shuō cáo cāo, cáo cāo dào.
Literal: Speak of Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives.
Figurative: The Chinese equivalent of "speak of the devil," drawn from the novel's portrait of Cao Cao as swift and unexpectedly present. Said when a person appears just as they are being talked about. One of the clearest examples of how thoroughly the Romance's characters entered everyday speech.
Tags: literature novels classics classical history strategy

Literal: to do what one says — to be as good as one's word
Figurative: 说 shuō (to say) + 到 dào (reach the point of) + 做 + 到. Literally "say it to the point, do it to the point." A high compliment: this is a person whose words and deeds match, who does not promise idly. The structure leans on 做到 (to achieve, to follow through).

Literal: to start telling it makes a long story: it is a long story
Figurative: Lit: to-speak-of-it-the-words-grow-long. The standard preface to a complicated explanation, the Chinese equivalent of "well, it's a long story."

Literal: say one, not two — a person whose word is final; absolute authority
Figurative: Lit: say-one-not-two. To speak once and have it stand; not to be contradicted. Describes a figure of absolute authority within their domain. Can be used admiringly (a decisive leader) or critically (an autocrat). 他在公司里说一不二。Tā zài gōngsī lǐ shuō yī bù èr. "In the company, what he says goes."
Tags: cosmology philosophy daoism yin-yang grammar vocabulary language communication rhetoric

Literal: to refuse to own up to one's debts even in death — utterly unwilling to acknowledge fault
Figurative: Lit: die-not-recognize-account. Said of someone who, when caught out, doubles down rather than admitting anything. The 死 here is "to-the-death," intensifying the refusal.

Pinyin: sǐ ér fù shēng, zài shì wéi rén
Literal: to die and come back to life; to be reborn into the world
Figurative: 再世 (again-in-the-world) is the classical expression for reincarnation or miraculous revival. Used both literally (near-death recovery) and figuratively (total transformation of a situation or person). 再世英雄 (a hero reborn in a new era).

Literal: to die away and come back: to the point of fainting and reviving
Figurative: Lit: die-go-live-come, pairing 死 and 活. Describes extremity of feeling or pain so severe one seems to faint and revive: to cry 哭得死去活来 (to weep oneself into a faint), to be beaten half to death.

Literal: dying for face, living in torment — to suffer rather than ask for help because of pride
Figurative: A seven-character folk saying rather than a classical 成语, but extremely widely used. Describes the pattern of letting one's face-consciousness cause unnecessary suffering , not asking for help, not admitting failure, not seeking medical attention, because doing so would cost face.

Literal: to die other than by one's allotted fate: to meet an unnatural death
Figurative: Lit: die-by-not-fate. 于 marks the cause of death, and 非命 (not one's natural span) signals an accident, violence, or disaster rather than a peaceful end.

Literal: to make one's home in all four seas — at home anywhere; cosmopolitan; rootless wandering
Figurative: 四海 = the four seas = everywhere under heaven. 为 = to treat as; to make into. The whole globe is one's household. Used for travelers, exiles, and those rootlessly at ease anywhere. Both admiring (cosmopolitan freedom) and elegiac (loss of fixed roots) , depending on context.
Tags: family society home cosmology space language

Literal: four faces, eight directions — from every direction; from everywhere
Figurative: The most common chengyu using 方. 四面 (the four faces of a square; the four sides) + 八方 (the eight directions). Used for crowds, news, demands, attacks , anything converging from every direction. 来自四面八方的客人 (guests from all over).
Tags: cosmology culture language space geometry meaning characters direction philosophy

Literal: Chu songs on all four sides — besieged on every side; utterly isolated
Figurative: From the fall of Xiang Yu, the Hegemon-King of Chu, at the battle of Gaixia (202 BCE). Surrounded by Han forces, Xiang Yu heard his enemies singing the songs of his own homeland of Chu from every direction, and concluded that Chu had already fallen and his men had deserted to the enemy.
Tags: communication culture characters cosmology space language han dynasty identity classics history literature ancient biography

Literal: reaching in four and through eight — accessible in every direction; well-connected
Figurative: 四通 (passing through in the four directions) plus 八达 (extending out the eight ways). Used of roads, railways, and transport networks that radiate to everywhere, and by extension of any hub that connects in all directions. A 交通四通八达 city is one you can reach and leave by any route.
Tags: cosmology space language motion communication meaning characters

Literal: seemingly right but actually wrong; plausible but false
Figurative: Lit: seem-right-but-wrong. Used for arguments, claims, or reasoning that appear correct on the surface but are fundamentally flawed. The danger zone of logical errors , specious reasoning that passes for truth. Appears in classical philosophy and remains common in intellectual criticism.
Tags: grammar copula logic focus cleft past

Literal: if you escort the Buddha, escort him all the way west: finish what you start, see help through to the end
Figurative: A colloquial saying drawing on the westward journey of Buddhist pilgrimage. Urges you not to abandon a kindness or a task halfway, but to carry it to completion.

Literal: to send off the old and welcome the new: ring out the old year, ring in the new
Figurative: A New Year and year-end phrase, balancing 送 (sending off) the old against 迎 (welcoming) the new. Common on greeting cards and in festival speeches.

Literal: to send off those leaving and welcome those arriving: the endless round of social hospitality
Figurative: Traces to the Lǐjì (Book of Rites). Describes the constant ceremony of receiving guests and seeing them off, often with a faint note of how exhausting such social duty becomes.

Literal: follow the karmic current — to go with the flow; to accept what fate brings; non-attachment
Figurative: Lit: follow-karmic-connection. A Buddhist and Daoist attitude of non-attachment: accepting outcomes without forcing them, trusting the flow of conditions rather than imposing a rigid agenda. Has become a widely used life philosophy and response to uncertainty or disappointment. 随缘吧，强求没用。

Literal: the years spare no one — time is merciless; age catches up with everyone
Figurative: 岁月 suìyuè (years and months , a classical compound for the flow of time) + 不饶 bù ráo (shows no mercy, does not spare). A cousin-phrase to 时不我待, but the mood is different: less urgent, more resigned. Where 时不我待 urges action, 岁月不饶人 acknowledges what cannot be undone.

Literal: the years pass like a weaver's shuttle — time flies
Figurative: Lit: years-months-like-shuttle. 岁月 = years and months (time). 梭 suō = the weaver's shuttle that flies back and forth at great speed. The Chinese "time flies," usually said with a mixture of nostalgia and wonder at how quickly life passes.

Literal: the one of whom I speak — the beloved, the one I yearn for
Figurative: From the Shijing (诗经) poem 蒹葭 ("Reeds"). One of the most famous lines of classical poetry, and the locus classicus for 伊 as feminine third person. The poem itself is gender-ambiguous in the classical text but read across two millennia as referring to a beloved woman across the river.

Literal: all before one is swept aside: to carry all before one, irresistible
Figurative: Lit: wherever-faced, grass-flattens. 所向 is "wherever one turns," 披靡 the way grass bends flat before the wind. Said of an army or a force so strong that everything in its path gives way.

Literal: stones from other hills — outside perspectives can polish your own jade
Figurative: From the Book of Songs (诗经): "stones from other hills can be used to grind jade." External viewpoints, foreign models, and outside criticism all carry value that self-regard misses. 他山 (other hills) + 之 (possessive particle) + 石 (stones).

Literal: Grand Duke Jiang fishes: those who are willing will take the bait
Figurative: From 太公钓鱼，愿者上钩. The sage Jiang Ziya fished with a straight, baitless hook, waiting for King Wen to seek him out. Said of letting the willing come of their own accord rather than forcing them.

Literal: an age of great peace and prosperity — the ideal the Taiping name invoked, and failed to deliver
Figurative: 太平 (great peace) + 盛世 (flourishing age, era of prosperity). The four-character compound describes the classical Chinese political ideal: an era in which the realm is at peace, governance is just, harvests are abundant, and the common people live without fear.
Tags: intensifier meaning cosmology characters history qing rebellion religion

Literal: to flower briefly and vanish
Figurative: Literally "the night-blooming cereus shows itself once," for something splendid that lasts only a moment and is gone. The flower opens for a single short while in the night, then withers. A poignant image of fleeting brilliance, the shadow side of "a little while."
Tags: time modern perception characters vocabulary timing daily-life

Literal: to chat and laugh with verve: lively, easy conversation
Figurative: Lit: talk-laugh wind-rises, as if a fresh breeze sprang up from the talk. Describes a person who holds a room with relaxed, witty conversation. A warm compliment to a host or a speaker.

Literal: to sigh that one need look no further: the very acme of perfection
Figurative: Lit: sigh-that-viewing-stops-here. From the Zuozhuan, where a guest praised a performance as so fine that watching could end there, nothing better remaining to see. High praise for the best of its kind.

Literal: dignified and upright: open, honorable, with nothing to hide
Figurative: Reduplicated from 堂正. Said of someone who acts squarely and aboveboard, facing things head-on rather than scheming in the shadows. 堂堂正正做人 "to live as an upright person."

Literal: hide your brightness and nurture your obscurity — keep a low international profile while building strength
Figurative: 韬光 (conceal one's brilliance) + 养晦 (cultivate obscurity, from 晦 = darkness, the dark of the moon).

Literal: peaches and plums fill the world: a teacher's students are everywhere
Figurative: Lit: peach-plum-fill-the-world. 桃李 (peach and plum trees) stand for a teacher's 弟子, the disciples cultivated over a lifetime. To say someone's 桃李满天下 is high praise for a great educator.

Literal: the Oath of the Peach Garden — sworn brotherhood
Figurative: The scene in which Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei swear an oath of brotherhood in a peach orchard, vowing to live and die for one another and their shared cause.
Tags: literature novels classics classical history strategy

Literal: ask a price, return a price: to haggle, bargain
Figurative: Acts out the back-and-forth of the marketplace, one side naming a figure and the other countering. Extended to any drawn-out negotiation over terms.

Literal: unable to laugh or cry: caught between amusement and dismay
Figurative: Lit: crying-laughing-both-wrong. Neither weeping nor laughing fits the situation, the awkward state of finding something at once absurd and exasperating. 令人啼笑皆非 "leaves one not knowing whether to laugh or cry."

Literal: clarified butter poured over the crown — sudden, total illumination
Figurative: 醍醐, the finest essence refined from milk, was a Buddhist metaphor for the ultimate teaching; pouring it over the head is enlightenment received in one stream. Used for explanations so good they reorganize your understanding: a lecture, a mentor's single remark.

Literal: grand in structure and fine in thought: a work both vast and meticulous
Figurative: Lit: body-large-thought-fine. Praise for a major work, a book or system, whose overall framework is grand while its detailed reasoning is precise. Here 体 is the structure or framework of the whole.

Literal: the body without a patch of whole skin: wounded all over, or torn apart in criticism
Figurative: Lit: body-without-intact-skin. Literally beaten until no skin is unbroken; figuratively, an argument or piece of work refuted or criticized so thoroughly that nothing is left standing.

Literal: to carry out the Way on Heaven's behalf
Figurative: The slogan on the great banner of the Liangshan outlaws, claiming that in punishing the corrupt and protecting the weak they act as the agents of Heaven's justice where the earthly state has failed.
Tags: literature novels classics classical song rebellion

Literal: heaven-bestowed good fate — a heaven-sent destined match; a blessed union
Figurative: Lit: heaven-bestow-good-fate. The most auspicious framing for a destined romantic match , one that heaven itself has arranged and blessed. Used in wedding toasts, blessings, and romantic contexts when the match seems particularly right. 他们的婚姻真是天赐良缘，两个人都幸福极了。

Literal: heaven and earth as my witness — swearing to one's sincerity before the cosmos
Figurative: A folk oath formula invoking Heaven and Earth as moral witnesses. 我天地良心地告诉你. "I'm telling you in all sincerity, with heaven and earth as my witness." Reveals how folk religion makes the cosmos itself a moral guarantor.
Tags: folk-religion gods popular ethics virtue confucianism human-nature philosophy mind wang-yangming cosmology taoism nature heaven classical existence

Literal: heaven overturned, earth capsized — a total upheaval; world-reversing change
Figurative: 翻 fān (to overturn; to flip) + 覆 fù (to capsize). When the cosmos itself is described as flipped, the image captures change so total that the existing order has been inverted. Used for dramatic historical upheavals or situations where everything has changed beyond recognition. 经历了这场变革，国家发生了天翻地覆的变化。
Tags: cosmology taoism philosophy nature heaven classical existence

Literal: Heaven is high and the emperor is far away
Figurative: In a remote place, central authority cannot reach, so local powers do as they please. A wry comment on how rules dissolve with distance from the capital, still used for any situation where oversight is too far off to matter and people act with impunity.
Tags: vocabulary history emperor imperial statecraft royalty

Literal: Heavenly Empress, Holy Mother — Mazu's full honorific
Figurative: The full formal title combines 天后 (Heavenly Empress, the highest imperial designation) with 圣母 Shèngmǔ (Holy Mother, a term shared with the Blessed Virgin in Catholic contexts, creating interesting resonance in Fujian where Portuguese missionaries arrived in the 16th century).

Literal: self-evident truth; axiomatic — too obvious to argue about
Figurative: Lit: heaven's warp and earth's weft. 经 jīng = warp threads (the vertical structural threads in a loom); 义 yì = weft and righteous pattern. Together they constitute the fabric of moral reality , what is simply given. "孩子要孝顺父母，这是天经地义的事。
Tags: cosmology heaven mandate grammar modal permission communication

Literal: heaven's decree is hard to defy; fate is difficult to resist
Figurative: 天命 tiānmìng (Mandate of Heaven; fate) + 难 nán (difficult) + 违 wéi (to defy; to go against). The phrase works in both the political and personal register.

Literal: the mandate has found its home — used of the rightful heir to power, the person heaven has chosen
Figurative: 所归 suǒ guī (where it belongs; where it returns to). As a chengyu, 天命所归 is a verdict, not a prediction. It is said after the fact: this person succeeded, therefore heaven wanted them to succeed.

Literal: heaven south, earth north — from all corners of the world; talking about everything under the sun
Figurative: 南 nán = south; 北 běi = north. The phrase works in two ways. Used of people: 天南地北的朋友 (friends from all corners of the world , scattered to the four directions, heaven-south and earth-north).

Literal: Heaven and humanity in sympathetic resonance — cosmic and human realms in constant responsive dialogue
Figurative: 感 gǎn = to feel, to resonate; 应 yìng = to respond. The Han Confucian doctrine , systematized by 董仲舒 Dǒng Zhòngshū , that Heaven responds to human affairs and humans respond to Heaven's movements, all mediated through the five phases and Yin-Yang cycles.
Tags: yin-yang five-phases cosmology philosophy confucianism taoism nature heaven humanity classical

Literal: Heaven and humanity as one body — the complete unity of cosmic and human orders
Figurative: A variant formulation of 天人合一, with 体 (body; substance) replacing 合一 (united as one). 一体 emphasizes organic embodied unity , Heaven and humanity are not merely in accord but constitute a single body, a single substance.
Tags: philosophy confucianism taoism cosmology nature heaven humanity classical

Pinyin: tiān shí dì lì rén hé
Literal: Heaven's timing, Earth's advantages, human harmony — the three conditions for success
Figurative: From Mencius (2A.1): the convergence of the right moment from Heaven, favorable terrain from Earth, and human solidarity. A practical expression of 天人合一 in strategic thought: success requires alignment with all three orders simultaneously.
Tags: philosophy confucianism taoism cosmology nature heaven humanity classical

Pinyin: tiānxià dà shì, fēn jiǔ bì hé
Literal: the great tendency of all-under-heaven: long divided, must unite; long united, must divide
Figurative: The opening principle of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). A cyclical theory of political history: unity and division alternate as inevitably as the seasons. Endlessly cited in Chinese political discourse to frame any current period as part of a longer historical rhythm.

Literal: all under heaven is at peace — universal peace and order
Figurative: 天下 tiānxià (all under heaven , the entire world as governed territory) + 太平 (great peace). The ideal end-state of Confucian governance and the dream of every dynasty: a world so well-ordered that there is nothing left to struggle against.
Tags: intensifier meaning cosmology characters heaven mandate direction grammar motion politics history worldview

Literal: the world belongs to all — the realm is the public good, not private property
Figurative: Sun Yat-sen's personal motto, drawn from the ancient Book of Rites. Inscribed on buildings and monuments across Taiwan and mainland China. The phrase directly opposes the Confucian concept of dynasties as family property (家天下 jiā tiānxià, "the realm as one family's possession").

Literal: all crows under heaven are equally black — it's the same everywhere; they're all the same
Figurative: Usually cynical: no matter where you go, officials/bosses/people of that type are all equally corrupt/problematic/the same. 当官的天下乌鸦一般黑 (Officials everywhere are equally corrupt , all crows under heaven are black.) A statement of resigned cynicism about systemic problems.

Pinyin: tiānxià wú bù sàn zhī yánxí.
Literal: No feast under heaven goes on forever; every banquet must end.
Figurative: A proverb woven through the novel and epitomising its theme of impermanence: every gathering, however joyful, must break up, just as the splendour of the Jia family must pass. Used widely in Chinese to console at partings and to acknowledge that good times, like all things, come to an end.
Tags: literature novels classics classical qing romance

#fields:Hanzi: 天下无难事只怕有心人
Pinyin: tiānxià wú nán shì, zhǐ pà yǒuxīn rén
Literal: under heaven there are no difficult things — only fear the determined person
Figurative: Determination overcomes all obstacles , there is nothing under heaven so hard that a truly committed person cannot accomplish it. A companion to 功夫不负有心人. 有心人 yǒuxīn rén = a person of resolve and intention. Used as encouragement in the face of daunting tasks: 天下无难事，只怕有心人，你一定能做到。

Literal: the rise and fall of the realm is the responsibility of every common person
Figurative: Attributed to the late Ming / early Qing Confucian scholar 顾炎武 Gù Yánwǔ (1613–1682), though the current form was popularized by Liang Qichao in the late Qing. A founding text of Chinese civic patriotism.
Tags: ming great-wall zhenghe politics history worldview

Literal: the ends of the earth — sky-edge, sea-corner
Figurative: Lit: sky-edge sea-corner. The farthest, most remote reaches of the world. High frequency in romantic poetry and pop songs about separation and longing.

Literal: seamless; flawless — not a flaw to be found
Figurative: Lit: heaven's robe has no seams. The garments of heavenly beings are woven whole , no stitching, no joins. Used to praise flawless plans, flawless stories, and flawless alibis. When applied to an alibi, the idiom carries a slight edge: seamlessness itself can be suspicious.

Literal: a favored child of Heaven: one singularly blessed by fortune
Figurative: Lit: Heaven's-spoiled-child. Originally said of the Xiongnu nomads who boasted Heaven's favor; now used of anyone who seems destined for success, sometimes with a touch of envy.

Literal: a union made by Heaven: a match made in heaven
Figurative: Lit: Heaven-made union. A classical blessing for a marriage, suggesting the couple was destined to come together. Still used today on wedding scrolls and congratulations.

Literal: to stir up trouble and drive a wedge: to set people against each other
Figurative: Lit: stir-up and sow-division. To deliberately create a gap between people who were close, by rumor or provocation. 离间 (jiàn) is to open a rift where there was none.

Literal: iron buddies: rock-solid male friends
Figurative: 铁 (iron) intensifies 哥们儿. The metaphor is metal: a friendship that won't bend or rust. Reserved for the few friends you would drop everything for.

Literal: listen and yet not hear — to hear without registering; selective inattention
Figurative: 听 (the act of listening) + 而 (and yet, connecting contrast) + 不闻 (not actually hearing). The distinction between 听 (the directed act) and 闻 (what the ear actually receives) sharpens into an idiom: you can perform the physical act of listening without anything penetrating.

Literal: to leave it to Heaven — to accept fate without struggle
Figurative: Lit: listen-Heaven follow-fate. To stop fighting and let things take their natural course. Can be stoic acceptance or passive resignation depending on context. One of the most common fate-related expressions in everyday Chinese.
Tags: philosophy fate life classical ethics perception daily-life confucianism cosmology history politics

Literal: spirit communication — the shamanic gift
Figurative: 通 tōng (to connect, to pass through) + 灵 líng (spirit; efficacious; miraculous). The ability to communicate with spirits , the defining capacity of a shaman. In contemporary Chinese, 通灵 also appears in discussions of psychic ability, mediumship, and supernatural sensitivity more broadly.

Literal: through to feeling, reaching to reason: sensible, reasonable, understanding
Figurative: 通 (to be through to) + 情 qíng (human feeling; the way people are) + 达 dá (to reach) + 理 lǐ (reason; principle). A person who is 通情达理 understands both how people feel and what reason requires, and weighs the two fairly.
Tags: principle philosophy meaning characters emotion mind romance motion communication

Literal: plain and easy to understand
Figurative: High praise for writing or speech: 通俗 (accessible, popular) and 易懂 (easy to understand) together describe an explanation pitched so clearly that anyone can follow it. The standard compliment for good teaching.

Literal: sharing the same sickness, they pity each other: fellow sufferers sympathize
Figurative: From the Wú Yuè Chūnqiū. People who endure the same hardship feel a natural bond, the way two patients in one ward understand each other without explanation.

Literal: to share joys and hardships
Figurative: Literally "together the sweet, shared the bitter", to go through good times and bad side by side. It captures the deepest sense of 跟 as "with", a togetherness that holds through difficulty. Here 同 ("together") plays the accompanying role 跟 carries in speech.
Tags: society connections meaning characters grammar conjunction communication spoken

Literal: of one heart and one virtue — fully unified in purpose and conduct
Figurative: Lit: same-heart-same-virtue. The phrase for a group whose members share both inner orientation (心) and outward conduct (德). Used of teams, families, and political coalitions to describe rare and full unity , not just agreement on a goal but alignment on the moral terms by which it will be pursued.

Literal: to work together with one heart
Figurative: Literally "same heart, joined strength", to pull together toward a shared goal in full unity. It is the spirit behind 一起努力 ("work hard together") raised to its ideal: not just acting jointly, but acting as one mind and one effort.

Literal: in the same boat, crossing together: united by a common difficulty
Figurative: Lit: same-boat-jointly-cross. People who, sharing one boat, must row together to reach the far shore. The classical image for setting aside differences in the face of a shared crisis.

Literal: pain in the heart and ache in the head: bitterly grieved and resentful
Figurative: Lit: pain-heart-ache-head. To feel grief and indignation so deep that heart and head both ache. Used for bitter regret or anger over a wrong or a loss. 对这种浪费，他感到痛心疾首 "He was bitterly grieved at such waste."

Literal: clear and logical at every point: well-reasoned and articulate
Figurative: Lit: every-head-is-the-way. Said of speech or analysis that is orderly and convincing from start to finish, with each point landing soundly. 说得头头是道 "to argue every point convincingly."

Literal: heavy on top and light on the feet: top-heavy and unstable
Figurative: Lit: head-heavy-feet-light. Used of anything badly balanced, with too much weight or emphasis at the top: a wobbling structure, a lopsided plan, or a dizzy, unsteady feeling.

Literal: throw a peach, return a plum: to repay a kindness in kind; mutual gift-giving
Figurative: This idiom shares the verb 投 tóu (to throw; to give) that drives 投票, though it does not contain 票 itself, so it sits here as a near neighbor on the 投 thread rather than a 票 idiom. 投桃报李 comes from the Shījīng (Book of Songs): you toss me a peach, I send back a plum.

Literal: to advance by leaps and bounds: to progress at great speed
Figurative: Lit: sudden-fly-fierce-advance. Said of rapid, dramatic progress in study, technology, or an economy. 科技突飞猛进 "technology advances by leaps and bounds."

Literal: nothing but an empty name — a title with no substance behind it
Figurative: 徒 (merely, only) + 有 (have) + 虚名 (empty name). The sharpest everyday formulation of what 正名 opposes. A famous general who wins no battles is 徒有虚名. A top university whose graduates learn nothing is 徒有虚名.
Tags: confucianism confucius analects philosophy language ethics politics classical

Literal: the Tumu Crisis — the catastrophic defeat in which a Chinese emperor was captured by nomads
Figurative: The 1449 capture of Emperor Yingzong at Tumu Fortress (土木堡 Tǔmùbǎo) by Oirat Mongols under Esen Khan. A turning point that ended Ming offensive posture against the steppe and initiated the Great Wall rebuilding program. Used as a metonym for military disaster born of imperial overreach.

Literal: push out the old and bring forth the new
Figurative: To discard the outdated and create something new, the constant renewal that drives a thing forward into its modern form. Used of art, technology, and institutions that modernize by building fresh work on inherited foundations rather than simply repeating the past.
Tags: adjectives change modern vocabulary time history era daily-life

Literal: shed the womb, swap the bones: a total transformation
Figurative: From Daoist alchemy, on the adept reborn into an immortal frame. Modern usage praises a genuine, root-and-branch change for the better.

Literal: the awl-tip comes through the bag — talent that emerges despite obstacles
Figurative: From the Shǐjì (史记, Records of the Grand Historian). 颖 yǐng = the pointed tip of an awl. 脱 tuō = to escape; to break free. An awl placed in a bag will always eventually poke through: genuine talent, given any opportunity, will emerge and make itself visible.

Literal: Confucian on the outside, Legalist on the inside — the structural formula of Chinese imperial governance
Figurative: A modern scholarly formulation summarizing two thousand years of Chinese governance. 外 wài = outer, exterior; 内 nèi = inner, interior. The outer face of government (edicts, titles, rituals, examination texts) was thoroughly Confucian.

Literal: returning the jade intact to Zhao — restoring something to its owner undamaged
Figurative: From the Shiji biography of 蔺相如 Lin Xiangru, who carried the priceless 和氏璧 jade to the powerful state of Qin, saw through Qin's bad faith, and brought the jade safely home to Zhao through sheer nerve and cunning.
Tags: grammar daily-life language classics history han literature ancient biography

Literal: finished egg: to be done for, ruined, all over
Figurative: Not a four-character chengyu but a fixed colloquial expression. 完 (wán, to finish) + 蛋 marks total collapse: 完蛋了 (wándàn le) means we're finished, it's all over.

Literal: perfect and without flaw — utterly complete
Figurative: 完美 (perfect) + 无 wú (without) + 缺 quē (defect, lack, gap). Flawless to the point that nothing is missing and nothing could be improved. The two halves reinforce each other: 完美 asserts wholeness, 无缺 denies any gap.

Literal: the matter is finished and all is well — done and dusted
Figurative: 完 (to finish) + 事 shì (matter) + 大吉 dàjí (greatly auspicious, all is well). Said with relief when a task is over and one can stop worrying about it , "that's that, we're done." Sometimes carries a faint note of cutting corners, of treating the mere finishing as the whole point.

Literal: evergreen through ten thousand ages — enduring forever
Figurative: 万古 (ten-thousand ages, all of history) + 长青 (ever-green, perennially fresh). Used for ideas, institutions, or relationships that are wished to last beyond ordinary time.

Literal: the ten-thousand-li Great Wall — symbol of colossal collective effort
Figurative: 万里 wànlǐ (ten thousand li) is figurative hyperbole. The wall's actual total length across all dynasties is approximately 21,196 km. Used metaphorically for any enormous undertaking requiring sustained collective effort.
Tags: fortification settlement geography characters direction space daily-life qin unification first-emperor history dynasty great-wall ming architecture

Literal: the ten-thousand-li long march — the 1934–1935 retreat of the Red Army; any prolonged and arduous undertaking
Figurative: 万里 (ten thousand li , vast) + 长征 (long expedition, long march). The Chinese Communist Party's Long March (1934–1935) covered approximately 12,000 kilometers as the Red Army retreated from Nationalist forces. 万里 again functions as rhetorical superlative rather than measurement.

Pinyin: wàn shì jù bèi, zhǐ qiàn dōngfēng
Literal: all ten thousand things are ready; only the east wind is lacking
Figurative: From the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). Before the Battle of Red Cliffs (208 CE), Zhuge Liang tells Zhou Yu that the plan is complete in every respect , except that the wind is blowing in the wrong direction to set the enemy fleet alight.

Pinyin: wàn shì jù bèi, zhǐ qiàn dōngfēng.
Literal: Everything is ready; we lack only the east wind.
Figurative: From the eve of Red Cliffs, when the allies' fire-attack plan was fully prepared but needed a wind from the east to carry the flames into Cao Cao's fleet. The line is now a common chengyu for a situation in which all preparations are complete and only one final, decisive condition is missing.
Tags: history dynasty han statecraft strategy classical

Literal: all things renewed — the entire world refreshed and reborn
Figurative: 万 (ten thousand; all) + 象 (phenomena; appearances) + 更新 (to renew). The 更 is gēng, first tone. A classic New Year phrase; appears on Spring Festival banners alongside 春回大地 (spring returns to the earth).
Tags: grammar adverb comparison degree timing classical

Pinyin: wàn zhàng gāo lóu píng dì qǐ
Literal: A tower ten thousand zhang tall rises from flat ground
Figurative: The folk proverb that answers impatience: every immeasurable height begins on ordinary earth.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy daoism daodejing laozi education learning

Literal: ten thousand hearts as one — united as one body
Figurative: 万众 wànzhòng = the ten thousand people / the multitudes. 一心 = one heart / one mind. Used for collective unity in times of national effort or crisis. A rallying phrase in political rhetoric and public discourse , the aspiration that multiplicity collapses back into the cosmological One.
Tags: cosmology scale language philosophy taoism confucianism

Literal: ten thousand purples, a thousand reds — a riot of color; abundant beauty
Figurative: From the Song dynasty poet Zhu Xi 朱熹: 等闲识得东风面，万紫千红总是春 , "It is easy to recognize the face of the east wind: ten thousand purples and a thousand reds , it is all spring." The phrase moved from the poem into common use as the standard expression for spring's visual abundance.
Tags: cosmology scale language measure-words classifiers nouns

Literal: the music of a doomed state — decadent art that signals decline
Figurative: From the Liji 礼记: licentious music signals a state in moral collapse. Used today to criticize art deemed nihilistic or culturally destructive.

Literal: mend the sheep pen after the sheep is lost
Figurative: From the Zhanguo Ce: a man loses sheep through a hole in his pen and is told he is too late to repair it. A neighbor corrects the fatalist: remediation after a loss is not too late, it is exactly right.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms planning ethics colloquial daily-life

Pinyin: wáng yáng bǔ láo, wéi shí wèi wǎn
Literal: mend the pen after the sheep is lost — it is not yet too late
Figurative: The extended form of the idiom, almost always cited together. The second half (为时未晚, not yet too late) is the direct answer to the fatalist in the original story. The full eight-character phrase is common enough to function as a single fixed saying.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms planning ethics colloquial daily-life

Literal: lose a sheep, gain an ox
Figurative: A related phrase (not a classical chengyu in the same sense) used to describe a small loss that leads to an unexpected larger gain: the silver lining formulation. Where 亡羊补牢 is about repair, 亡羊得牛 is about serendipitous compensation. The shared 亡羊 makes the pair memorable.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms planning ethics colloquial daily-life

Literal: a constant stream of coming and going — uninterrupted traffic
Figurative: 往 wǎng (to go toward) + 来 (to come) + 不绝 (without cessation). Describes a place or relationship with continuous back-and-forth movement: traffic, commerce, correspondence, social connection. 街上人来人往，好不热闹 "People coming and going on the street , what a lively scene!"

Literal: rebirth in the Pure Land — the aspiration fulfilled at death
Figurative: The central Pure Land aspiration: to depart this world and arrive in Amitābha's Pure Land at death. In eulogies and memorial contexts: "She has been reborn in the Pure Land" 她已往生净土 is the standard Buddhist formulation for death.

Literal: the past is like drifting smoke
Figurative: Literally "bygone matters are like smoke", the past fading and dispersing beyond grasp. Here 往 takes its time sense, 往事 ("past events"), and the phrase carries a gentle melancholy about how what is gone slips away. The mirror of 往 reaching backward rather than ahead.

Literal: to work with selfless devotion; absorbed work
to see only the dust and never catch up: to be hopelessly outdistanced
Figurative: Literally "to gaze at the dust and be unable to reach." One can see only the dust kicked up by someone far ahead, with no hope of catching them. Used to admit that another is so far superior or so far in front that one cannot hope to match them.

Literal: to quench thirst by gazing at plums
Figurative: From a tale of Cao Cao, who told thirsty troops that plum groves lay ahead, so the thought of sour plums made their mouths water and eased their thirst. It means consoling oneself with an empty hope or imagined prospect. The 望 of gazing-toward is the same root that gives 希望 its reach.
Tags: perception feeling evaluation characters history han biography warlord poet poetry statecraft strategy vocabulary daily-life communication

Literal: hoping your daughter will become a phoenix — parental ambition for daughters
Figurative: The female counterpart to 望子成龙 wàng zǐ chéng lóng (hoping your son will become a dragon). 凤 fèng (phoenix) is the female auspicious creature paired with 龙 (dragon). The phoenix (凤凰 fènghuáng) represents feminine grace, beauty, and virtue.

Literal: gazing till the eyes would bore through: aching with anticipation
Figurative: Eyes straining at the road so hard they might pierce the distance. Describes longing for someone's return or news that will not come.

Literal: to hope ones son becomes a dragon: to long for ones child to succeed greatly
Figurative: Literally "to hope the son becomes a dragon," the dragon being the emblem of supreme success and distinction. The classic expression of parental ambition: the deep hope that ones child will rise high in life. A close partner phrase, 望女成凤, hopes the daughter becomes a phoenix.
Tags: perception feeling evaluation characters family confucianism nouns

Literal: alarming words to startle the listener: scaremongering
Figurative: Here 危 carries its older sense of high-pitched, alarming speech. Used to dismiss someone exaggerating a threat to frighten an audience. Mildly critical register.

Literal: danger lies in dawn-and-dusk: peril is imminent, near death
Figurative: Sānguó Zhì era usage. 旦夕 is the span of a single day; the danger is so close it could fall within hours. Used for a dying patient or a regime about to collapse.

Literal: the leather cord worn through three times — the archetype of devoted scholarship
Figurative: 韦 wéi = leather; 编 biān = cord, binding; 三绝 sān jué = worn through three times. Classical books were written on bamboo strips bound together with cords of leather or silk.

Literal: to compromise to keep the peace: to bend and yield so the whole holds together
Figurative: Lit: bend-crooked-seek-wholeness. To swallow grievances and make concessions in order to preserve a relationship or an arrangement intact. Here 全 is the intact whole one bends in order to save.

Literal: to do evil; to commit crimes and wrongdoing
Figurative: Lit: do-wrong-make-evil. 非 (wrong) and 歹 dǎi (bad, evil) pair up to name flagrant wrongdoing. Said of those who run riot doing harm: 为非作歹的歹徒 "evildoers who run amok."
Tags: negation logic meaning characters production writing

Literal: to be a henchman for the tiger; to help the powerful oppress others
Figurative: Lit: for-tiger-act-as-ghost-of-the-slain. In Chinese folklore, the ghost of someone eaten by a tiger becomes a 伥 , a spirit that lures future victims to the tiger. To 为虎作伥 is to be co-opted into serving the very power that devoured you.

Literal: to rid the people of a scourge
Figurative: To eliminate a menace for the public good, as a hero kills a man-eating beast. Praising tone, used for someone who removes a real threat.

Literal: to be a teacher and model for others: to set an example worthy of imitation
Figurative: 为人 wéi rén = to act as, to be for others. 师 shī = teacher. 表 biǎo = model; the standard others measure themselves against. To serve as a moral and intellectual example, especially said of teachers who must embody what they teach.

Pinyin: wéi xué rì yì, wéi dào rì sǔn.
Literal: In pursuit of learning, every day something is gained. In pursuit of the Dao, every day something is dropped.
Figurative: Chapter 48. The contrast with Confucius's emphasis on continuous learning and accumulation of knowledge is probably deliberate. The Daodejing does not reject learning but insists that the Dao requires a different movement: subtraction rather than addition, unlearning rather than accumulation.

Literal: prepare before the rain comes
Figurative: From the Book of Songs (诗经, Shījīng): the bird weaves its nest before the rains arrive. The counterpart to 亡羊补牢 , prevention before the fact. Together the two idioms cover the complete cycle of crisis management: prepare if you can, and repair decisively if prevention fails.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms planning ethics colloquial daily-life tense aspect time

Literal: review the old to understand the new — the scholar's relationship to tradition
Figurative: 温 (wēn, to warm; to review , warm water used to reheat food, hence to re-examine) + 故 (gù, old; former) + 知 (zhī, to know) + 新 (new). From the Analects of Confucius, Chapter 2.11: 子曰，温故而知新，可以为师矣。
Tags: meaning history memory characters change classical daily-life

Literal: the writing does not match the topic: off the point, irrelevant
Figurative: Lit: writing-not-match-topic. Said of an essay or answer that wanders away from what was asked, or of a reply that misses the actual question. The classic teacher's note on a stray composition.

Literal: the four treasures of the study: brush, ink, paper, inkstone
Figurative: 文房 is the scholar's study, the writing 房; 四宝 are its four treasures: 笔 (brush), 墨 (ink), 纸 (paper), 砚 (inkstone). The phrase names the classical toolkit of Chinese calligraphy and painting.
Tags: arts music classical confucianism literature calligraphy writing history aesthetics culture home daily-life settlement characters

Literal: accomplished in both letters and arms: master of both pen and sword
Figurative: Literally "civil and martial, both complete." The classic praise for a complete person who excels at both scholarship and fighting, the brush and the blade. The ideal whole human being in the traditional view, equally at home in the study and on the field.

Literal: writing carries the Way — literature serves moral truth
Figurative: The classical Chinese theory of literature: writing is not merely aesthetic entertainment but a vehicle for moral truth (道 Dào). Proposed by Han Yu (韩愈) in the Tang Dynasty and central to the Chinese literary tradition.

Literal: refined in manner and solid in substance — the cultivated gentleman
Figurative: From the Analects: 文质彬彬，然后君子. "When refinement (文) and substance (质) are balanced, then you have the gentleman." The ideal of 文 is not mere surface polish but the harmonious integration of outward culture with inner integrity. 彬彬 = harmonious, balanced.

Literal: hear the cock and rise to practice swordplay: diligent self-discipline
Figurative: From the Jin Shu account of Zǔ Tì (祖逖), who woke at the rooster's first crow to drill with his sword. A praise word for someone who studies or trains relentlessly.

Literal: as stable as Mount Tai — utterly immovable, rock solid
Figurative: Mount Tai (泰山, Shandong), the most sacred of the Five Peaks and site of imperial Heaven-sacrifice. Used to praise a person's composure, a government's stability, or a company's financial health.

Literal: to aspire to rule China — lit. "to inquire about the cauldrons of the Central Plains"
Figurative: From a Spring and Autumn anecdote: the king of Chu asked Zhou envoys about the weight of the Nine Cauldrons (九鼎), signaling his ambition to displace the Zhou. 问鼎 became permanently associated with political ambition at the highest level.
Tags: history confucianism classical dynasty ancient politics ritual philosophy classics bronze-age origins

Literal: the crux of the problem; the key issue
Figurative: A very common phrase pairing 问题 with 关键 (key, crux) to point at the heart of a matter: 问题的关键在于… ("the crux of the problem lies in…"). Used constantly in analysis and discussion to single out what really matters, the decisive point on which everything turns.

Literal: questioning the heart and finding no guilt — to have a clear conscience; to be at peace with what one has done
Figurative: 问 (to question; to examine) + 心 + 无愧 (without guilt; nothing to be ashamed of). To question one's own 心 and find no 愧 (guilt, shame) is the state of moral peace that comes from acting according to 良心. Used as an aspiration and as a claim. 我做这件事问心无愧。(In doing this, I have nothing on my conscience.)
Tags: ethics virtue confucianism human-nature philosophy mind wang-yangming

Literal: I don't think it matters either way; I have no preference.
Figurative: A useful everyday phrase pairing 觉得 with 无所谓 (it makes no difference, I don't mind). Used to signal an easygoing, no-strong-opinion stance when asked to choose. Shows how 觉得 frames even a non-opinion as a personal impression.

Literal: to go one's own way; to act as one always has
sleep on brushwood and taste gall — sustained self-discipline in pursuit of a long-deferred goal
Figurative: From the story of 越王勾践 Yuè Wáng Gōujiàn, king of Yue, defeated and humiliated by the king of Wu around 494 BCE.
Tags: history confucianism classical dynasty ancient politics ritual philosophy classics

Pinyin: wū lòu piān féng lián yè yǔ
Literal: the roof leaks, and then it rains all night — misfortunes come in clusters
Figurative: The Chinese equivalent of "when it rains, it pours." A leaking roof is already misfortune; continuous rain compounds it. Often quoted as half-proverb with the paired line: 船迟又遇打头风 (the boat is delayed and then hits a headwind). Very natural in everyday speech.

Literal: to groan without being sick: to complain for no reason
Figurative: A literary critic's jab at writers who manufacture sorrow they do not feel. Now applied to anyone who dramatizes trivial troubles or affects suffering for effect.

Literal: nothing comes to the right of it — unrivaled; the best of its kind
Figurative: 无 (nothing; none) + 出 (to go beyond; to surpass) + 其 (its; this) + 右 (right side). In classical Chinese ranking, the person or thing of highest rank occupied the rightmost position in certain formal arrangements. "Nothing surpasses it to the right" means nothing ranks higher.

Literal: all-pervading; present everywhere; reaching every corner
Figurative: 无 wú (without; no) + 处 chù (place) + 不 bù (not) + 到 (arrive). There is no place that is not arrived at. The double negative , no place that has not been reached , produces the emphatic positive: total pervasiveness.

Literal: everywhere; omnipresent — present in every place
Figurative: Lit: no-place-not-present. The double negative (无处 "no place" + 不在 "not present") creates a strong universal affirmative: present in every place without exception. Used for things that are all-pervasive , technology, a scent, an influence. 他的影响力无处不在。

Literal: impossible to grasp; no way to get a handle on it
Figurative: Lit: no-way-from-grasp. Used when a situation is too fluid, complex, or uncertain to control or predict. The physical image of reaching for something and finding no surface to grip carries directly into this idiom.

Literal: no ground on which to hold oneself: too ashamed to show one's face
Figurative: 无地 = no place; 自容 = to hold or hide oneself. So ashamed that there is nowhere on earth to put oneself. 容 here is the holding sense turned inward: no space will contain a person's shame. 听到批评，他羞愧得无地自容。(At the criticism, he was so ashamed he wished the ground would swallow him.)

Literal: unrelated to the important — trivial; beside the point; not worth worrying about
