Figurative: Lit: no-connection-tense-important. Used to dismiss irrelevant details or minor concerns. 这些细节无关紧要，我们不要在这里浪费时间。"These details are beside the point , let's not waste time on them." Often used as a diplomatic way to redirect a conversation.

Literal: of no help to the matter: useless, achieving nothing
Figurative: Lit: no-help-to-the-matter. Here 于 means "to, with respect to," so the phrase is literally "brings no benefit to the situation." Said of an effort or remedy that fails to change anything.

Literal: a treasure beyond price: a priceless thing
Figurative: 无价 (without price) marks what no sum could buy. Used for a rare heirloom, a one-of-a-kind artwork, or, warmly, for a person or a friendship.

Literal: nothing can be done about it — helpless; resigned; having no recourse
Figurative: 无 (nothing) + 可 (can) + 奈何 (what can be done; how to deal with). The expression of pure helplessness: there is no available action. 无可奈何，只能接受。(There was nothing to be done; one could only accept it.) One of the most-used classical phrases in modern speech.
Tags: grammar modal ability permission classical syntax communication pragmatics spoken

Literal: unsung hero — a hero without a name
Figurative: Lit: without-name hero. Someone who performs heroic deeds without receiving fame or recognition. The tension between 名 (name, recognition) and 实 (substance, actual contribution) compressed into a phrase.

Literal: powerless; unable to do anything about it
Figurative: Lit: have-no-ability-to-act-with-force. 无能 = lacking ability; 为力 = to exert effort/force. The standard idiom for expressing helplessness in the face of a problem. 对于这件事，我也无能为力 "I am also powerless over this matter." Formal and literary; widely used.
Tags: modal ability permission grammar adverb communication

Pinyin: wú shì bù dēng sānbǎo diàn
Literal: one doesn't visit the Three Jewels hall without a reason — never come empty-handed or without purpose
Figurative: The 三宝殿 is the hall of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, Sangha) , you don't enter it for nothing. The proverb is used to say: if someone is coming to see you or asking something, they must want something.

Literal: governing through non-action — the ideal Daoist political order
Figurative: The political application of 无为: the sage ruler does so little that people think they accomplished everything themselves. 太上，下知有之 (Daodejing 17): "The best ruler , the people merely know he exists." The phrase is widely used today for management styles that empower rather than micromanage.
Tags: grammar classical taoism philosophy daoism wuwei syntax religion immortality daodejing laozi

Literal: no gap worth striking — flawless, impeccable, impossible to fault
Figurative: 无 (no) + 懈 (slack; gap; weak point) + 可 (worth) + 击 (to strike). If there is no gap worth attacking, the argument or plan is airtight. 他的计划无懈可击。(His plan is flawless.) Common in formal debate and written argument.
Tags: grammar modal ability permission classical syntax

Literal: five lights, ten colors — multicolored and dazzling; richly varied
Figurative: 五光 (five kinds of light) and 十色 (ten colors) together evoke a brilliant, shifting display. Used both literally, for lights and decorations that glitter in every hue, and figuratively for a world or a scene that is varied, glamorous, and a little dazzling.

Literal: the five lakes and four seas: from every corner of the land
Figurative: A sweep of the whole country. Used warmly for people gathered from everywhere: 我们来自五湖四海。
Tags: nature settlement characters cosmology philosophy language

Literal: five limbs to the ground — to prostrate fully; to admire with complete humility
Figurative: 五体 (the five parts of the body: the two knees, the two elbows or hands, and the head) plus 投地 (cast to the ground). It names the Buddhist full prostration in which all five touch the floor, the deepest bodily gesture of reverence.
Tags: body health meaning characters cosmology philosophy language

Literal: the five phases generating and overcoming each other — the self-regulating logic of the cosmos
Figurative: The technical summary of the two cycles. 相生 xiāngshēng = mutual generation; 相克 xiāngkè = mutual overcoming/control. Together they describe a homeostatic system: generation without overcoming leads to excess; overcoming without generation leads to stagnation.

Literal: five shades, six colors — a riot of colors; multicolored
Figurative: Lit: five-shades-six-colors. The standard idiom for anything vibrantly multicolored. 五 and 六 are figurative numbers (like English "many"); the compound just means extremely colorful. 市场上五颜六色的花朵 "the market's riot of colorful flowers."

Literal: Wu Song fights the tiger — fearless strength against great odds
Figurative: The most famous single episode in the novel: the hero Wu Song, drunk and alone on Jingyang Ridge, kills a man-eating tiger with his bare hands.
Tags: literature novels classics classical song rebellion

Literal: highly skilled in martial arts: a formidable fighter
Figurative: Literally "martial skill high and strong." Describes a person of outstanding fighting ability, a master whose technique is far above the ordinary. 武艺 is the craft of arms, the practised techniques of combat; 高强 marks it as superior.

Literal: things change, stars shift — time passes and the world turns over
Figurative: From Wang Bo's Tang-dynasty Pavilion of Prince Teng poem: 物换星移几度秋, "things change, stars shift, how many autumns now?" The stars' slow precession as the clock of dynasties. Used for nostalgia at scale: returning to a transformed hometown, rereading an old diary.
Tags: motion daily-life characters astronomy cosmology nature

Literal: when things reach their extreme, they necessarily reverse — the law of cyclical transformation
Figurative: 物 wù = things; 极 jí = extreme, apex; 必 bì = necessarily; 反 fǎn = to reverse. This is the fundamental law of Yin-Yang cosmology, applicable to all phenomena: the hottest summer carries the seed of winter; the most powerful dynasty carries the seed of its decline; a pendulum at its extreme cannot stay…
Tags: philosophy divination cosmology classics yin-yang five-phases

Literal: let everything exhaust its use — no waste; make the most of every resource
Figurative: 物 wù = things; resources; material. 尽 jìn = to exhaust; to use fully. Let every thing fully deploy its capacity, leaving nothing wasted. A principle of material ethics as much as economics: the proper relationship between a person and the world's resources is stewardship, not waste.

Literal: the goods fine and the price cheap: excellent value for money
Figurative: The four-character verdict every shopper hopes to pronounce: good quality and a low price at once. Standard praise in advertising and casual recommendation alike.
Tags: society social daily-life characters things science nature

Literal: things remain but people have changed — the bittersweet feeling of returning to a place where everything looks the same but everyone is gone
Figurative: Lit: things-are-people-not. A key phrase in classical Chinese poetry for the emotional experience of historical rupture: looking at unchanged landscapes after dynasties have fallen. Deeply appropriate to the Yuan-Ming transition, when the same cities stood but an entire ruling order had vanished.

Literal: things gather by kind: like attracts like, birds of a feather flock together
Figurative: Lit: things-by-kind-gather. From the idea that creatures of a sort come together; often paired with 人以群分 "people divide into groups," and used, sometimes pointedly, of who keeps company with whom.

Literal: To Stray onto the Wrong Road
Figurative: The four-character idiom for taking a wrong turn, whether morally, professionally, or literally. Where 迷途知返 describes the recovery, 误入歧途 describes the moment things went wrong.

Literal: looking at flowers through mist — seeing something obscurely, without clarity
Figurative: 雾 (mist, fog) + 里 (inside, within) + 看花 (looking at flowers). The object of perception is real, but the medium prevents clear sight. Used for situations where the truth is obscured , murky political signals, ambiguous intentions, confusing circumstances.

Literal: the evening sun descends in the west — dusk; things in decline
Figurative: 夕阳 (setting sun) + 西 (west) + 下 (to descend). A classic image from Tang dynasty poetry: the sun dropping below the western horizon. Used literally for beautiful sunsets and metaphorically for the decline of an era, a career, or a life.

Literal: the Western Pure Land — and by extension, any paradise or blissful realm
Figurative: The formal name 西方极乐世界 Xīfāng Jílè Shìjiè is abbreviated to 西方极乐 in common usage. In pure religious context: Amitābha's Buddha-field. In broader cultural use: any ideal realm of beauty, abundance, and peace.

Literal: every breath mutually connected — closely and inextricably interconnected
Figurative: Lit: breath-breath-mutually-connected. 息 = breath. The image: two systems breathing in such synchrony that they cannot be separated. Used for things that are organically and necessarily connected. 这两个问题息息相关，解决一个就能推动另一个。"These two issues are inextricably linked , solving one will advance the other."

Literal: grinning cheekily: to behave with a flippant, unserious grin
Figurative: A face stuck in a smirk, used to describe someone who refuses to take a moment seriously. Often a parent's rebuke to a child who jokes through a scolding.

Literal: to grow so used to a thing that it seems ordinary
Figurative: Lit: practice-take-to-be-normal. What was once strange or hard becomes routine through repetition, until one no longer notices it. Often said of bad habits or hardships one has stopped questioning.

Literal: move the post, establish credibility — demonstrate that stated commitments will be honored
Figurative: Shang Yang's wooden post demonstration before his Qin reforms: post a reward, honor it fully, establish that the state means what it says.
Tags: ancient dynasty history philosophy legalism statecraft politics classics

Literal: joy beyond what one hoped — overjoyed by surprise
Figurative: 喜 (delight) arriving from outside (外) the range of expectation (望). The precise word for good news you did not dare hope for: the scholarship, the recovered wallet, the friend at the airport gate. Stronger and more specific than 很高兴.
Tags: space meaning family characters emotion culture feeling spoken daily-life

Literal: as long as you like it, that's enough
Figurative: A warm everyday phrase, not a classical chengyu, used when giving a gift or making a choice for someone: if you like it, that's all that matters. It captures a generous, easygoing attitude and is one of the most common natural uses of 喜欢 in spoken Chinese.

Literal: brimming with joy: radiant with a festive, happy spirit
Figurative: Lit: festive air spilling over. 洋洋 paints joy overflowing in every direction. Said of a face, a household, or a whole town lit up with celebration, a stock phrase at weddings and the New Year.

Literal: glad to hear and pleased to see — popular and well-liked
Figurative: Describes something the public genuinely enjoys and welcomes, literally "glad to hear it and happy to see it." 喜 (glad) and 乐 lè (happy) pair with 闻 (hear) and 见 (see). Often used of art, entertainment, or activities that are widely and warmly received.
Tags: emotion culture family characters vocabulary feeling daily-life

Literal: joy takes shape in the face: visibly delighted
Figurative: Lit: joy 喜 takes form 形 upon 于 the complexion 色. Happiness that cannot be hidden and shows plainly on the face. Here 形 is verbal, "to take shape, to appear," a clear window onto the verb sense of the character.
Tags: aesthetics culture color philosophy perception geometry meaning characters classical cohesion

Literal: first come, first served
Figurative: Literally "the early-comers and the later-arrivers", the order of precedence set by who came first. It rests on the same 先 ("first") and 后 ("after") that frame 然后, here applied to fairness in turn-taking and priority. The natural order of a queue.

Literal: first courtesy, then arms — try diplomacy before resorting to force
Figurative: From the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义). The classical strategic principle: open with 礼 (courteous communication), and only if that fails escalate to 兵 (military force or coercive action).

Literal: what enters first becomes master: first impressions dominate later judgment
Figurative: Lit: first-enter-become-master. The idea that lodges in the mind earliest takes the seat of authority and colors everything after it, the classical name for the grip of a first impression or a prior bias.

Literal: petty men first, gentlemen after — settle terms up front
Figurative: The contract-signing proverb: state the money, the split, and the deadlines with un-gentlemanly explicitness now, so that everyone can afford to be a gentleman later. Spoken at the start of partnerships between friends precisely because friendship is what it protects.

Literal: the note beyond the strings: an unspoken meaning, the overtone behind the words
Figurative: Lit: outside-the-string's sound. The sense a speaker implies without saying it outright, like the overtones a plucked string sets ringing. To catch the 弦外之音 is to hear what someone really means.

Literal: obvious; plain to see: needing no explanation
Figurative: Lit: evident-and-easy-to-see. The 而 joins "evident" to "easily seen," so plain that it is grasped at a glance. Often opens a sentence stating something taken as self-evident.

Literal: to appear in person and teach by example: to instruct from one's own experience
Figurative: Lit: show-the-body-and-expound-the-teaching. Originally Buddhist, of a deity appearing in bodily form to preach. Now it means to teach others by drawing on what one has personally lived through.

Literal: to complement each other: two things that reinforce and complete one another
Figurative: Lit: mutually-assist mutually-complete. Said of two factors that work together so that each makes the other stronger, like theory and practice or form and content.

Literal: to be close and loving — mutual affection between people
Figurative: Lit: mutually-close mutually-love. The standard phrase for loving harmony in a family or couple. Often used in toasts and wedding speeches.

#fields:Hanzi: 相濡以沫，不如相忘于江湖
Pinyin: xiāng rú yǐ mò, bùrú xiāng wàng yú jiānghú
Literal: Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes than to sustain each other with spit
Figurative: From 大宗师. The first half, 相濡以沫, has become an independent chengyu meaning "mutual support and care in difficult circumstances" (the fish sustaining each other in a drying puddle). Used positively for devoted couples or friends who help each other through hardship.

Literal: to depend on one another for life; to be each other's only support
Figurative: 相依 "mutually depending" plus 为命 "for life." Said of two people whose survival depends on each other: a widow and her child, two siblings orphaned together, an old couple in their final years. Carries deep emotional weight; not used lightly. Often appears in family stories and biographical writing.

Literal: incense smoke; the vitality of a temple's active veneration
Figurative: Literally "incense fire" or "incense smoke," but 香火 carries meanings beyond the physical act of burning. A temple with 香火鼎盛 xiānghuo dǐngshèng (incense burning vigorously) is a temple with a healthy, active congregation, good reputation, and real spiritual efficacy.
Tags: folk-religion religion gods culture history ritual ancestors mazu goddess coast family

Literal: to think of squares and devise methods: to try every possible means
Figurative: Lit: think-method-set-up-method. To rack one's brains for a way through, doing whatever it takes. 方 and 法 here both carry the "method" sense, doubled for emphasis.
Tags: legal religion meaning characters space geometry

Literal: to let the mind wander into improper territory; lost in fantasy
Figurative: 想 xiǎng (to think; to imagine) + 入 rù (to enter; to go into) + 非非 fēifēi (beyond right and wrong; in Buddhist usage, the realm beyond ordinary thought).

Literal: a small dish on a plate: a piece of cake, an easy matter
Figurative: Lit: small-dish-one-saucer. A 小菜 is a minor side dish, trivial next to the main course, so 小菜一碟 means a task so easy it is hardly worth mentioning. 这对我来说是小菜一碟 "this is a piece of cake for me."

Pinyin: xiǎohái méi niáng, shuō lái huà cháng
Literal: the child has no mother: it's a long story
Figurative: A 歇后语 (xiēhòuyǔ) two-part saying. The literal image, a motherless child, sets up the punchline 说来话长, "it's a long story." Spoken as a preface when the backstory is tangled and the speaker hardly knows where to begin.

Literal: just a kid, only a child
Figurative: Colloquial set phrase. The trailing 家 marks a category of person; said dismissively or fondly of someone too young to know better. "你一个小孩子家懂什么。"

Literal: childish, immature in manner
Figurative: Describes adult behavior that is petty or babyish. The 气 (qì) suffix turns a noun into a temperament. Everyday spoken register: "他这样太小孩子气了。"

Literal: the petty man gets his moment — power in unworthy hands
Figurative: 得志 is achieving one's ambitions; attached to 小人 it names the special insufferability of the schemer promoted. The stock description of the new supervisor swaggering through a department, and of every court favorite in the historical novels.

Literal: to make a big production of a small topic — to overreact
Figurative: 小 xiǎo (small) + 题 tí (topic, subject) + 大 dà (big) + 做 (to make, to treat). Originally from the examination tradition, where a trivial topic was expanded into a grand essay; now it means blowing a minor matter out of proportion.
Tags: education meaning communication characters confucianism daily-life adjectives grammar social

Literal: with extreme care and caution; treading very lightly
Figurative: Lit: small-heart wing-wing. The 翼翼 reduplication comes from the Shijing (Classic of Poetry) where it described birds folding their wings carefully.

Literal: a dagger hidden in a smile: friendly on the surface, treacherous beneath
Figurative: Lit: laugh-inside hide-knife. Traced to the Tang minister Lǐ Yìfǔ, whose mild smile masked a ruthless heart. Names a person whose warmth is a weapon, the dark twin of 微笑.

Literal: hold the emperor to command the lords — rule through a puppet figurehead
Figurative: Cao Cao's signature strategy: control a powerless legitimate ruler and issue your own orders in their name. Now a standard idiom for anyone who wields real power from behind a respectable figurehead, in politics or business. It names the gap between formal authority and actual control.
Tags: history han biography warlord poet poetry statecraft strategy

Literal: absent-minded; not mentally present
Figurative: Lit: heart-not-present-there. 焉 yān is a classical demonstrative "there." The heart/mind (心 xīn , the seat of consciousness in Chinese tradition) is absent from the place where the body sits. Used to describe distraction, daydreaming, or emotional distance during a conversation or task. 他上课时总是心不在焉。

Literal: heart-urgent, fire-scorching — desperately impatient and anxious
Figurative: Lit: heart-urgent-fire-scorch. The sensation of being so anxious that you feel fire scorching your insides. Used for people in unbearable suspense, waiting for important news.

Literal: heart anxious as if burning: consumed with worry
Figurative: 焚 (fén) is to set ablaze. The heart so 急 it feels on fire, used for someone waiting in agony for urgent news. Literary and intense.

Literal: quick heart, straight mouth — frank and direct by nature
Figurative: Lit: heart-fast-mouth-straight. A description of someone whose inner state and outer speech are perfectly aligned: no strategic filtering, no diplomatic softening. Used as a compliment among people who value directness, and occasionally as an excuse after saying something pointed.

Literal: heart vast, spirit at ease — expansive peace and contentment in beautiful surroundings
Figurative: 旷 kuàng = open; vast (like an open plain). 怡 yí = pleased; comfortable. The specific feeling of contentment and openness experienced in a beautiful landscape, after a burden lifts, or at a moment of rare clarity. Common at scenic spots: 站在山顶，令人心旷神怡。

Literal: heart receives, spirit understands — to understand without words; to grasp intuitively
Figurative: Lit: heart-receive-spirit-comprehend. The ideal of Chinese social understanding: no explicit statement is needed. You see, you understand, you nod. This is 意思 operating at its highest level , the meaning is fully communicated without ever being spoken. 他点了点头，心领神会。

Literal: heart full and wishes fulfilled: perfectly content and satisfied
Figurative: Lit: heart-full-intent-satisfied. Pairs 心 and 意 again, both filled to the brim. Said of someone wanting for nothing, the calm fullness of having one's desires met.

Literal: heart and mind unsettled: distracted and uneasy
Figurative: Lit: heart-spirit-not-settled. Said of a restless, distracted state in which the mind cannot come to rest, often from worry or anticipation. The opposite of 镇定.

Pinyin: xīn wài wú lǐ, xīn wài wú wù
Literal: outside the mind there is no principle; outside the mind there are no things
Figurative: Two formulations of Wang Yangming's central thesis in their most direct form. 心外无理 xīn wài wú lǐ directly contradicts Zhu Xi: principle is not outside the mind awaiting investigation.

Literal: may what the heart wishes come true
Figurative: 心 xīn (heart) + 想 xiǎng (think; wish) + 事 shì (matter; affair) + 成 chéng (to succeed; to be accomplished). A blessing structure: heart-wishes turn into accomplished realities. Among the most common felicitations in Chinese , standard at New Year (新年快乐，心想事成！), birthdays, and before examinations.
Tags: mind emotion philosophy vocabulary modal evaluation communication

Literal: with one's whole heart and every thought — to dwell on something constantly
Figurative: A doubled, rhythmic phrase stacking 心 (heart) and 念 (thought): every beat of the heart, every flicker of mind, bent on one object. 她心心念念想回家 (her every thought is set on going home).

Literal: heart imprinting on heart — deep mutual understanding; soul connection
Figurative: 印 yìn = seal; to stamp. Like two wax seals pressed together making a perfect impression , silent, complete correspondence between two people's inner worlds. 他们心心相印，不需要多说话就能理解彼此。

Literal: hearts share the rhinoceros horn — telepathic understanding; being on the same wavelength
Figurative: From a Tang poem by Li Shangyin (李商隐): 身无彩凤双飞翼，心有灵犀一点通. The rhinoceros horn was believed in classical natural philosophy to have a channel running through its center , an image of two hearts with a shared passage between them, allowing understanding to flow without words.

Literal: mind like a monkey, will like a horse — a restless, unsettled mind
Figurative: A Buddhist-Daoist image, central to the novel's allegory, of the mind as an unruly monkey and the will as a bolting horse, leaping and galloping where it pleases. The Monkey King is literally the 心猿, the mind-monkey, who must be tamed.
Tags: literature novels classics classical buddhism pilgrimage

Literal: the heart knows and the belly is clear — everyone understands, nobody says it
Figurative: Knowledge distributed through the torso: heart knowing, belly bright. The phrase for open secrets: the office 心知肚明 about why the manager left; both negotiators 心知肚明 about the real bottom line. Understanding at its most silent.

Literal: flourishing and thriving: full of vigor and growth
Figurative: Lit: joyful-joyful, facing-flourishing. 欣欣 is the look of glad, vigorous growth; 向荣 is turning toward flourishing. Said of plants in full bloom, and by extension of a thriving enterprise or society.

Literal: the new replaces the old: metabolism; constant renewal
Figurative: Lit: new and old, replacing and discharging. The scientific term for metabolism, the body taking in the new and expelling the spent. Figuratively, the natural cycle by which fresh things supersede worn-out ones in any system.

Literal: to open the mouth like a river — to speak carelessly; to say whatever comes to mind without regard for truth
Figurative: 信 xìn here shifts sense: 信 kǒu = to trust one's mouth, to follow wherever the mouth goes (the archaic sense of 信 as "to follow freely"). 开河 kāi hé = to open a river, to let it flow unobstructed.

Literal: pick up casually with a free hand — to write or create with effortless skill
Figurative: Lit: trust-hand-pick up-come. Used of writers, calligraphers, and scholars who produce refined work without apparent effort. The idiom implies deep mastery: the hand moves freely because the mind no longer needs to deliberate. Often said of someone who writes beautifully on demand.

Literal: arrayed like stars, spread like chess pieces — dotted everywhere
Figurative: 星罗 (netted like stars) + 棋布 (laid out like go stones). The standard descriptor for anything scattered densely across a landscape: lakes on a delta, islands in an archipelago, convenience stores in Shanghai. The two images, night sky and go board, are both grids the classical eye knew intimately.

Literal: a single spark can set the prairie ablaze
Figurative: 星星 here is the spark sense of 星. The image of fire racing across a plain is ancient (the Book of Documents already warns of fire on the grassland), but the phrase's modern fame comes from Mao Zedong's 1930 essay taking it as a title, arguing a small revolutionary force could ignite the country.

Literal: a walking corpse, a moving piece of flesh — alive in body but dead in spirit
Figurative: Lit: walking-corpse, walking-flesh. Said of someone who has lost the inner life that makes a person alive in any meaningful sense , going through motions without thought, feeling, or purpose. Sharp, almost cruel; reserved for those judged to have given up entirely.
Tags: food body daily-life characters movement motion ethics

Literal: every trade produces its champion — every line of work has its top practitioner
Figurative: Lit: every-row produces a 状元 (the top scholar in the imperial exam). The folk-wisdom rebuttal to anyone who says one trade is beneath another: every trade has its master, every craft has its top practitioner, and excellence is available wherever you are.

Literal: like drifting clouds and flowing water — natural, effortless, unforced
Figurative: Lit: walking-clouds, flowing-water. The classical praise for prose, calligraphy, conversation, or any skilled action that has reached the point of unforced motion. The sister-image to 自然 (naturalness): the result is fluid because nothing is being held against the grain.

Literal: walk throughout the world — to travel the world boldly
Figurative: The romantic image of the 江湖 adventurer or itinerant scholar: someone who has traveled all under Heaven, accumulating experience and connections. The phrase captures the Chinese ideal of the person who has moved through the world and is at home everywhere.

Literal: a lone form, a single shadow: solitary and without companions
Figurative: Lit: the form is alone, the shadow is single. The mirror image of 形影不离: here there is only one form and its one shadow, no one alongside. A literary, somewhat melancholy phrase for a person who is utterly on their own.

Literal: all shapes and colors: of every kind, all sorts
Figurative: Lit: shape-shape, color-color. The reduplication piles up variety: people, goods, schemes, opinions of every imaginable kind. 形形色色的人 = all sorts of people. Often carries a faint edge of "a mixed bag," not all of it admirable.

Literal: form and shadow never part: inseparable
Figurative: Lit: form and shadow do not separate. A shadow follows its form everywhere; two people who are 形影不离 are constant companions, always together. Warm and affectionate, used for close friends, devoted couples, or a child who will not leave a parent's side.
Tags: motion nature characters perception geometry meaning grammar conjunction communication spoken direction space

Literal: spirits high, expression ablaze — in jubilant high spirits
Figurative: Originally literary criticism: Liu Xie's Wenxin Diaolong used 兴高而采烈 to praise the poet Ji Kang's lofty inspiration and brilliant style. The phrase migrated from describing writing to describing faces, and now marks any scene of visible collective joy: children on the last day of school arrive 兴高采烈.

Literal: the lessons of rise and fall — the standard analytical frame for the Taiping in modern Chinese historiography
Figurative: 兴 (rise, flourish) + 亡 (fall, perish) + 教训 (lesson, warning). Not a fixed classical chengyu but a recurring analytical phrase in modern Chinese historical writing, particularly in discussions of the Taiping.

Literal: a matter of life and death: bearing directly on survival
Figurative: Literally "bearing on life itself." Here 性命 means life, the vital nature that animates the body. The phrase marks something as gravely serious, a matter on which survival hangs, as in 性命攸关的决定, a life-or-death decision.

Literal: much ill fortune, little good — the outlook is grim
Figurative: 多 and 少 as a probability report: on the scale of outcomes, the bad end is heavy. The stock phrase of thriller narration and worried families when someone has gone missing; expect it in every wuxia novel's darkest chapter.

Literal: brothers and sisters; siblings
Figurative: The full set of siblings named in birth-order pairs: 兄 (elder brother), 弟 (younger brother), 姐 (elder sister), 妹 (younger sister). A staple four-character phrase, and one of the few common ones to carry 姐 directly.

Literal: sharing joys and sorrows: bound together by a common fate
Figurative: Lit: joy-sorrow-mutually-connected. Two parties so closely tied that whatever befalls one befalls the other, the deep 关系 in which fortunes rise and fall as one.

Literal: to watch from the sidelines with folded arms: to look on without lifting a finger
Figurative: Lit: sleeve-hands-aside-watch. With hands tucked in the sleeves, the onlooker stands by and does nothing while others struggle. A reproach for passivity and refusal to help.

Literal: a mind as open as a valley — profound receptivity; the deepest form of intellectual humility
Figurative: The Daoist counterpart to the Confucian 谦谦君子. Where the Confucian formulation focuses on the social expression of humility in hierarchical relationships, 虚怀若谷 focuses on the inner orientation , the mind that has genuinely emptied itself of the need to be right, to have known first, to defend its exi…

Literal: to have only its surface: impressive on the outside but hollow within; all show and no substance
Figurative: 虚 xū = empty; hollow; in vain. 有其表 yǒu qí biǎo = to have (only) its outer appearance. The phrase describes something or someone that looks fine on the surface but lacks real worth underneath. 这家公司虚有其表，其实早就负债累累。

Literal: the noisy guest usurps the host: a secondary thing overshadows the main one
Figurative: Lit: clamoring-guest-seizes-host. Said when something minor draws all the attention away from what should be central, like a sideshow that swallows the main event or a flashy detail that buries the point.

Pinyin: xuē jiān nǎodai wǎng lǐ zuān
Literal: to sharpen one's head and bore in: to push to the front of the queue
Figurative: A colloquial saying, not a classical 成语, paired here with 加塞儿 (jiāsāir, to cut the line). Mentioned to contrast the orderly 排队 ideal with the elbows-out reality of a crowded queue.

Literal: Learning cannot stop — the process of cultivation has no natural endpoint
Figurative: Opening line of the Xunzi and of the 劝学 chapter, the programmatic statement of Xunzi's entire educational philosophy. 已 yǐ: to stop, to cease. The philosophical force follows from the 性恶论: if goodness is not innate but must be cultivated, then the cultivation is never complete by its own logic.

Literal: to study and constantly practice what one has learned — the joy of learning
Figurative: The opening phrase of the Analects (1.1). 时 shí means "at the right times" or "constantly/regularly"; Confucius is describing not cramming but sustained, rhythmic practice. 习 xí originally depicted a young bird practicing flight: iteration until mastery.

Pinyin: xué ér shí xí zhī, bù yì yuè hū?
Literal: Is it not a pleasure to learn and repeatedly practice what you have learned?
Figurative: Opening line of the Analects (1.1). The word 说 here is read yuè, an archaic form of 悦 "pleased, delighted." The passage continues: "Is it not a joy to have friends come from afar? Is it not a mark of the noble person not to be resentful when others do not recognize him?" Three questions that establi…

Literal: excel in learning, then enter officialdom
Figurative: From the Analects (子张 chapter): the formulation attributed to Confucius's disciple Zixia establishing the connection between scholarly achievement and public service. 优 (yōu) means to excel, to have surplus capacity; 仕 (shì) means to serve in office.
Tags: history confucianism tang song ming qing

Literal: learning fills five carts — immensely learned; erudite
Figurative: 学 (learning) is 富 (rich enough) to fill 五车 (five cartloads of books). The image comes from an age when books were bamboo strips, so that a serious library was measured by the cartload. Originally said of the philosopher Hui Shi, whose writings were said to fill five carts.
Tags: literacy culture calligraphy cosmology philosophy language

Literal: learning has no boundary — there is always more to know
Figurative: Lit: learning-has-no-stopping-point. The classical formulation of intellectual humility , no matter how much one has learned, the frontier of knowledge remains inexhaustible. Used to encourage continued study and to discourage complacency.

Literal: learn in order to apply — practical application of knowledge
Figurative: Lit: learn-by-means-of-reach-use. The Confucian insistence that learning is not ornamental but practical: knowledge must be applied in action to have value. The opposite of empty book-learning (书呆子 shū dāizi, "bookworm" in the pejorative sense).
Tags: confucianism education culture philosophy daoism daily-life grammar

Literal: frost on top of snow — to make a bad situation even worse
Figurative: 雪 xuě (snow) + 上 shàng (on top of) + 加 jiā (to add) + 霜 shuāng (frost). Frost piled on snow already covering the ground: one hardship stacked on another. The everyday equivalent of "to rub salt in the wound" or "when it rains, it pours." 他刚失业，妻子又生病了，真是雪上加霜。

Literal: to send charcoal in the snow: timely help when it is needed most
Figurative: The image is bringing fuel to someone freezing in a blizzard. Praises aid that arrives at the moment of real need, the warm counterpart of 锦上添花 (adding flowers to brocade), which only embellishes what is already fine. Still in everyday use.
Tags: motion social daily-life characters direction grammar nature weather winter

Literal: blood and flesh linked: tied as closely as flesh to blood
Figurative: A near-twin of 骨肉相连, stressing the living, circulating closeness between people, or between an individual and a cause they cannot separate from.

Literal: to advance step by step in order
Figurative: Literally "following the sequence, advancing gradually", to progress in proper order without rushing. It is the principle behind any 先…然后…最后 plan: each step in its turn, the next only after the last. A watchword in learning and training.
Tags: motion meaning direction characters vocabulary conjunction timing communication

Literal: trained to a standard: well-drilled, disciplined
Figurative: 素 here means a long-cultivated grounding. Praises a team, unit, or staff whose competence is visibly the product of systematic 训练 rather than luck.

Literal: not a crow or sparrow to be heard — dead silence
Figurative: The silence so complete even the loudest birds have stopped. The stock description of a classroom after a hard question, a courtroom before a verdict, a banquet after an unwise toast. Its cousin 悄无声息 describes stealth rather than hush.
Tags: phonology perception communication characters language vocabulary

Literal: strict in disciplining oneself: hold yourself to a high standard
Figurative: Lit: strict-toward-disciplining-self. Often paired with 宽以待人, "lenient toward others," to describe the admired character who is hard on the self and gentle with everyone else.

Literal: words that always hit the mark; speech that is measured and unfailingly accurate
Figurative: From Analects XI.14: Confucius describes a man who rarely speaks , 不言则已，一言必中: but when he does, always hits the target. 中 zhòng here means "center; bull's-eye," not "middle." The standard for speech that earns its right to be heard: few words, each one aimed and landing.
Tags: grammar modal logic classical ethics philosophy

Literal: words cannot exhaust meaning — the inadequacy of language; what remains unsaid
Figurative: Lit: words-not-exhaust-meaning. A classical lament about the limits of language , that what one truly means always exceeds what words can carry. Found in literary correspondence, essays, and poetry. Often appears at the end of letters: 语言有限，言不尽意。

Literal: to teach by word and by example: to instruct both through speech and through one's own conduct
Figurative: Lit: words pass it on, the body teaches it. Describes the ideal of a teacher or parent who not only explains in words (言传) but also models the lesson through their own actions (身教). The deeper teaching is the one carried by example.
Tags: transmission communication culture characters education religion society

Literal: to speak and be trustworthy — to be as good as one's word
Figurative: 言 yán (to speak; words) + 而 ér (and; then; connecting two qualities) + 有 yǒu (to have; to possess) + 信 xìn (trustworthiness).

Literal: let the words return to the main story: to get back to the main topic
Figurative: Lit: words return to the proper narrative. A storyteller's phrase, after a digression, for steering back to the central thread. Notably 传 takes the zhuàn reading here, since 正传 means the main body of the tale, the narrative proper, not a casual transmission.

Literal: brief words, complete meaning — concise and comprehensive
Figurative: 简 jiǎn = brief, few; 意 yì = meaning, intention; 赅 gāi = complete, thorough (a relatively rare character used almost exclusively in this idiom). The highest praise for a piece of writing or a speaker: nothing wasted, nothing missing.

Literal: words heard, plans followed — to comply with every word and plan
Figurative: 言 (words) + 听 (heeded) + 计 (plans, strategies) + 从 (followed). Whatever someone says is accepted; whatever they plan is implemented. Used to describe a relationship of complete compliance , a ruler who accepts all counsel from a trusted advisor, or a person who follows another uncritically.

Literal: words and actions align — to practice what you preach
Figurative: 言 yán (words) + 行 xíng (actions) + 一致 yīzhì (consistent; in agreement). The Confucian virtue of correspondence between speech and conduct. Used as a positive description of trustworthy, reliable people, and as a standard against which behaviour is measured.

Literal: covering one's ears to steal the bell — self-deception
Figurative: From the Lüshi Chunqiu: a thief found the great bell of the fallen Fan clan too heavy to carry, decided to break it up, and covered his own ears against the clang so no one would hear.

Literal: eyes blurring, vision tangling — dazzled, overwhelmed by abundance
Figurative: Lit: eye-flower-tangle-disorder. Used for the sensory overload of a busy market, a fireworks display, a dazzling performance: too much beauty or activity to take in at once. Almost always positive in tone (the overload of richness, not chaos).

Literal: to feel proud and elated; to finally breathe out after long suffering
Figurative: Lit: raise-eyebrows-exhale-qi. The physical sensation of relief and pride after enduring hardship or injustice. The eyebrows lift, the breath that was held in tension is finally released. Used for vindication, promotion after years of struggle, or national pride after historical humiliation.

Literal: play up strengths, avoid weaknesses: lean into what you do well
Figurative: Common in advice and strategy contexts; the practical companion to 取长补短.

Literal: obey openly, defy in secret — to comply in appearance while resisting in private
Figurative: 阳 yáng (openly) + 奉 fèng (to obey; to comply) + 阴 yīn (covertly) + 违 wéi (to disobey). To nod and agree to someone's face while quietly doing the opposite behind their back. The phrase turns on the 阴 / 阳 contrast of overt and covert: the visible compliance is 阳, the hidden defiance is 阴.

Literal: to support the family and feed its mouths: to provide for one's household
Figurative: Lit: support-family-keep-alive-mouths. Here 活 is causative, to keep alive by feeding. The duty of the breadwinner to put food on the table and sustain everyone under the roof.

Literal: to chew and gnaw on words — nitpicking at wording; pedantic attention to phrasing
Figurative: 咬 = to bite; 嚼 = to chew. Vividly imagines someone masticating language rather than simply reading it. Can be used approvingly (careful, attentive reading) or critically (pedantry, missing the point). Context determines the register.

Literal: the medicine arrives, the illness is gone: an instant, effective cure
Figurative: A praise phrase for a skilled doctor or a decisive remedy. Extended to any solution that fixes a problem cleanly and at once.

Pinyin: yào fēng dé fēng, yào yǔ dé yǔ
Literal: want wind, get wind; want rain, get rain — getting whatever one wishes
Figurative: Used to describe someone who gets everything they ask for: a pampered child, a powerful person, someone in a position where nothing is refused. The parallelism of 要…得… (want…obtain…) is the construction backbone. Can be admiring or envious. 他在家里要风得风，要雨得雨，什么都不缺。

Literal: mastery of one's work comes from diligence: skill is born of effort
Figurative: Lit: work, refined-through, diligence. From Han Yu's essay on study: 业精于勤，荒于嬉, "mastery comes from diligence and is ruined by play." A maxim that one's craft or learning is perfected only through steady, hard application.

Literal: Lord Ye Loves Dragons
Figurative: He decorated his palace with dragons, until a real one appeared. The idiom for loving what you only love in the abstract.

Literal: to cancel with one stroke of the pen: to write off entirely
Figurative: Lit: one-stroke-cross-out. With a single line drawn through the ledger, a debt or a past grievance is wiped clean. Used of forgiving a debt or letting an old matter be settled and forgotten.

Literal: to cross over in a single step — to clear an obstacle in one move
Figurative: Not a classical 成语 but a fixed conversational formula. Often used in development and policy rhetoric: 一步跨过工业化 "to leap past industrialization in a single step." Carries a faint flavor of skipping stages: sometimes admiring (decisive progress), sometimes ironic (rushing through what should have been…

Literal: one step, one footprint — steady, methodical progress
Figurative: Lit: each step leaves exactly one footprint; nothing rushed, nothing skipped. A modern proverb for diligent, unhurried work that builds on itself. Often used in career advice, study guidance, and praise for craftsmen.

Literal: one sings, a hundred answer: a single voice draws a crowd of agreement
Figurative: One person 唱 starts the note and a hundred others 和 (hè) chime in. Used for an idea or call that instantly wins broad, eager support.

Literal: one sings, the other echoes: to chime in and back each other up
Figurative: Originally one voice leads and another harmonizes (和 hè, to respond in tune). Now usually mildly negative: two people egging each other on or colluding to push the same line.

Literal: fixed and unchanging; rigidly the same — set in stone; never varying
Figurative: 成 chéng here carries its classical sense of "established; fixed; accomplished." Lit: "once established, not changing." The phrase carries a critical edge, describing something or someone that has refused all adaptation.

Literal: touch and it ignites — a situation on the verge of explosion
Figurative: Lit: one-touch-immediately-fire. A crisis situation where the slightest action will trigger an explosion: political tensions, a fragile negotiation, volatile emotions. Originally describing hair-trigger mechanisms, now widely applied to any situation of extreme tension.
Tags: culture daily meaning change body characters

Literal: to succeed in one step
Figurative: Literally "one stamp of the foot and it is done," to accomplish something in a single easy stroke. Most often used in the negative, to warn that hard things cannot be done all at once: 学语言不能一蹴而就 ("you can't master a language in one go"). The single-action 一 again, the cousin of 一下子.

Literal: a dot and a drop: bit by bit, little by little
Figurative: Lit: one-dot-one-drop. The small increments by which patient effort accumulates. 一点一滴地积累 "to build up bit by bit."

Literal: not moving a muscle: perfectly still, motionless
Figurative: Lit: one-move-not-move. The everyday phrase for total stillness, a person frozen in place, an animal holding its breath. The doubled 动 frames the stillness as the complete absence of motion.

Pinyin: yī ér zài, zài ér sān
Literal: once, then again, then a third time — time after time; repeatedly
Figurative: The fullest expression of Chinese repetition idiomatics. 一而再 (once to twice), 再而三 (twice to three times): the escalating structure conveys frustration or persistence. Almost always used with a negative coloring: someone has done something they shouldn't have, repeatedly. 他一而再，再而三地失约，让人很失望。

Pinyin: yī fēn qián yī fēn huò
Literal: you get what you pay for — one fen of money, one fen of goods
Figurative: The Chinese equivalent of "you get what you pay for." 分 fēn is both a fraction of a yuan and a measure of fairness. A practical consumer proverb that endorses quality over cheapness.

Literal: one man guards the pass: a position so strong that a single defender holds off an army
Figurative: From the line about the road to Shu, 一夫当关，万夫莫开, "one man holding the pass, ten thousand cannot force it open." It praises a place of such natural strength that a lone defender can block a whole host, and by extension any well-held strategic point or a person stubbornly guarding a position.

Literal: to lump together and judge as one: to treat distinct cases as if identical
Figurative: Literally "to discuss everything by one measure." Almost always negated: 不能一概而论 bùnéng yī gài ér lùn "you cannot lump them all together," a standard caution against treating different cases with a single blanket judgement.

Literal: one by one; one after another
Figurative: The triple form stresses that things happen or are dealt with individually, in sequence. 学生一个个走进教室 "the students filed into the classroom one by one."

Literal: to feel like old friends at first meeting: instant rapport
Figurative: 一 (yī, one) + 见 (jiàn, to meet) + 如 (rú, as if, like) + 故 (an old friend, drawing on the 故人 sense). To meet someone for the first time and feel as though you have known them for years.

Literal: to fall in love at first sight
Figurative: Lit: one-look-concentrate-feeling. 钟 zhōng here means to gather or focus one's feeling on someone. The standard phrase for instant romantic attraction on a first meeting.

Literal: not letting a single item slip: accounting for every piece, leaving nothing out
Figurative: 漏 lòu = to leak; to omit. A colloquial set phrase built on 件, used when an inventory, a checklist, or a list of tasks is completed in full with no item missed. 他把行李一件不漏地清点了一遍。(He counted every piece of luggage without missing one.)

Literal: one item at a time: piece by piece, one matter after another
Figurative: A reduplicated measure-word phrase rather than a classical chengyu, but extremely common in speech. Doubling 件 turns it into an adverbial sense of taking things one at a time. 我们一件件地处理这些问题。(Let us handle these problems one by one.)

Literal: one move, two gains — kill two birds with one stone
Figurative: Lit: one-raise/move-two-gains. 举 here is a verbal measure word (one lift/movement). A perfect analogue of "kill two birds with one stone." 这样做一举两得 "Doing it this way achieves two goals at once." Among the most common four-character idioms in business and daily speech.
