Literal: in one breath; without stopping; in one go
Figurative: Lit: one-mouth-breath. Describes doing something continuously, without pause, in one uninterrupted exhalation of effort. 他一口气跑了十公里 "He ran ten kilometers without stopping." 一口气读完这本书 "Read the whole book in one sitting." The most common and versatile 气 idiom in everyday speech.

Literal: a string of / a series of — multiple linked events
Figurative: 一连 = one stretch of consecutive events; 串 chuàn = a string of threaded items (the classifier for strings of things: 一串葡萄 a bunch of grapes). Together: a chain of multiple connected events. 一连串的问题 "a string of problems." 一连串的失败 "a series of failures." Extremely common in news and commentary.

Literal: the whole road with following winds: bon voyage, may your trip go smoothly
Figurative: A maritime image (favorable wind for the sails) generalized to all travel. Ubiquitous farewell phrase, slightly less formal than 一路平安.

Literal: one horse takes the lead: to be out front, to take the initiative
Figurative: The lead horse of the charge. Praises someone who steps forward first and sets the pace for others.

Literal: descended from one bloodline: an unbroken line of inheritance
Figurative: Lit: one-vein-mutually-inherit. Said of ideas, schools, or traditions that pass down through a single connected lineage with nothing broken in between. The image is of a single connecting thread, the same 系 logic of strands held together across generations.

Literal: Not Give Even a Hair
Figurative: Refuse to give even a single hair from your body. Mencius's phrase for the Yangist philosophy of radical self-preservation, and the word for a miser that it became.

Literal: cast from one mould: exactly alike, identical
Figurative: Lit: one-mould-one-shape. Said of two things so alike they might have come from a single cast: 这对双胞胎长得一模一样 "the twins look exactly alike."

Literal: one glance makes it clear — obvious at a single look
Figurative: 一 (one) + 目 (eye-glance) + 了然 (clearly understood). Describes things immediately comprehensible , a diagram that explains itself, an argument whose logic is visible. The phrase appears in Qing dynasty texts and entered general usage by the early Republic period.
Tags: perception daily-life grammar body radical logic cohesion meaning characters aspect complement communication

Literal: the difference of a single thought — a momentary lapse that changes everything
Figurative: 一念 (one thought-moment) + 之差 (the difference of). The idea that a whole fate can turn on a single passing impulse , one wrong thought acted on, one good one suppressed.

Literal: one promise is worth a thousand gold — a promise that is absolute
Figurative: A promise from a person of integrity is as valuable as a thousand pieces of gold. From the story of Ji Bu 季布 in the Shiji: "It is better to have one promise from Ji Bu than a hundred gold pieces from another." Used to praise reliability and personal honor.

Literal: a single vote vetoes it: one negative vote overrides the rest; absolute veto power
Figurative: 一票 yí piào = a single vote. 否决 fǒujué = to vote down; to veto. A decision rule in which one opposing vote is enough to block a proposal outright, the power a permanent member holds on the UN Security Council.

Literal: one stone, two birds — accomplish two goals with a single action
Figurative: The Chinese and English idioms are structurally identical. The image of a single stone bringing down two birds appears to have developed independently in both traditions, though the Chinese form likely circulated in literary Chinese before modern contact. In use: 这个方案真是一石二鸟。
Tags: daily-life grammar culture cosmology philosophy daoism yin-yang vocabulary taoism confucianism measure-words classifiers nouns

Literal: in a short time; for a little while
Figurative: A colloquial set phrase, "one moment, half a spell," meaning a brief span of time, most often in the negative: 这事一时半会儿说不清 ("this can't be explained in a moment"). It builds directly on the 会儿 of 一会儿, stretching it into a fixed expression for "any time soon."

Literal: to accomplish nothing: not one thing brought to completion
Figurative: Lit: one-matter-without-success. Said of a person who, despite time and effort, has nothing finished to show for it. A common note of self-reproach or worry over a life that feels stalled.

Literal: to press forward without turning back
Figurative: Literally "going straight on, nothing ahead can stop it", an image of fearless forward drive. The 往 here is pure forward motion, the direction-of-travel sense, intensified into dauntless momentum. Said of armies, reformers, and anyone who advances undeterred.

Literal: to have nothing at all
Figurative: Literally "one/whole (一) lack (无) that-which-is-had (所有)": the components of 所有 in their original possessive sense. Cuī Jiàn's 崔健 1986 song 《一无所有》, often called the founding track of Chinese rock, turned the idiom into a generational catchphrase: 我曾经问个不休，你何时跟我走 sung by a narrator who owns nothing.

Literal: single-minded; wholeheartedly devoted — one heart, one mind
Figurative: Lit: one-heart-one-intention. Used for unwavering focus or devotion , to a person, a task, or a cause. 他一心一意地爱着她。(He loves her with his whole heart and mind, without wavering.) The antonym is 三心二意 sān xīn èr yì , "three hearts, two intentions" , indecisive and halfhearted.

Pinyin: yī yán jì chū, sìmǎ nán zhuī
Literal: once a word is spoken, four horses cannot chase it back — a promise is binding
Figurative: 驷 sì = a team of four horses (the fastest vehicle in ancient China); 追 zhuī = to chase, to pursue. Once you have spoken, no speed can retrieve the words. Used to impress on someone that speech is irreversible: a commitment made out loud becomes binding.

Literal: a word worth nine cauldrons — a promise of great weight; a person whose word is binding
Figurative: 一言 (a single word) is as weighty as 九鼎 (the Nine Cauldrons). The Nine Cauldrons were the bronze vessels cast by Yu the Great, symbols of sovereignty over the nine provinces and among the heaviest objects of state.

Literal: one word and it is settled: a deal is a deal
Figurative: Lit: one-word-makes-settled. Said to seal an agreement on the spot: a single word given, and the matter is fixed, with no going back. The everyday way to say "deal, it's settled."
Tags: meaning timing evaluation characters business commerce numbers vocabulary

Literal: to cover it all in one word — in a word; to sum up
Figurative: From the Analects II.2, where Confucius summarizes the 300 poems of the Shijing: 诗三百，一言以蔽之，曰思无邪。 — "The three hundred poems can be covered in one phrase: 'no depraved thoughts.'" 以 marks the instrument (one word) used to accomplish the action (cover/sum up).
Tags: grammar classical syntax conjunction particle literary

Literal: a single glance, ten thousand years — a look that lasts forever
Figurative: Lit: one-glance-ten-thousand-years. Modern romantic register, especially in song lyrics and pop fiction: the glance at first meeting that settles a lifetime. Builds on 眼 as the measure word for a single act of looking.

Literal: one thread running through all — a single principle governing everything
Figurative: Source: Analects 4.15. Confucius tells Zengzi 吾道一以贯之 , "My way is threaded through by one." When Zengzi explains to other disciples, he names that one thing as 忠恕 zhōngshù (loyalty and reciprocity).

Literal: to walk one's own way alone — to push through with one fixed idea, ignoring all advice
Figurative: Lit: one-intention-alone-walk. Said of someone who refuses to listen, refuses to compromise, refuses to take counsel , and walks straight into the consequences. The 孤 "alone" is what makes it pejorative: not principled persistence (which would be praiseworthy) but stubborn isolation.

Literal: to know a little, to half-understand: superficial knowledge
Figurative: Lit: one part 一 known 知, half 半 understood 解. A shallow, fragmentary grasp of something, knowing a bit but not the whole. 对这门学问他只是一知半解 = he has only a superficial grasp of this subject. Usually mildly critical of half-baked understanding.

Literal: not missing a single character — word-for-word; complete and verbatim
Figurative: 漏 lòu = to leak; to omit; to miss. 他把合同一字不漏地读了一遍。(He read the contract verbatim, not missing a single character.) Used to emphasize thoroughness, total quotation, or painstaking completeness. Related: 一字不差 yī zì bù chā (not one character wrong, absolutely accurate).

Literal: one character, a thousand gold pieces — words of immense value
Figurative: 字 here is a classifier for characters/words. 金 (gold pieces) is the unit of price. From the story of Lü Buwei's 吕不韦 text 《吕氏春秋》: he challenged anyone to change a single character and offered a thousand gold pieces if they could improve it. Used to praise literary excellence.
Tags: writing language meta measure-words classifiers nouns

Literal: word by word, line by line: spoken or read with careful deliberation
Figurative: Lit: one-character-one-sentence. Describes speaking, reading, or copying out so slowly and clearly that each character and each phrase lands on its own. 一字一句地说 "to say it word by word."

Literal: to leave behind endless harm
Figurative: 贻 (to bequeath) + 害 + 无穷 (endless): a mistake or evil whose damage runs on without limit. Compare the proverb 害人之心不可有，防人之心不可无 (never hold a heart that harms others, never drop the guard against being harmed), which frames the moral middle ground 害 sits on.

Literal: to repay enmity with virtue — to return kindness for a wrong
Figurative: Lit: with-virtue-repay-enmity. From the Analects (论语), where Confucius is asked his view of this maxim and pointedly disagrees: "Then how would you repay virtue? Repay enmity with directness (直), repay virtue with virtue (以德报德)." The chengyu remains in common use as a moral ideal, but Confucius's re…
Tags: confucianism daoism ethics virtue philosophy grammar classical syntax conjunction particle literary

Literal: to win people over by virtue (rather than by force)
Figurative: Lit: with-virtue-make-people-submit. The Confucian alternative to coercion: a leader whose 德 is genuine attracts willing followers; one who relies on force only gets compliance. The classical contrast is 以力服人 "to make people submit by force" , which produces obedience without loyalty.

Literal: to match Heaven through virtue — the moral logic of dynastic legitimacy
Figurative: The Zhou theological principle: the Mandate of Heaven (天命) is not permanent; it follows virtue. A ruler who loses virtue loses Heaven's backing. This gave Chinese political culture its recurring logic of dynastic rise and fall as moral narrative.

Literal: to hold harmony as precious — harmony as the highest value
Figurative: From the Analects I.12 (有子's saying): 礼之用，和为贵，先王之道，斯为美。 — "In the application of ritual, harmony is what is precious; this is the beauty of the ways of the former kings." Often cited as the Confucian reason why formal rules (礼) exist: they are instruments toward harmony, not ends in themselves.
Tags: grammar classical taoism philosophy daoism wuwei syntax conjunction particle literary

Literal: to treat one another with proper courtesy
Figurative: 以 yǐ (using; by means of) + 礼 + 相 xiāng (mutually) + 待 dài (to treat). A formal phrase for the reciprocal practice of 礼貌 between parties , between hosts and guests, between rival firms after a difficult negotiation, between countries after a diplomatic strain.

Literal: to throw an egg at a rock: to attempt the hopelessly outmatched
Figurative: Here the egg is 卵 (luǎn), the classical word for egg, but the image is the same fragile shell shattering on stone. Describes a doomed fight against overwhelming force.

Literal: to put people first; human-centered governance
Figurative: Lit: use-person-as-root. A classical Confucian governance principle revived as modern policy language. 本 běn (root; foundation) is the underground portion of a tree, the part everything else rests on. The person, not the state or ideology, is the root of all legitimate policy.

Literal: win against many with few — overcome a larger force; quality over quantity
Figurative: 以 (by means of) + 少 (few) + 胜 (overcome, win) + 多 (many). The archetype is military: a smaller but better-prepared force defeating a larger one. The Battle of Red Cliffs (208 CE), in which Sun Quan and Liu Bei's combined forces defeated Cao Cao's much larger army, is the classic example.

Literal: to set a standard through personal conduct — lead by example
Figurative: 以 (by means of) + 身 (one whole person; conduct) + 作则 (set a rule/standard). 身 is the entire person understood as embodied conduct , the leader is not separate from the example set. Among the most-cited leadership principles in Chinese management and parenting discourse. 作为领导者，必须以身作则。
Tags: grammar classical syntax conjunction particle literary body health daily-life vocabulary

Literal: use history as a mirror — learning from the past to illuminate the present
Figurative: A classical Chinese phrase with new resonance in the post-Cultural Revolution context. 鉴 (mirror, warning reflection) + 史 (history).

Literal: use history as a mirror — learn from the past to govern the present
Figurative: Taizong's most famous political aphorism: "Using copper as a mirror, one can straighten one's appearance; using history as a mirror, one can understand the rise and fall of dynasties; using people as a mirror, one can perceive one's own gains and losses." The "people as mirror" referred to his minis…

Literal: taking Heaven as the standard — modeling conduct on the cosmic pattern
Figurative: 则 zé (standard; rule; model; then). The classical injunction to take Heaven's order as the measure for human conduct. Appears in Mohist and Confucian texts as a basis for ethical argument: if a practice conforms to Heaven's pattern, it is right; if it violates that pattern, it is wrong.
Tags: philosophy confucianism taoism cosmology nature heaven humanity classical

Literal: to make friends through writing — cultural exchange as the basis of friendship
Figurative: 以 (by means of) + 文 (writing, culture) + 会 (to meet, to gather) + 友 (friend). From the Analects (Book XII): Zēngzǐ says the exemplary person uses 文 (cultural cultivation) to gather friends. In classical usage, 文 here means poetry, ritual texts, and the cultivated arts.

Literal: see the great through the small — the particular reveals the universal
Figurative: Lit: use-small see-great. A principle of classical aesthetics and moral observation: close attention to a small thing , a grain of sand, a single conversation, a minor act of character , reveals large truths.

#fields:Hanzi: 以小人之心，度君子之腹
Pinyin: yǐ xiǎorén zhī xīn, duó jūnzǐ zhī fù
Literal: measuring a gentleman's belly with a petty man's heart — projecting one's own baseness
Figurative: Adapted from a Zuozhuan phrase: assuming others' motives are as small as one's own. The polite deployment is self-accusation: 是我以小人之心度君子之腹了, "I misjudged you by my own petty standard," the graceful way to withdraw a suspicion that proved unfair.

Literal: mind transmitted by mind — the direct transmission of awakening from master to student
Figurative: The second Chan axiom, paired with 不立文字. Awakening cannot be transferred via words or rituals; only by a direct, living encounter between an awakened mind and a genuinely seeking student.

Literal: to repay virtue with resentment
Figurative: An inversion of the Confucian ideal: 德 (virtue, kindness) is answered with 怨 (resentment). The phrase appears in the Analects' discussion of how to respond to good and to harm.

Literal: leaning on age to trade on age — exploiting seniority
Figurative: Lit: lean-on-old-sell-old. The critical idiom for elders who demand deference they have not earned, throwing their age around as a trump card to win arguments or avoid accountability.

Literal: duty leaves no room to decline: an obligation one cannot refuse
Figurative: 义 = duty, righteousness; 不容 = brooks no, leaves no room for; 辞 = to decline, to refuse. A moral duty so clear that refusing it is not an option. Note the 不容 (will brook no) construction: 容 in the negative means "to leave room for." 帮助他是我义不容辞的责任。

Literal: righteousness admits no looking back — to press forward without hesitation because duty demands it
Figurative: 义 yì (righteousness) + 无 wú (there is no; without) + 反顾 fǎngù (to look back; to turn back). When 义 demands an action, there can be no hesitation, no reconsidering once the course is set.

Literal: righteous in cause and stern in speech: to speak with upright authority
Figurative: Lit: principle-upright-words-stern. Said of someone whose argument rests on a just cause and whose wording is firm and severe, leaving no room for doubt that they hold the moral high ground.

Literal: to follow every step slavishly
Figurative: Literally "you walk, I walk; you hurry, I hurry", from the Zhuangzi, where a disciple copies his master's every move. It paints the extreme of 跟 as "follow": imitating so closely that one has no step of one's own. Often mildly critical of mere copying.

Literal: different mouths, the same sound — unanimous
Figurative: Everyone says the same thing at once: the committee that answers in chorus, the witnesses whose accounts match. Neutral to positive in tone; suspicious unanimity would be phrased differently. The mirror image of 众说纷纭, where every mouth says something else.
Tags: body culture phonology perception communication characters society connections meaning language vocabulary

Literal: wildly fanciful ideas; to have one's head in the clouds
Figurative: 异 yì (strange; different; fantastical) + 想 xiǎng (thought; imagine) + 天 tiān (sky; heaven) + 开 kāi (to open). Fantastical thoughts that open the sky itself: thinking so far outside reality that heaven itself cracks open.

Literal: sending plum blossoms by postal relay — a token of remembrance sent across great distance
Figurative: From a Tang poem, but the Yuan postal relay system (驿站 yìzhàn) was the most elaborate in East Asian history, running thousands of stations across the empire with fresh horses. The phrase evokes distance, longing, and the slender thread of connection maintained across vast space.

Literal: meaning runs deep and long — deeply meaningful; thought-provoking; pregnant with implication
Figurative: Lit: meaning-flavor-deep-long. Used for words, actions, or expressions that reward reflection , where the surface content is less than what is being communicated. 他的话意味深长，我想了很久。"His words were deeply meaningful , I thought about them for a long time." Common in literary and critical contexts.

Literal: to teach according to aptitude: tailor instruction to each learner
Figurative: Lit: based-on-talent-apply-teaching. A principle traced to Confucius, who answered the same question differently for different students. The enduring ideal of the teacher who meets each pupil where they are rather than drilling all alike.
Tags: education religion society characters logic cohesion meaning

Literal: adapt measures to local conditions: act according to what the place calls for
Figurative: Lit: follow-the-land, make-it-fitting. 因 here is the older sense, to take an existing ground as one's basis. The phrase counsels suiting your plan to local circumstances rather than forcing one rigid method everywhere.

Literal: make do with the crude and the simple: get by with what little there is
Figurative: 因 to rely on, 陋 crude, 就 to settle for, 简 the simple. Said of working within tight means, building or running something on a shoestring without waiting for better tools.

Literal: act according to what the time requires
Figurative: A closely related four-character phrase drawing explicitly on the 时中 tradition. Where 与时俱进 emphasizes forward movement alongside the era, 因时制宜 emphasizes responsive calibration: making decisions that fit the specific circumstances of the moment.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms modern culture politics change philosophy

Literal: lose much over a trifle: sacrifice the great for the sake of the small
Figurative: Lit: because-of-the-small, lose-the-big. A warning against penny-wise foolishness: chasing a minor gain or saving while letting something far more valuable slip away.

Literal: yin off, yang astray — a chain of coincidences producing an unexpected result
Figurative: 阴 yīn + 差 chā (off; awry) + 阳 yáng + 错 cuò (wrong). A tangle of small errors and coincidences, some hidden (阴), some accidental (阳), that combine to produce an outcome nobody intended, often a missed chance or a strange twist of fate. 因为阴差阳错，他们错过了那班火车。
Tags: meaning daily-life communication characters cosmology yin-yang nature weather

Literal: yin-wrong yang-off — a chain of mishaps and coincidences leading to an unexpected outcome
Figurative: A series of errors and coincidences (some of a yin nature, hidden and unintended; some of a yang nature, overt and accidental) that together produce an unexpected result, usually unfortunate. 因为阴错阳差，他们错过了相遇的机会。

Literal: yin-yang weird energy — passive-aggressive; sarcastic; speaking in an off-putting, odd manner
Figurative: A vivid colloquial phrase for someone whose speech or behavior is consistently passive-aggressive, sarcastic, or oddly unsettling. 他说话总是阴阳怪气的，让人不舒服。

Literal: Yin and Yang complementing and nourishing each other — the ideal of balanced opposition
Figurative: 济 jì = to aid, to cross over, to benefit. The image is of two forces that are not in conflict but in mutual assistance , each making the other possible. This is the aspirational state, whether in the body, a relationship, a government, or the cosmos.

Literal: voice and smiling face: the remembered presence of someone now gone
Figurative: Lit: sound-face-smile-appearance. The way a person's voice and warm expression linger in memory, used above all of the departed. 音容宛在 "the voice and face seem still present" is a common condolence.

Literal: to cite the classics and quote the canon: to argue from authoritative texts
Figurative: Lit: draw on classics, rely on canon. Praise for someone whose argument is grounded in scripture and the classic texts, though it can also tease a person for being bookishly pedantic.

Literal: stretch the throat and sing loudly: to sing out at full voice
Figurative: 吭 is the throat; the image is of someone tipping the head back to let the voice carry. Used warmly for hearty, unrestrained singing.

Literal: too busy to cope: more coming in than one can attend to
Figurative: Lit: responding and receiving without a spare moment. 应接 is "to attend to"; 不暇 is "no leisure." Said when guests, sights, or tasks arrive faster than one can handle them. The yìng reading, "to meet."
Tags: motion connections daily-life characters modal meaning ability

Literal: everything one could expect is there
Figurative: 应有 (what ought to be there) + 尽有 (is exhaustively there). The stock phrase for a well-provisioned shop or feature-complete product: 这家超市商品应有尽有 "This supermarket has everything you could want." The structural mirror of 一无所有: total presence against total absence.
Tags: modal meaning ability characters quantifiers adverb numbers

Literal: to split apart at the meeting of the blade: solved with ease
Figurative: Lit: meeting 迎 the blade 刃, it splits 解. Like bamboo that splits cleanly the moment the knife touches it: once the hardest part is cracked, everything else falls apart of its own accord. Used when solving one key difficulty makes all the rest resolve effortlessly.

Literal: worried about the country and the people — the Confucian official's moral burden
Figurative: The phrase encodes the Confucian ideal of public-spirited concern: not personal ambition but sorrow at the state's condition and compassion for the people's suffering.

Literal: preparedness prevents disaster — forewarned is forearmed
Figurative: Lit: have-preparation-lack-disaster. One of the most practical and frequently cited classical Chinese proverbs. The 有/无 binary frames the logic: having preparation eliminates (brings to non-existence) disaster. 出门前要检查好，有备无患。"Check everything before you go , preparedness prevents problems."

Literal: should there come a day: one day, someday
Figurative: Lit: there-is morning one-day. 朝 here is zhāo, a morning standing for some future day. A set way of saying "one day," usually pointing to a hope or ambition: 有朝一日我会成功 "one day I will succeed."

Literal: having a mouth but unable to speak — in a position where one cannot explain oneself
Figurative: The frustration of having the means to speak but being unable to, because of social constraints, grief, or incriminating circumstances. One of the most vivid expressions for the experience of being misunderstood with no way to clear one's name.

Literal: mouth but no heart — speaking without malice; thoughtless but innocent
Figurative: Lit: have-mouth-lack-heart. Describes someone who says careless or blunt things but means no harm , the words come from the mouth, not the heart. Used to excuse or explain unintentionally offensive speech. 他说话直，有口无心，别放在心上。"He speaks bluntly , no malice intended."

Literal: there is coming and there is going — mutual exchange; reciprocity
Figurative: 往 wǎng = to go; toward. 来 and 往 together make up the full back-and-forth of social exchange: gifts, visits, words, favors. A relationship characterized by 有来有往 is balanced and healthy , neither party gives without receiving. Often used to encourage reciprocity in social or diplomatic contexts.

Literal: name without substance — nominal but hollow
Figurative: Lit: have-name-lack-substance. For positions, titles, or claims that exist in name only , without the actual power, content, or reality they imply. The Chinese equivalent of "all title, no game." 他是经理，但有名无实，什么权力都没有。

Literal: every request met with response — to never refuse a reasonable ask
Figurative: Lit: have-request-must-respond. Said of a generous, responsive person or deity (Guanyin is described this way). 她对学生有求必应，从不拒绝。"She responds to every student's request and never refuses." High praise for helpfulness and generosity.
Tags: modal meaning ability characters grammar existence possession

Literal: to see a thing through to the end
Figurative: Literally "to have a beginning and have an end", to finish what one starts rather than abandon it midway. The 终 of completion again, valued as a virtue of persistence. The opposite is 有始无终, all start and no finish.

Literal: to have eyes but no pupils — to fail to recognize what is right in front of you
Figurative: Lit: have-eyes-without-pearls (珠 = pearl, here pupil). Said of someone who has missed an obvious quality or opportunity: failed to spot a talent, dismissed a worthy person. Often self-deprecating: 我真是有眼无珠 "I had eyes but couldn't see."

Pinyin: yǒu yuán qiānlǐ lái xiāng huì
Literal: those with fate meet across a thousand miles — destiny brings people together regardless of distance
Figurative: The full saying: 有缘千里来相会，无缘对面不相识。"Those with karmic connection will meet across a thousand miles; those without it won't recognize each other face to face." One of the most beloved Chinese sayings about fate and connection.

Literal: governance that favors the literary — an administration that prioritizes civil culture over military force
Figurative: 右文 (to favor the literary arts: to place the civil over the martial) + 之 (possessive particle) + 治 (governance; rule).

Literal: the lingering sound circles the roof-beams — music that haunts after it ends
Figurative: From the Liezi: the singer Han E, paying for a meal with song, left a melody that circled the beams of the city gate for three days (余音绕梁，三日不绝). The standard praise for a performance that stays with you, extended freely to speeches, films, and any experience with a long afterglow.
Tags: phonology perception music characters arts vocabulary confucianism

Pinyin: yú hé xióng zhǎng bùkě jiān dé
Literal: you can't have both the fish and the bear's paw — you can't have everything you want
Figurative: From Mencius: both fish (common) and bear's paw (prized delicacy) are desirable, but you cannot have both. The Chinese equivalent of "you can't have your cake and eat it too." Frequently invoked when someone has to choose between two things they want equally. 鱼和熊掌不可兼得，你只能选一个。"You can't have both.

Literal: to make fish-meat of the common people: to oppress and exploit them
Figurative: Here 鱼肉 is a verb: to treat people as meat to be carved up. A classical condemnation of tyrannical officials, traceable to the Shǐjì. Still used to denounce abuse of power.

Literal: fish leaping Dragon Gate — passing a crucial test and transforming one's destiny
Figurative: 鱼 yú (fish) + 跃 yuè (to leap) + 龙门 lóngmén (Dragon Gate). The legend: a carp that braves the current and clears the great waterfall at Dragon Gate on the Yellow River is transformed into a dragon.

Literal: The Foolish Old Man Moves the Mountains
Figurative: Two mountains blocked his door. He and his sons began to move them, one basket at a time. A mocker laughed. He said: when I die my sons will continue; when they die, their sons.

Literal: to advance together with the times
Figurative: A classical phrase that became a political slogan in 2001, used to justify the Communist Party accommodating private enterprise, and criticized for justifying whatever the party currently does.
Tags: chengyu classical idioms modern culture politics change philosophy

Literal: to stand aloof from strife: to live without contending against the world
Figurative: Lit: with the world, no contention. Describes a person who seeks neither fame nor advantage and stays clear of rivalry, content with a quiet life. Carries a Daoist flavor of withdrawal and unforced ease.

Literal: spring bamboo shoots after rain: springing up everywhere at once
Figurative: The image of bamboo shoots erupting after spring rain. Modern usage describes new businesses, buildings, or trends multiplying rapidly.

Literal: words are weighty, feeling is deep — earnest, heartfelt advice
Figurative: Lit: words-weighty-heart-long. Used to describe sincere, deeply felt words from someone who genuinely cares: a mentor's advice, a parent's warning, a teacher's final lesson before a student departs. The heaviness (重) of the words comes from the depth (长) of the feeling behind them.
Tags: language literature communication characters grammar culture

Literal: Jade and stone burn together — the innocent perish with the guilty
Figurative: Lit: jade-stone both-burn. The image is of a fire that cannot distinguish the precious from the worthless, the innocent from the guilty: everything burns. Used when a catastrophe (war, political upheaval, unjust punishment) destroys indiscriminately.
Tags: nature culture virtue confucianism aesthetics royalty classical

Literal: Haste Does Not Bring Success
Figurative: Speed desired, arrival missed: Confucius on why rushing produces the opposite of what you intend.

Literal: to lodge soldiers among farmers: keep a militia by having peasants farm in peacetime and fight in war
Figurative: A classical statecraft principle: soldiers feed themselves from the land in quiet years, so the army costs little until it is needed. Used today of any scheme that hides one function inside another.

Literal: the original seal unmoved: left exactly as it was, untouched
Figurative: 原封 is the original seal on a package. To leave something 原封不动 is to return or keep it intact, never opened or altered. Everyday modern usage.

Literal: the original form is fully revealed: a true nature laid completely bare
Figurative: Lit: original-shape-completely-appears. Said when a disguise drops and someone's real, usually unflattering, character or identity becomes plain for all to see.

Literal: from source and root: in full and exact detail, from start to finish
Figurative: The doubled 原 (source) and 本 (root). To tell something 原原本本 is to give the whole account faithfully, leaving nothing out and adding nothing.

Literal: climb a tree to look for fish — to seek something by completely wrong means; a futile approach
Figurative: Lit: climb-tree-seek-fish. Here 缘 means "to climb along" rather than "karmic connection" , a completely different sense of the character (the edge-clinging, tree-climbing meaning). A cautionary idiom from Mencius. Used when someone's method is fundamentally unsuited to their goal.

Pinyin: yuǎn qīn bù rú jìn lín
Literal: a distant relative is no match for a close neighbor — proximity creates community
Figurative: 远亲 (distant kin) + 不如 (not as good as) + 近邻 (near neighbor). A proverb rather than a classical chengyu with a single attributed source, but documented in Song dynasty collections and widely cited since.

Pinyin: yuǎn shuǐ jiù bù liǎo jìn huǒ
Literal: distant water cannot put out a nearby fire
Figurative: From the Hán Fēizǐ. Help too far away is useless against an urgent crisis; a homely proverb on the gap between resources and immediate need.

Literal: walk far and fly high — to go far away; to escape and seek freedom
Figurative: Lit: far-walk-high-fly. The image of a bird launching into open sky. Used when someone leaves a constraining situation (a bad job, a difficult relationship, a suffocating hometown) to seek a better life elsewhere. Carries a tone of liberation and sometimes wistfulness.
Tags: direction geography nature classical analects confucianism

Literal: a covenant of three clauses — simple, clear rules agreed upon in advance
Figurative: Liu Bang's proclamation upon entering Qin territory: abolishing Qin's thousands of regulations in favor of just three (no murder, no assault, no theft). Now: any simple, clear agreement or set of rules established upfront between parties. 我们约法三章：不准迟到，不准说谎，不准逃课.

Literal: moonless and windy — a dark night fit for crime or treachery
Figurative: 月黑 (the moon is black, that is, no moon) + 风高 (the wind is high). A set scene-setting phrase for a night when something sinister is afoot. The full classical line is 月黑风高杀人夜 (a moonless, windy night, a night for killing). Storytellers use it to signal that the next thing to happen will be dark.

Literal: better and better — a wish or observation of continuous improvement
Figurative: Not classical 成语 but a near-fixed conversational formula and a cultural mantra of optimism. The opening line of a famous song by Sun Yue (孙悦) used at the 2000 Lunar New Year gala, 越来越好 ("Better and Better"), fixed it in popular memory.

Literal: the more one sinks, the deeper one falls — to become increasingly trapped
Figurative: A 越…越… frame applied to 陷 (xiàn, to sink, to become trapped). Used for any situation where each step makes escape harder: debt, addiction, scandal, a bad relationship.

Literal: to overstep the sacrificial vessel and take the cook's place — to do someone else's job, to overstep one's role
Figurative: From the Zhuangzi (庄子). 俎 zǔ is the sacrificial chopping block , the priest's tool , and 庖 páo is the kitchen's domain. The original image is of a priest abandoning the altar to do the cook's work.

Literal: dizzy head, spinning direction — disoriented; thrown off; bewildered
Figurative: 晕 (yūn, dizzy) + 头 (tóu, head) + 转 (zhuàn, to spin) + 向 (xiàng, direction). The character 向 alone , not 方向 , is doing the directional work in the chengyu. Used when someone is overwhelmed, confused, or has lost track of what is going on.

Literal: to make further efforts; to keep working hard; to do even better next time
Figurative: 再接 (take it up again) + 再厉 (sharpen again; work harder again). Used as encouragement after success or after failure: "keep it up" or "do even better." Common in school settings, performance reviews, and sports. 你这次考得很好，希望你再接再厉。

Literal: both singing and dancing: to celebrate with song and dance
Figurative: 载…载… is a classical frame meaning doing two things at once. Standard description of festive crowds at a 春节 (chūnjié) gala or village celebration.

Literal: rebellion is justified — Mao's most radical formulation
Figurative: Mao Zedong's phrase, originally from a 1939 speech, given new prominence and murderous application during the Cultural Revolution. "马克思主义的道理千条万绪，归根结底，就是一句话：造反有理。

Literal: a duty one cannot shirk
Figurative: Literally "the responsibility cannot be passed to another," a duty that falls squarely on you and that you ought to shoulder. Used when one accepts an obligation as rightfully one's own, the firm sense of "should" hardened into "must."

Literal: fasting — the Chinese term for Ramadan's fast
Figurative: 斋 zhāi (fasting; vegetarian abstinence, a word also used for Buddhist fasting) + 戒 jiè (precept; prohibition). 斋月 zhāiyuè is the Chinese for Ramadan (the Fasting Month). 开斋节 Kāizhāi Jié is Eid al-Fitr (the Festival Breaking the Fast).

Literal: look ahead and glance behind — to be overly cautious; to hesitate by considering every angle
Figurative: 瞻 zhān (to look ahead; to gaze forward) + 前 qián (front) + 顾 gù (to look back; to attend to) + 后 hòu (back). Looking anxiously in both temporal directions , toward the past and the future , before acting. Used critically of someone who deliberates so carefully they become paralyzed.

Literal: cut the grass and pull the root: to eliminate a problem at its source
Figurative: Lit: cut-grass-remove-root. Weeds cut at the surface grow back; only by tearing out the roots are they truly gone. The idiom urges finishing a job completely so trouble cannot return, often with a ruthless edge.

Literal: to show one's emerging talent — horns beginning to protrude
Figurative: The image is a young animal whose horns are just breaking through the hide. Used for a young talent beginning to stand out. Very common in Chinese writing about emerging professionals or artists.

Literal: cannot stand on its feet: untenable
Figurative: Literally "the feet cannot hold their stand." Used of an argument, excuse, or theory that collapses under scrutiny. Colloquial and very frequent.

Literal: to stand firm; to gain a foothold
Figurative: Literally "to stand steady on one's heels." A common set phrase, not a classical four-character idiom: to establish oneself securely in a place, job, or market before making a move. Everyday modern usage.

Pinyin: zhàn zài fēng kǒu làng jiān
Literal: to stand where the wind and waves meet: at the eye of the storm
Figurative: To be exposed at the most dangerous, contested forefront of events, where pressure and scrutiny are fiercest. Modern journalistic register, common in commentary.

Literal: hang lanterns and tie up silks: to decorate festively for a celebration
Figurative: Lit: hang-lanterns-tie-colored-silks. The classic picture of a place dressed up for a wedding, a festival, or New Year, with lanterns strung and bright silk streamers tied everywhere. Here 结 is the literal tying of decorations.
Tags: daily-life nature characters connections meaning society

Literal: if this goes on for long — a warning about sustained bad behavior
Figurative: Lit: long-this-by-going. Used to warn that if a current (usually bad) situation continues indefinitely, serious consequences will follow. 长此以往，身体会垮掉的 "If this keeps up, your health will collapse." Almost always negative; rarely used for positive sustained trends.

Literal: a long wind breaking through the waves — bold ambition and perseverance
Figurative: From the Tang poet Li Bai: 长风破浪会有时，直挂云帆济沧海. "There will come a time when the long wind breaks through the waves; I shall set my cloud-sail straight across the vast sea." The image is unstoppable ambition riding the great winds, no obstacle too large to overcome.

Literal: a long-winded discourse: a lengthy, overdrawn speech or piece of writing
Figurative: Literally "long chapters, big discoursing." A speech or text that goes on at excessive length. Usually mildly critical: the listener or reader feels the argument could have been made in a fraction of the words.

Literal: long life without ageing — immortality
Figurative: The obsession that drove the First Emperor, who sent expeditions in search of the elixir of immortality and is said to have died from mercury pills meant to grant it. The chengyu names the dream of eternal life free from ageing, a recurring theme in Daoist alchemy and in the legends around 秦始皇.
Tags: history qin first-emperor ancient art archaeology

Literal: long sighs and short groans: to sigh repeatedly in distress
Figurative: Describes a person worn down by worry, audibly lamenting their troubles. Literary and slightly old-fashioned in tone.

Literal: to set about; to begin tackling (a task)
Figurative: 着 zháo (second tone, resultative) + 手 hand. Literally "to have the hands land on something" , to get a grip on a task and begin. The image is of hands making contact with work.

Literal: to focus on; to have one's eye on; to consider from the angle of
Figurative: 着 zháo + 眼 eye. "To land the eye on" a target or consideration. Most commonly found as 着眼于 (focused on, with an eye to) or 着眼点 (focal point, angle of concern). Common in political and analytical writing: 着眼长远 "with an eye to the long term." A formal way to name what frame or priority is operative.

Literal: the Well-Governed Era of Zhenguan — the Confucian ideal of enlightened imperial rule
Figurative: Taizong's reign era (627–649 CE), celebrated as the model of good governance in Chinese political tradition. The formula "[reign-era name] 之治" became the standard way to name historical periods of exceptional governance, as in 文景之治 and 开元盛世.

Literal: the true Son of Heaven, destined to rule
Figurative: The legitimate ruler chosen by Heaven, as opposed to a usurper or pretender. Used in historical fiction and now, loosely and often jokingly, for "the one true destined person" in any field. It rests on the idea that the emperor's authority comes from the 天命 (Mandate of Heaven), not from force alone.
Tags: vocabulary history emperor imperial statecraft royalty

Literal: the true face comes fully to light
Figurative: 真相 (the true state of affairs) + 大白 (made fully plain, the white of 明白). The headline phrase when a mystery resolves or a cover-up collapses. Its verb form 水落石出 ("the water recedes and the stones emerge") describes the same moment hydrologically.
Tags: knowing daoism philosophy virtue clarity mind learning spoken

Literal: with sincere heart and genuine intent — utterly in earnest
Figurative: Lit: real-heart-real-intent. The standard four-character emphatic for sincerity. 我真心实意地感谢你 "I sincerely thank you with my whole heart."

Literal: true knowledge and penetrating insight — genuinely wise judgment
Figurative: Lit: real-knowing-burning-seeing. 灼 = scorching, here "piercing." High praise for someone whose understanding cuts through to the essential.

Literal: revitalize China — the rallying cry of national renewal
Figurative: Attributed to Sun Yat-sen and the Revive China Society (兴中会). One of the most durable slogans in modern Chinese political history, used by the Nationalist government, the Communist government, and by Xi Jinping's "China Dream" (中国梦 Zhōngguó Mèng) rhetoric.

Literal: to argue with apparent conviction: to speak plausibly while in the wrong
Figurative: Lit: assured-and-having-words. Describes someone who defends a weak or unjustified position with a confident flow of arguments, sounding righteous though the case does not hold. Mildly critical in tone.

Literal: to argue without end: an endless, unresolved dispute
Figurative: Literally "dispute and discuss without ceasing." Describes a debate that drags on with no side yielding and no resolution in sight. 不休 bù xiū "without stopping" stresses the wearisome, going-nowhere quality of the argument.

Literal: rising like steam, day by day — prospering and flourishing continuously
Figurative: 蒸 zhēng = steam; to rise in vapor. The image of steam rising without ceasing, day after day. Used of businesses, careers, nations, or any enterprise that is consistently growing and thriving. A very positive set phrase, commonly used in well-wishes and assessments of success.

Literal: upright and eight hundred — perfectly serious; genuinely proper
Figurative: 正经 (proper, serious) intensified by 八百 (eight hundred), where the large number simply amplifies the quality. The phrase insists that something is done in earnest, no joking, the real and proper thing: 正经八百地谈 (to discuss in all seriousness).

Literal: hitting exactly what I hoped for — exactly what I wanted
Figurative: Lit: exactly-hit-one's-heart/intention. Note: 中 here is zhòng (tone 4, to hit). The expression describes something that lands exactly where you hoped (a proposal, a result, a turn of events) as if it aimed directly at your wishes. 这个方案真是正中下怀 "This plan is exactly what I had in mind."

Literal: Zheng He's expeditions to the Western Oceans — shorthand for Chinese maritime greatness
Figurative: Used as a historical reference point in modern discussions of Chinese global engagement, maritime strategy, and the "peaceful rise" narrative. The voyages are cited as evidence that Chinese power projection has historically been tributary rather than colonial.

Literal: government flowing smoothly, people in harmony — the ideal of good governance
Figurative: From Fan Zhongyan's (范仲淹) "Yueyang Tower Preface" (岳阳楼记, 1046 CE): 政通人和，百废具兴 , when governance flows and the people are in harmony, all that was ruined can be restored. The four-character condensation became a standard formula for describing a well-governed state.

Literal: limbs apart and shattered to bits: fragmented, in pieces
Figurative: Here 离 means scattered or come apart. Describes something broken into incoherent fragments, a wrecked argument, a shattered country, a disjointed text.

Literal: branches linked, leaves joined — close-knit family or unity
Figurative: Lit: branches-connect-leaves-join. A literary phrase for family solidarity or any close-knit organic unity, like branches of a tree that are all connected at the root. Uses 连 in its original botanical/linking sense.

Literal: recognize a fault and at once correct it
Figurative: Praise for the rare person who, the moment they see their error, fixes it without excuse. Echoes the Confucian ideal of 过则勿惮改, do not fear to mend a fault.

Literal: knowing a kindness and planning to repay it — grateful; not forgetting a debt of gratitude
Figurative: 知 zhī (to know; to be aware of) + 恩 ēn (kindness; grace; favor) + 图 tú (to plan; to intend) + 报 bào (to repay; to respond). The compound 知恩 , knowing that a kindness has been done to you , is the first act; 图报, planning how to return it, is the second.

Literal: to know the law and break it anyway: to offend with full awareness
Figurative: Lit: know-law-violate-law. Said of someone who understands exactly what the law forbids and breaks it regardless, which makes the offense worse, not more excusable.

Literal: know yourself and know your opponent — thorough strategic understanding
Figurative: From Sun Tzu's Art of War (孙子兵法·谋攻篇): 知彼知己，百战不殆 (zhī bǐ zhī jǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài) , "Know your opponent and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will not be imperiled." The fuller phrase is often compressed to 知己知彼.
Tags: identity ethics meaning characters knowing philosophy confucianism education classics statecraft strategy ancient legalism vocabulary daily-life communication

Pinyin: zhī jǐ zhī bǐ, bǎi zhàn bù dài.
Literal: Know yourself and know the enemy, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril.
Figurative: The single most quoted line in the Art of War and one of the best-known Chinese sayings worldwide. The full passage continues that one who knows only himself will win some and lose some, and one who knows neither will lose every time.
Tags: classics philosophy statecraft strategy ancient legalism

Literal: to retreat on seeing the difficulty: to back off when the odds are clearly against you
Figurative: Lit: know-hard-and-withdraw. On recognizing how hard a thing is (知难), one 而 wisely pulls back (退). It can praise prudent judgment or, more pointedly, chide a lack of nerve.

Pinyin: zhī rén zhě zhì, zì zhī zhě míng.
Literal: To know others is wisdom; to know oneself is enlightenment.
Figurative: From chapter 33. The Daodejing consistently ranks inward mastery above outward conquest: knowing others is mere cleverness, but knowing oneself is true clarity (明 míng, the brightness of genuine insight); overcoming others takes force, but overcoming oneself takes real strength.
Tags: daoism laozi classics philosophy wuwei cosmology

Literal: to know books and understand rites — educated and well-mannered; the Confucian ideal
Figurative: 知书 zhī shū = to know books; to be literate and learned. 达礼 dá lǐ = to have arrived at an understanding of 礼; to know and practice proper conduct. Together: the classical ideal of the cultivated person, academically educated and socially formed.

Literal: to know heaven's decree — Confucius at fifty; the age of understanding one's place in the order
Figurative: From Analects 2.4: 五十而知天命 (wǔshí ér zhī tiānmìng , at fifty, I understood heaven's decree). The phrase is not about political legitimacy here but about a different kind of knowing: what heaven put you on earth to do, what your capacities and limits are, what it is pointless to resist.

Literal: Unity of knowing and acting.
Figurative: Wang Yangming's most cited formulation. The argument is conceptual, not motivational: genuine moral knowing is not a cognitive state that precedes action but an orientation that is already action-shaped. The person who "knows" something is wrong but consistently does it does not truly know it.
Tags: wang-yangming mind knowing neo-confucianism confucianism philosophy ethics human-nature history ming virtue

#fields:Hanzi: 知之为知之，不知为不知。
Pinyin: zhī zhī wéi zhī zhī, bù zhī wéi bù zhī.
Literal: To know what you know and know what you don't know — that is real knowledge.
Figurative: From the Analects of Confucius. The full saying ends 是知也 ("this is wisdom"). It teaches intellectual honesty: genuine knowledge includes a clear sense of the limits of one's knowledge.

Literal: knowing sufficiency brings lasting happiness — contentment is the source of joy
Figurative: From Laozi (老子·道德经, Chapter 33): 知足者富 (zhī zú zhě fù) , "Those who know sufficiency are wealthy." The fuller proverb 知足常乐 is not directly from the Daodejing text but is a Taoist-derived commonplace built on that chapter's logic.
Tags: knowing philosophy confucianism education body motion radical daoism religion immortality

Literal: Those who know sufficiency are wealthy.
Figurative: Chapter 33. The full passage offers four paired contrasts: knowing others is wisdom (智 zhì), knowing oneself is enlightenment (明 míng); overcoming others requires force (力 lì), overcoming oneself requires strength (强 qiáng); knowing sufficiency is wealth (富 fù), acting with determination is will (志…

Literal: to enforce the law like a mountain: to uphold it firmly and without bending
Figurative: Lit: enforce-law-like-mountain. Praise for an official or judge who applies the law unshakably, immovable as a mountain, favoring no one and yielding to no pressure.

Literal: strategize on paper — armchair theorizing without practical ability
Figurative: From the Battle of Changping (260 BCE): Zhao Kuo (赵括) could discuss military theory fluently but had no battlefield experience. His appointment as Zhao's commander, reversing the caution of the veteran Lian Po, led to the encirclement and massacre of 400,000 Zhao troops.
Tags: ancient dynasty history philosophy legalism statecraft politics classics

Literal: point at a deer and call it a horse — deliberate falsification to identify loyalists
Figurative: Zhao Gao presented a deer to the court and declared it a horse, watching who agreed and who dared contradict him. Those who said "deer" were later executed.

Literal: pointing with hands and gesturing with feet — bossing others around with showy gestures
Figurative: Lit: point-hand-draw-foot. Said of someone who criticises and orders others about while making theatrical gestures. Carries a strong note of irritation: the speaker is performing authority rather than exercising it.
Tags: arts calligraphy culture characters body movement space

Literal: to point and gesture: to criticize or gossip about others behind their backs
Figurative: The reduplicated 指点 zhǐdiǎn (to point out, to instruct) turns sour here: to keep pointing fingers and passing judgment on what is not one's business.

Literal: sharing the same goals and ideals — kindred spirits
Figurative: Describes friends or partners who share the same ambitions (志 zhì) and follow the same path (道 dào). The classical ideal of friendship: not mere companionship but a meeting of values and direction. Used for close friends, allies, and collaborators who are truly aligned in what they want and believe.
Tags: connections society meaning characters vocabulary social daily-life

Literal: determined to get it; fully committed to winning
Figurative: 志 zhì (will; ambition) + 在 (located in) + 必 bì (certainly) + 得 dé (to obtain). The ambition is so fixed that obtaining the goal is taken as given, not from arrogance but from total commitment. Used to describe someone who has made a full decision and will not waver. 他对这个项目志在必得，不成功不罢休。

Literal: to codify ritual and compose music — founding a cultural order
Figurative: The achievement credited to the Duke of Zhou during his regency. Used as a compound phrase to describe the founding moment of Zhou cultural civilization, and by extension any act of creating the formal cultural infrastructure of a new order.
Tags: history ancient confucianism classical dynasty ritual philosophy bronze-age

Literal: Master the decrees of Heaven and use them — human agency as the response to natural necessity
Figurative: From 天论 (On Heaven). Contrasted with the alternative: 大天而思之, "exalting Heaven and longing for it." Xunzi argues that the latter is passive and futile; the former is the correct response to a world governed by regular, impersonal natural processes.

Literal: govern the state, pacify the realm — the task of statecraft
Figurative: 治国 (govern the state) + 安邦 (stabilize the realm; 邦 bāng, polity, domain). The paired formulation for the ruler's task: governing the state and maintaining peace across the whole domain. A classical political phrase that appears in pre-Qin texts.

#fields:Hanzi: 治世之能臣，乱世之奸雄
Pinyin: zhìshì zhī néngchén, luànshì zhī jiānxióng
Literal: a capable minister in peace, a villainous hero in chaos
Figurative: The famous double-edged appraisal of Cao Cao, conceding his talent while condemning his ambition. The phrase is quoted as a character type in itself: the gifted person whose abilities turn dangerous when the rules break down. 奸雄 jiānxióng, "villain-hero," is the role Cao Cao defines.
Tags: history han biography warlord poet poetry statecraft strategy

Literal: Extending innate moral knowledge.
Figurative: The core practice of Wang Yangming's philosophy. 致 means "to extend" or "to bring to bear fully." The practice is not the construction of moral knowledge through study but the removal of whatever obstructs the 良知 that is always already present.
Tags: wang-yangming neo-confucianism confucianism philosophy ethics human-nature knowing mind history ming

Pinyin: zhì zhě qiān lǜ, bì yǒu yī shī
Literal: even a wise person's thousand deliberations will have one mistake
Figurative: From the Shiji (史记, Records of the Grand Historian), the strategist Li Zuoche (李左车) speaking to Han Xin: "The wise person's thousand deliberations will have one mistake; the fool's thousand deliberations will have one success." Literal: to place oneself outside the matter: to stay aloof, keep clear of it
Figurative: Lit: place-body-affair-outside. To keep oneself out of an affair, neither helping nor interfering. Often mildly critical, of someone who stands apart when they ought to be involved.

Literal: a pillar standing firm in the middle of the current — a mainstay; steadfast support
Figurative: Lit: mid-current-firm-pillar. The image of a rocky pillar in the middle of a fast-moving river, standing unmoved while the water rushes past. Used to describe a person, organization, or principle that holds firm and provides stability amid turmoil.

Literal: many mouths melt gold
Figurative: From the Guoyu and other classical texts: collective speech is so powerful it can melt metal. A more extreme formulation of the same principle as 三人成虎: the force of accumulated voices is overwhelming, even against something as solid as reputation or fact.

Literal: as everyone knows; it is common knowledge
Figurative: A formal phrase, literally "what the crowd all knows," used to introduce a widely accepted fact. 众 (the masses) + 周知 (universally known). Common in writing and speeches as a way of appealing to shared knowledge, the Chinese equivalent of "as is well known."

Literal: when wills unite, a city wall is formed — collective will is an impregnable defense
Figurative: From the Guoyu (国语 Guóyǔ), a pre-Qin historical text. 众 (the many; the people) + 志 (will; resolve) + 成 (form; become) + 城 (city wall). When a people are of one mind, they become as strong as a city's walls. Used in political speeches, team motivation, and times of national crisis. 面对困难，我们众志成城，一定能克服。

Literal: to follow the overturned cart's tracks again: to repeat a past disaster
Figurative: Lit: again-tread-overturned-ruts. The chóng reading. To make the same ruinous mistake that wrecked others before, having failed to learn from it.

Literal: weightier than Mount Tai: of the gravest possible significance
Figurative: From Sima Qian: a death may be 重于泰山 (weightier than Mt Tai) or 轻于鸿毛 (lighter than a goose feather), depending on what it is given for. The zhòng reading, weight as worth.

Literal: the Duke of Zhou spits out his food — a ruler's eagerness to receive talent
Figurative: From a passage in the Shiji: the Duke of Zhou was so eager to receive visiting scholars and advisors that when eating he would stop mid-meal, spit out his food, and go to meet them, lest a talented man leave without an audience.

Literal: to take joy in helping others
Figurative: Literally "to help others as one's joy," to find genuine pleasure in aiding people. A prized social virtue, often used to praise the selflessly helpful. Built on 助 (to aid), the same character at the heart of 帮助.

Literal: turn danger into safety: pull through a crisis
Figurative: A four-character mirror of 居安思危, read in the other direction. The relief phrase after a patient stabilizes or a company survives. Common in news and speeches.

Literal: Zhuang Zhou dreams of being a butterfly — life is like a dream, identity is fluid
Figurative: The canonical chengyu referring to the butterfly dream in 齐物论. Used in poetry and classical prose to evoke the dreamlike quality of human life, the unreliability of fixed identity, or the philosophical argument that the boundary between self and world is not as firm as it seems.

Literal: to fake a shape and put on a show: to playact, to put on airs
Figurative: Lit: feign-mould-make-shape. To strike a false pose, going through the motions of sincerity or effort while meaning none of it. A pointed way to call out pretense.

Literal: trace back to the root and seek the source
Figurative: 追 (pursue) + 本 (root) + 溯 (go upstream) + 源 (source). Used for rigorous investigation of origins: of a word, a practice, a family line, a historical claim. The metaphor of going upstream to find the source of a river runs through classical Chinese thought about genealogy and textual scholarship.

Literal: the son carries on the father's trade: inheriting the family calling
Figurative: Said when a child takes up the parent's profession or business, from a craftsman's shop to a family firm. Neutral to approving, depending on whether the inheritance is seen as continuity or constraint.

Figurative: From the 秋水 chapter. Used in modern Chinese as a rhetorical challenge when someone claims to understand an experience or perspective that is not their own: "You haven't been through what I've been through; how can you know how I feel?" Literal: within the words and between the lines: the meaning an author implies but does not state
Figurative: Lit: inside-the-characters, between-the-lines. The unspoken sense that lives in the spaces of a text. 字里行间流露出真情 "true feeling shows between the lines."

Literal: weighing every character, deliberating every sentence — writing with extreme care and precision
Figurative: 斟酌 zhēnzhuó = to deliberate; to weigh carefully. Used for careful writing, diplomatic language, or painstaking editing. A compliment to someone who writes with rigor. 这份合同是字斟句酌写成的。(This contract was written with extreme care.)

Literal: to find one's own pleasure: content in one's own way
Figurative: Lit: self-obtain-its-joy. Said of someone happily absorbed in a quiet pursuit of their own, needing no audience or approval, perfectly content alone.

Literal: to support oneself by one's own labor: to earn one's own keep
Figurative: Lit: self-eat-one's-strength. To live on what one's own effort earns rather than leaning on others, high praise for honest self-reliance.

Literal: to feel good about oneself — often wryly, overly self-satisfied
Figurative: A common modern expression using 感觉 gǎnjué (feeling), a close relative of 觉得. Literally "self-feeling is good," it describes someone with a high (often too high) opinion of themselves. Usually said with a touch of irony about another person's unearned confidence.

Literal: to contradict oneself: spear against one's own shield
Figurative: Lit: self-mutually-spear-shield. From the fable of a peddler who swore his spear (矛) could pierce anything and his shield (盾) could stop anything, until a bystander asked what would happen if he used the one on the other.

Literal: to act on one's own judgment; to go one's own way regardless of others
Figurative: 自 zì (self) + 行 xíng (to act; carry out) + 其是 qí shì (what one considers right). Doing what one believes to be correct without consulting or deferring to others.

Literal: to talk to oneself: to mutter under one's breath
Figurative: Lit: self-speak-self-say. The 自 repeats to stress that both the speaking and the listening are oneself, used of someone murmuring aloud with no one else there.

Literal: free and at ease: unhurried, answerable to no one
Figurative: Lit: self-free-self-present. A doubled 自 that paints a life lived on one's own terms, comfortable and unconstrained, like a bird with the whole sky to itself.

Literal: what you make, you suffer: to reap the consequences of your own actions
Figurative: Lit: self-do-self-bear. The Chinese counterpart of "you made your bed, now lie in it." Said of trouble that a person has brought entirely upon themselves.

Literal: look at flowers from a galloping horse — a superficial, rushing view
Figurative: 走马 (galloping horse) + 观花 (observe flowers). The mounted rider moves too fast to see the flowers properly , their gaze skims the surface without stopping to appreciate what is there. A criticism of rushed, inattentive engagement with a subject.

Literal: full of wisdom and many stratagems — highly resourceful and clever
Figurative: 足 zú (sufficient; full of) + 智 zhì (wisdom; intelligence) + 多 duō (many; much) + 谋 móu (stratagem; scheme; counsel; 谋 contains 言, speech, over 某, a certain person, suggesting deliberate planning). The ideal military or political advisor: smart and strategically inventive, always with another plan.

Literal: the ringleader of the crime and the chief of the disaster: the main culprit
Figurative: Lit: crime-chief-disaster-head. The principal wrongdoer, the one most to blame for an offense or calamity. Here 首 is the head, the ringleader. 他是这场事故的罪魁祸首 "He is the chief culprit behind this accident."

Literal: look left, glance right — looking around hesitantly or alertly; distracted attention
Figurative: 左 (left) + 顾 (to look back; to turn and look) + 右 (right) + 盼 (to look; to gaze with expectation). The eyes move ceaselessly left and right , taking in everything around, unable or unwilling to settle on a single point.

Literal: thinking left and right — to turn something over and over in the mind; to deliberate from all angles
Figurative: 左 zuǒ (left) + 思 sī (to think) + 右 yòu (right) + 想 xiǎng (to think). The spatial metaphor makes tangible what overthinking feels like: the mind moving left, then right, finding no ground to rest on.

Literal: meet a spring on the left and on the right — resourceful; successful in every direction
Figurative: 左右 (left and right) + 逢 (to encounter; to meet with) + 源 (a spring, source of water). Wherever you turn, you find a source of nourishment or support. Originally from Mencius (孟子·离娄下): a scholar who has deeply internalized principle will find it arising naturally from every direction.

Literal: left and right both difficult — caught in a dilemma; no good option in either direction
Figurative: 左右 (left and right) + 为 (to be; causing) + 难 (difficult). Whichever direction you move , left or right , you face difficulty. The idiom captures the specific kind of dilemma where the problem is bilateral: pleasing one side offends the other, taking one path closes the other.

Literal: to spin a cocoon and bind oneself: to trap yourself by your own doing
Figurative: Lit: make-cocoon-self-bind. As a silkworm spins the cocoon that encloses it, a person can create rules, habits, or schemes that end up trapping them.

Literal: having done the theft, the heart is uneasy — a guilty conscience betrays itself
Figurative: 做 + 贼 zéi (thief) + 心 xīn (heart) + 虚 xū (empty, weak, unsteady). One who has done wrong cannot keep an easy heart; the inner unease leaks out as nervousness and over-caution. The phrase observes that guilt is self-announcing, that the wrongdoer's own jumpiness gives the game away.
